#6341. A paleontologist hiking near Arches National Park may have found a new armored dinosaur

A new dinosaur bonebed discovered near Moab, Utah, may contain an unknown armored dinosaur species dating back 138 to 141 million years.

In mid-October 2026, the Utah Geological Survey (UGS) opened a new dinosaur excavation near Moab, in eastern Utah. The team calls the site the Ironstone Bonebed, and it lies north of Arches National Park.

The bonebed appears to contain the remains of a new species of armored dinosaur, the agency said. State Paleontologist Jim Kirkland is describing the animal and naming it in honor of Don DeBlieux, the Utah assistant state paleontologist.

The site is estimated at 138 million to 141 million years old. The UGS called it “currently tied as potentially the oldest Cretaceous dinosaur bonebed in North America.”

DeBlieux has said he spotted the first fossils while exploring the area on foot. They were a shoulder blade and an upper arm bone from an armored dinosaur.

He oversees the UGS field paleontology program and its fossil preparation lab. In 2002, he found a skull weathering out of sandstone near the middle of the Wahweap Formation, in southern Utah’s Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.

That skull became the horned dinosaur Diabloceratops eatoni. DeBlieux spent more than 800 hours over two years removing the rock from around the bone.

Kirkland has said the crew has identified about four kinds of dinosaurs at the new site so far.

Kirkland, who has held his post since 1999, is known for naming numerous dinosaur species, most notably Utahraptor. After 25 years of working side by side with him, DeBlieux will retire at the end of 2026.

Geologically, the new locality is nearly equivalent to Doelling’s Bowl, a UGS site some six miles (10 kilometers) to the east.

DeBlieux also found Doelling’s Bowl, in 2005, when he came across the vertebrae and a hip bone of a dromaeosaurid, a raptor-like predator.

A 2012 study of Utah raptors named it Yurgovuchia doellingi and reported a bone bed covering tens of acres (at least several hectares).

Plant-eating iguanodonts, including one compared to Iguanacolossus, dominate it, with at least ten individuals. At least three polacanthine ankylosaurs, a group of armored dinosaurs, were also found there.

The bonebed lies in the lower Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation, below a marker layer of calcrete. It yielded Mierasaurus bobyoungi, a long-necked sauropod descended from Jurassic turiasaurs of the Iberian Peninsula.

Kirkland and DeBlieux co-authored its 2017 description. By then, Doelling’s Bowl had also produced teeth from a large allosauroid predator and a new, still unnamed species of polacanthid ankylosaur.

“Ankylosaurs were so well protected that even their eyelids were armored,” Kirkland and Mark Loewen, then of the Utah Museum of Natural History, wrote in 2011.

At the time, the Cedar Mountain Formation had yielded more ankylosaur species than any other geologic formation in the world. Several more from it had been found but not yet described.

Gastonia burgei came from the basal Yellow Cat Member. It was closely related to Polacanthus foxi, from nearly age-equivalent rocks on England’s Isle of Wight.

Younger layers have produced other Cedar Mountain dinosaurs, including the ankylosaur Peloroplites cedrimontanus from the Ruby Ranch Member.

Utah’s first known nodosaurid, Animantarx ramaljonesi, was the first dinosaur discovered solely by technology. A radiological technician found it in 1994 by mapping low-level radiation across a quarry near the top of the formation.

Cedarpelta bilbyhallorum was then North America’s only known ankylosaurid from the Lower Cretaceous. Ankylosaurids are the branch of armored dinosaurs known for tail clubs and boxy skulls.

The UGS expects the new site to shed light on the transition from the Jurassic to the Cretaceous. A catastrophic event at the end of the Jurassic led to the near-complete extinction of Utah’s Morrison Formation dinosaurs, including Stegosaurus.

Across most of the western North American mountain belt, the gap between Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks spans 20 million to 25 million years.

In eastern Utah, microfossils, chemical signatures and uranium-lead dating of ancient soils cut it to five million to seven million years.

Kirkland, DeBlieux and two colleagues reported that revised dating in a 2025 conference abstract. In those rocks, an increase in larger coelurosaurs, a group of meat-eating dinosaurs, documents the extinction.

The ancient soils also point to a short wet interval after the drier Late Jurassic. Where Early Cretaceous wetlands formed in eastern Utah appears to have been controlled by movement of ancient salt deposits.

Kirkland has argued that the same salt tectonics explain why Utah’s oldest Cretaceous dinosaurs are restricted to northern Grand County.

As buried salt beds were squeezed into ridges, nearby ground subsided, and Lower Cretaceous sediments collected in the low areas.

Across much of the rest of North America, erosion was removing rock at the time. Salt movement peaked in the early Mesozoic, as reflected by the Salt Valley anticline at Arches National Park and the Moab fault.

The information was obtained from the Utah Geological Survey.

#6340. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#6339. City crows let people get closer, but country crows can be bolder in their own way

City crows tolerate people better than rural crows, but unfamiliar objects near food can make them more cautious.

City crows let people get closer than rural crows do. But when researchers put a lamp base in a pile of peanuts, city crows were less likely than rural crows to take a peanut.

The study of American crows around Ithaca, New York, suggests that a crow’s fears are shaped by its past experience.

Two experiments were run by Dave Colucci and Anne Clark, biologists at Binghamton University. In the first experiment, objects were left next to food on crow territories.

In the second, Colucci walked toward crows and measured how close he got before they flew.

The evidence for greater wariness in city crows comes from a single object.

It also comes from only one of the three measures used by the team. In addition, the city sites were closer to suburbs than to a downtown.

In crows, Colucci said, fear of anything new exists side by side with a great deal of curiosity. The fear does not always prevail, he added, so a new opportunity is sometimes seized.

Ten crow families were chosen from parking lots, parks, and dead-end streets near Ithaca.

Another 10 families lived on farmland and natural areas in the nearby town of Dryden.

American crows live in family groups that share a territory.

On most days of the week, Colucci scattered two cups of unsalted peanuts in the shell on each territory.

The same spot was used each time. He continued until the family had fed there three times in a row.

A single object was then set in the middle of the peanuts on four separate mornings. The crows were filmed by a hidden camcorder. Colucci watched from at least 164 feet (50 meters) away.

The trials were run in July and August of 2019 and 2020. Four objects were used: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a takeout box, and a lamp base.

The box was paperboard, and the lamp base was made to look like wood.

Every crow was expected to find the lamp base new. Bright colors, shiny surfaces and sharp angles are typical of human-made things.

These features are probably better known to crows living in cities. None of them was present on the lamp base.

When only peanuts were offered, nearly every crow that came within about 10 feet (3 meters) took one.

The team estimated the probability of eating at 99% for such city crows and 97% for rural crows.

With the lamp base in place, the estimated probability dropped to 76% among rural crows and 53% among city crows.

Wariness of new things is called neophobia by biologists. By this measure, the city crows had more of it.

The other two measures concerned only the first crow of each family to arrive and to eat. Their timing was compared with that on days when no object was present.

With the lamp base in place, the first crow to arrive and the first to eat were about as quick in city families as in rural ones.

To Colucci and Clark, that result suggests both places have some bold crows.

Results from earlier experiments on city and country birds have not agreed with one another. Lower wariness in cities has been reported in some of them, higher wariness or no difference in others.

Colucci and Clark wrote that some of those experiments used human-made objects, which city animals may know better.

A second idea was tested with the corn and the takeout box. An ear of corn should be ordinary to a crow that lives beside farm fields.

That ear of corn should seem strange to a crow whose home is beside a parking lot. For a takeout box, the reverse should be true.

More rural crows were put off by the takeout box, and more city crows were put off by the corn.

The team could be confident of that pattern only in the share of crows that ate. In how quickly the first crow arrived or ate, the pattern was too weak to be sure of.

A one-mile (1.6 km) stretch of road was also walked in each setting once a week for three weeks. Every human-made object was recorded.

A total of 341 objects was counted, with 169 along the city road and 172 along the rural road. A typical object nevertheless remained in place for a shorter time along the city road.

Objects turned over faster along the city road, but city crows were still more reluctant to eat beside the lamp base.

City crows are thus exposed to a constant turnover of objects, yet their wariness of new things hasn’t been reduced.

The authors suggested that most litter may be treated by city crows as one category.

In the second experiment, crows were approached on foot by Colucci 145 times over three summers. These approaches took place across upstate New York and Quebec.

During some approaches his gaze was fixed directly on the crow. During others his whole face was tilted toward the ground. A camera on his chest streamed video to a phone in his hand so that his direction could be maintained.

The average crow took flight while he was still about 150 feet (45 meters) away. A distance of 33 feet (10 meters) or less was reached in only eight approaches.

Closer approaches were tolerated by city crows than by rural crows, as is usual for city animals. Rural crows fled from far away regardless of the direction of his gaze.

In the most built-up areas, crows let him get about 82 feet (25 meters) closer when his face was down. The authors wrote that the true effect of his gaze could be either small or large.

A similar but smaller effect was found in a 2013 study of crows in Seattle. To the authors’ knowledge, a difference between two populations in the use of human gaze had not been shown before.

Hunting is one possible explanation for the behavior of the rural crows.

Within city limits in New York, crows may not be hunted. Hunting them in rural areas is legal from September 1 to March 31.

The rural response was described by Clark, an associate professor emerita of biological sciences, as a blunt defense against predators. “Don’t take any chances, don’t stop to assess; let’s just be safe,” she said.

Clark added that such a habit would not work for city crows. People pass by too often in a city for a crow to take flight every time.

The peanut experiment also provided evidence of greater caution among rural crows. With no object present, the first city crow reached the peanuts at about four times the rural rate.

The number of people living within about half a mile (800 meters) gave the best prediction of a crow’s reaction. When smaller or larger circles were used, the predictions were poorer.

A circle of that size is larger than the territory held by a crow family.

It was suggested by the authors that crows average their experience of people over a wide area. They then adjust to the person approaching them.

Individual people who have threatened them are also remembered by crows.

The study leaves open whether city crows gain any advantage from being more cautious around an unfamiliar object. Two possible explanations have been put forward by the authors.

One is that cities contain dangers which cannot be predicted even by a crow that knows its neighborhood well.

The other concerns the crows that first settled in towns about 70 years ago. Those birds may have had little fear of new things, with caution proving useful only later.

It is also uncertain whether the lamp base was equally new to both groups. Its shape is perfectly symmetrical, and such symmetry is rare in natural objects.

City crows might therefore have found it more familiar than the team had intended.

Were that the case, the authors wrote, the difference between city and rural crows could be underestimated.

Future research could test whether wariness slows crows down when new problems have to be solved. It could also test whether cities hold more unfamiliar threats.

For comparisons of urban wildlife with rural animals, a first step was recommended by Colucci and Clark. They wrote that the objects present in each environment ought to be identified first.

The full study was published in the journal Behavioral Ecology.

#6338. Peregrine falcons are much smarter than we thought, using fake attacks to tire out their prey

A new study reveals that peregrine falcons deliberately use false attacks against their prey, making them much easier to catch later on.

When a peregrine falcon dives at a flock of birds and comes away with nothing, it looks like a failed hunt.

At one bay in British Columbia, some of those failed hunts may never have been meant to succeed. A study of peregrines and small shorebirds called Pacific dunlins suggests that early attacks send the flock into the air too soon.

A few hours later, the dunlins are often back on the ground, and that’s when the falcons make the most kills. If the researchers are right, the early attacks make the dunlins easier to catch later.

Ron Ydenberg and two colleagues at Simon Fraser University’s Centre for Wildlife Ecology published the analysis in October 2023. Their case rests on the timing of flights and kills at a single bay.

Predators are “imagined as clever in novels and movies, like the velociraptors in Jurassic Park,” Ydenberg said. But biologists who work from evidence, he added, tend to doubt such ideas.

Between 20,000 and 40,000 dunlins spend the winter at Boundary Bay, feeding on mudflats that the tide covers twice a day.

As the tide rises, the dunlins have to feed closer to the shoreline, where a falcon can ambush them from cover.

Like other shorebirds, dunlins used to rest on shore at high tide. During the 1990s, as more peregrines wintered at the bay, the dunlins largely stopped.

Now they often spend daytime high tides circling in a loose flock high over the bay. Almost every dunlin the falcons were seen to kill was outside that flock.

But circling takes energy. On days when the dunlins made these flights, they averaged 3.1 hours in the air.

By the team’s estimate, the three most dangerous hours for a dunlin on the ground run from one hour before high tide to two hours after.

On those days, the dunlins spent 89% of the hour before high tide in the air and 95% of the hour after.

But in the second hour after high tide, the dunlins were in the air only 44% of the time. The falcons did best in that hour, making 43 of the 139 kills recorded in 905 hours of watching.

The dunlins had done a lot of their flying earlier, more than an hour before high tide, when the danger was low. Compared with the safest schedule, their flights started early and ended early.

To explain the early flights, the researchers used a 2007 model inspired by killer whales hunting sea lions.

In that model, a predator can gain by making attacks that have little chance of success. The prey still has to flee, then make up the lost feeding time by taking more risks later.

At Boundary Bay, that would mean falcons attacking before high tide to send the dunlins up early.

The team couldn’t test the idea, because even experienced observers can’t easily tell a serious attack from a half-hearted one.

In data the team hasn’t published, peregrine hunts at the bay peak two to four hours before high tide, hours before the kills do.

The records come from Dick Dekker’s winter visits to Boundary Bay between 1994 and 2012.

Falcon attacks were recorded on 151 days. The dunlin flocks were timed from dawn to dusk on 34 days, and they made their high-tide flights on 23 of them.

The authors wrote that Dekker became “the world’s foremost watcher of wild falcons.”

The authors offered two other explanations.

Less skilled falcons might be the ones attacking early, while skilled falcons hunt just after high tide. Or the dunlins might land early because feeding is especially good on a falling tide.

To test those explanations, researchers would have to track individual falcons closely, Ydenberg said. That doesn’t look practical at Boundary Bay, where the falcons weren’t marked.

He added that the idea could be tested in other predators and their prey, where the same logic should apply.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Ethology.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

#6336. New species of flying frog discovered in a mountain pond called Coca-Cola Lake

Scientists identified a new flying frog species in Indonesia's mountains. DNA, body features, and calls helped confirm the discovery.

A seasonal pond sits high in the mountains of Sulawesi in Indonesia. Climbers know it as Coca-Cola Lake.

A new species of flying frog has been collected there and it has been named Rhacophorus kurniatiae.

Body measurements barely separate this frog from its closest relative. The difference shows up when the animals breed. The relative builds a nest of foam.

The new species leaves its eggs in a loose mass of jelly instead.

No other flying frog on Sulawesi has been documented laying its eggs in a loose, irregular mass of jelly.

The frogs were collected on November 18, 2011, by Wahyu Trilaksono. Trilaksono is a herpetologist with Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency.

Four colleagues from Indonesia and the United States joined Trilaksono in describing the new species.

Thirty-one adults were collected in total. Every one of them came from that single pond.

Males measure 1.7 to 1.8 inches (43 to 47 millimeters) from snout to rump. Females are larger at 1.9 to 2.2 inches (49 to 57 millimeters). That is roughly the length of an AA battery.

The pond is found 6,155 feet (1,876 meters) up in the Mekongga Mountains. This range lies on the southeastern arm of Sulawesi.

The pond is not natural. It was created by a logging company as a place to store logs.

Rain and seepage fill the pond for part of the year. No stream runs into it or out of it. During the dry season, it shrinks to a few pools and exposed moss.

Loggers worked these mountains before they became a protected forest in 1994.

The 2011 trip belonged to a series of expeditions run for the ICBG Indonesia Project.

The project was a biological inventory of the mountains. Its Indonesian and American partners included the Museum of Wildlife and Fish Biology at the University of California, Davis.

The field team was led by Alan Hitch, who is a research affiliate at that museum. Hitch recalled reaching the pond on the way up the mountain. Green frogs were all over it.

“You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that,” Hitch said.

Biologists describe an event like this as explosive breeding. Adults gather suddenly along the edge of the water for a brief burst of mating. Heavy rain appears to trigger it at Coca-Cola Lake.

Asian flying frogs are tree frogs. Their name comes from gliding, which is done on large webbed feet. A foam nest is where the typical flying frog lays its eggs.

Rhacophorus boeadii is the closest relative of the new frog, and it breeds that way. Scientists named it last year from mountains in central Sulawesi.

Coca-Cola Lake is shared with a third flying frog. Its eggs are packed into compact balls of gel.

R. kurniatiae does neither of these things. Its eggs are laid straight into an irregular mass of jelly that contains no foam. The mass hangs above the water or is loosely attached to whatever is nearby.

The frogs showed no preference for any plant species or leaf shape. The embryos stay inside the jelly until they become tadpoles.

The authors wrote that the habit may reflect an adaptation to water that comes and goes.

The team needed to check whether the pond frogs were a species of their own. Twenty-eight body measurements were taken on preserved specimens for that purpose.

The 81 specimens came from six flying frog species found on Sulawesi and nearby islands.

Eighteen of them were the new frog. Its females were compared with R. boeadii females. None of the 28 measurements differed reliably between them.

Three measurements did differ among males. These were eye width, the length of the first toe and the width of the pad on the fourth toe.

The DNA was close as well. One stretch of mitochondrial DNA differed by 2.19% to 2.43% between the two species. The gap between the new frog and the other four species was about 4% to 5.7%.

Andrew Engilis Jr. is the curator of the UC Davis museum and a co-author of the study.

Species can sometimes “look the same, but their behavior is different and their genetics are different,” Engilis said.

Animals like these are known to biologists as cryptic species.

A few features do set the new frog apart on close inspection. A small flap of skin is present on each heel. A fold of skin runs along its limbs and its third finger carries more webbing.

The call of one male was recorded on a digital camera at 6:40 p.m. It lasted about 1.4 seconds.

Four notes made up the call. A single short pulse opened it. Three notes of three to five pulses each came next. The call of R. boeadii is a single note.

The team also wanted to compare the call with that of the third flying frog at the lake.

Call measurements published in 2015 by Hellen Kurniati were used for this. She was a long-serving herpetologist at Indonesia’s Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense.

The new species has been named in honor of Kurniati. She died before it was described.

Only one recording from one male was good enough to be analyzed. The authors wrote that the opening note may be that male’s own variation. It may not be a trait of the whole species.

R. boeadii is known from two mountain regions in central Sulawesi. R. kurniatiae has been found only on the southeastern arm.

Two major faults run close to the line between those ranges. Faults are long breaks in Earth’s crust where blocks of land slide past each other.

The authors suggested that the faults may have acted as barriers, splitting an ancestral frog population in two.

A similar pattern is seen in the flying lizards and macaques of Sulawesi.

Closely related species live on different arms of the island. The idea has not been tested for the frogs. More genetic analysis will be needed for that, the authors wrote.

So far, researchers have found the frog only at Coca-Cola Lake.

This raises potential conservation concerns, the authors wrote. They pointed to pressure from farming, deforestation and climate variability across Sulawesi.

The amphibians of Sulawesi have been studied less than those of Java, Sumatra and Borneo.

Thirty-three amphibian species are known from the region and six of them are flying frogs. The researchers expect the true number to be higher.

Several species have been added by recent fieldwork. One of them is a fanged frog that nests on land.

Engilis said the region is a candidate for national park status. Continued species discovery could help speed that process, Engilis added.

The authors called for targeted surveys of the island’s mountain habitats.

Other high ponds in the Mekongga Mountains could be surveyed in the future. Such work could show whether Coca-Cola Lake is the frog’s only home.

The full study was published in the journal Zootaxa.

#6335. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

K. Grice et al. Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

#6334. Your favorite foods may soon contain less sodium

Most of the sodium Americans eat comes from packaged and prepared foods. A new FDA rule could help cut sodium at the source.

Starting in December, a new FDA rule will let food makers replace some or all of the added salt in products such as bread, cheese, and canned vegetables.

That could make a difference because Americans get more than 70% of their sodium from packaged and prepared foods.

One option is a salt blend that replaces some sodium chloride with potassium chloride. Few Americans use salt substitutes at home.

Daniel W. Jones, a professor emeritus at the University of Mississippi School of Medicine, chaired the committee that wrote the 2025 U.S. blood pressure guideline, which recommends potassium-enriched salt substitutes.

In the journal JAMA, Jones said the FDA rule could help reduce sodium intake.

Table salt is sodium chloride. In a potassium-enriched salt substitute, some of that sodium chloride is replaced with potassium chloride.

Potassium chloride is a salt made with potassium in place of sodium.

According to Jones, a blend of 25% to 30% potassium chloride is recommended. A higher proportion is not accepted by American tastes, which is part of the reason.

Stores sell a wider range, from blends of equal parts to pure potassium chloride. The equal-part products are usually labeled “light” salt.

Wanpen Vongpatanasin of UT Southwestern Medical Center directs the center’s section on hypertension.

Vongpatanasin noted that blood vessels are affected by sodium and potassium in opposite ways. Sodium makes arteries stiffer, while potassium generally relaxes the blood vessels.

“You get a twofer with a potassium-enriched salt substitute,” Jones said.

A person who switches consumes less sodium and more potassium, he added. Both changes are considered healthy.

Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury, the units used in a reading such as 120 over 80. Jones noted that a blend with 25% potassium chloride lowers blood pressure by 5 to 7 points on average.

The top number is lowered by 8 to 10 points with most blood pressure drugs, he added.

Jones also explained the significance of such a drop for people with high blood pressure. Their risk of heart attack, heart failure, stroke, and kidney disease is reduced with every 10 points lost.

The reduction was estimated by Jones at about 15% to 20%.

The substitute was tested in a trial that was published in 2021 and conducted in 600 villages in rural China. The 20,995 participants had either survived a stroke or were at least 60 years old with high blood pressure.

The villages that received the potassium blend were selected at random and the remaining villages continued to use regular salt. One quarter of the blend consisted of potassium chloride.

The participants were followed for almost five years. About 29 strokes a year were recorded among every 1,000 people who cooked with the blend.

Roughly 34 strokes a year were recorded among every 1,000 people who used regular salt.

Deaths from any cause were also less frequent in the villages that used the blend. Blood pressure differed less than Jones’s average. The top number was about 3 points lower in villages using the blend.

Vongpatanasin and her colleagues examined how many people use these products. A national health survey of about 37,000 U.S. adults was analyzed for that purpose.

In the survey years 2013 and 2014, 5.4% of adults said they used a salt substitute. No other survey round recorded a higher share. By 2017 to 2020, that figure was 2.5%.

Use was low throughout and later fell by more than half. A substitute was rarely used by patients being treated for high blood pressure, either. Fewer than 1 in 10 of them reported it.

Taste is one reason. Vongpatanasin noted that potassium chloride can taste bitter or briny. The effect is stronger in larger amounts and for people who prefer heavily salted food.

She advised cooking with the substitute, along with other seasonings, instead of sprinkling it on cooked food. People become accustomed to the taste in about two weeks, Jones said.

Cost was also identified as a barrier in the 2025 guideline in which the World Health Organization suggested the switch. The guideline noted that the blends can cost more than regular salt and that public awareness is low.

A small consulting arrangement with the drugmaker AstraZeneca has been disclosed by Vongpatanasin.

She is also named as a co-inventor on a University of Texas patent for potassium magnesium citrate. No revenue has been generated by that patent to date.

Only a small part of dietary sodium is changed when a household switches completely to a substitute.

Roughly 11% of the sodium eaten by Americans is added during cooking or at the table. That estimate was reported by the FDA.

Average intake in the United States has been put at about 3,400 milligrams a day by the same agency. About 2,300 milligrams of sodium are contained in one teaspoon of table salt.

Federal dietary advice sets that amount as the daily limit, and the 2025 heart guideline aims for less than 1,500.

The recommendation of the WHO applies only to salt that people add themselves.

This limit was explained by Rain Yamamoto, a scientist in the nutrition and food safety department of the agency.

The advice is most relevant in countries where most salt is consumed through home cooking, Yamamoto said. The United States does not belong to that group of countries.

“Standards of identity” are maintained by the FDA for foods such as bread, sour cream, and mayonnaise.

The ingredients that a product needs before it can carry such a name are listed in each standard. Salt was allowed or required under 139 of those standards while a substitute was not permitted.

In October, the agency issued a final rule that lifted the restriction on substitutes in all 139 standards. Some or all of the salt in those foods may be replaced when the rule takes effect in December.

The affected foods include mayonnaise, salad dressing, many cheeses, canned vegetables, canned fish, bread, and pasta.

Potassium-enriched salt is not suitable for every patient. People with chronic kidney disease, especially end-stage disease, should not use potassium-based substitutes.

Other types of substitute such as herb blends can still be used by those patients.

Blood potassium can also be raised by several kinds of medicine. Some diuretics are included in that group and are commonly known as water pills.

Two common families of blood pressure drugs are included as well. These are the ACE inhibitors such as enalapril and the angiotensin receptor blockers such as losartan.

A doctor should be consulted first by patients on those drugs so that blood potassium can be monitored.

The WHO’s recommendation excludes pregnant women and children because evidence in these groups is limited.

Serious events linked to high blood potassium occurred at similar rates in both groups.

However, the trial had excluded people with serious kidney disease and people who were taking potassium supplements. Blood potassium was also not tested routinely during the trial.

No new labeling requirements were added by the FDA rule, which makes those exclusions relevant to packaged food.

A required warning about high potassium on those foods was declined by the agency. Potassium chloride will still be listed by name among the ingredients.

Use of a substitute is allowed by the FDA rule but no manufacturer is obliged to change a recipe.

No minimum level of replacement was set and no penalties were listed for companies that keep regular salt.

The rule leaves the choice of substitute to manufacturers.

Potassium chloride is mentioned in the rule as one example beside yeast extracts, MSG, and amino acids. Sodium in bread or cheese could therefore be lowered by a manufacturer with no potassium added.

A related question was left open by the 2021 trial in China. The blend was used for home cooking in that trial and people who ate most meals elsewhere had been excluded.

Packaged food that already contains the blend was not examined in that trial.

Concern about the rest of the diet was expressed by Sotiria Everett, who is a dietitian at Stony Brook University. Little effect is expected from cooking with a substitute if deli meats, cheese, and bacon are still eaten, she said.

A fruit or vegetable at every meal was recommended by Everett because potassium intake is then increased naturally.

The rule was published on October 13 and takes effect 60 days later in December. A report on progress toward the voluntary sodium targets of the FDA is also expected later in 2026.

The decision to use potassium salt in pursuit of those targets will be made by each manufacturer.

The full report was published in the journal JAMA.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) officially announced its decision to revoke the United States' measles elimination status on Nov. 17, 2026. The week prior, the Wall Street Journal reported that the PAHO had reached that decision.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6332. This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the new Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

#6330. America’s biggest data centers use nearly as much electricity as an entire state

A study estimates that 403 major U.S. data centers used 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a year, with natural gas and coal supplying more than half.

Every backed-up photo, every chatbot answer and every streamed show lives somewhere called the cloud, which sounds like nowhere at all. It is a set of windowless warehouses.

At the high end of the estimate, 403 of the largest U.S. data centers together used nearly as much electricity in a year as Indiana uses statewide.

More than half of that electricity came from burning gas and coal.

A team led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative mapped 403 of these buildings, known as hyperscale data centers.

The researchers then estimated what each one drew from the grid between May 2024 and April 2025.

The totals are estimates built from each building’s electrical capacity, not meter readings.

“Data centers are growing incredibly fast, driven largely by AI, and decisions about where to build them and how to power them are being made right now,” said lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics.

“But there’s very little facility-level information about their environmental footprint.”

“Our study helps fill that gap,” Guidi added.

Hyperscale data centers are the largest class of data center, the kind that runs cloud services and trains big AI models. The buildings in the sample had an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.

The team started with 675 candidate sites from a commercial database and kept the 403 it could confirm. Each address was matched to a rooftop and its footprint checked against OpenStreetMap.

Then the researchers looked at satellite and aerial images for the signs of a data center: big uniform roofs, cooling equipment and a substation next door.

Virginia had 142 of the 403, more than any other state. Oregon had 56 and Ohio 38.

No data center runs at its full rated capacity every hour, and the companies don’t publish their real loads. So the team multiplied each facility’s capacity by the hours in a year and by a load factor.

The researchers ran four versions of that factor, from a light load to one meant to bracket heavy AI training.

Across the four versions, the 403 facilities used an estimated 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year. The central estimate is about 82 terawatt-hours, or roughly 1.8% of all the electricity the country used.

Indiana, Michigan and Tennessee each use about 100 terawatt-hours a year. So at the high end these warehouses matched a whole state, and even the central estimate covers most of one state’s use.

The central figure is about 3.6 times a 2021 estimate of what hyperscale centers used in 2018. Projections of AI’s appetite for electricity look ahead; this study counts the buildings that exist now.

To work out where the electricity came from, and the power emissions behind it, the team assigned each data center to its regional grid operator.

The team then allocated the data centers’ electricity demand across power plants in each region based on how much electricity each plant generated.

The plant-by-plant generation and emissions figures came from the Environmental Protection Agency.

On that basis, 53.9% of the electricity came from fossil fuels: 38.2% from natural gas and 15.2% from coal.

Nuclear plants supplied 20.9%, and hydro, wind, solar, biomass and geothermal together supplied 25.3%. Nuclear and renewables together fell short of half.

The result was about 25.7 million metric tons (28.3 million U.S. tons) of carbon dioxide under the central version, and 21 to 31 million metric tons across all four.

A 2021 study estimated that U.S. hyperscale data centers were responsible for greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to about 10.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2018.

Virginia alone accounted for about 21 terawatt-hours, roughly a quarter of the total. Oregon followed with about 11, Ohio with about 9 and Iowa with about 7.

Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa together made up more than half of the electricity use, so the industry is heavily concentrated.

Oregon’s data centers drew more electricity than Ohio’s. Yet Oregon’s were tied to about 1.3 million metric tons of carbon dioxide and Ohio’s to 2.9 million, because Oregon’s grid runs far cleaner.

The fuel mix behind each state’s grid decides the carbon.

Virginia’s data centers were tied to about 7 million metric tons, the most of any state.

PJM, the grid operator serving Virginia, oversaw the region with the highest data center electricity demand. Its territory spans parts of 13 states and the District of Columbia.

There, about 60% of the attributed electricity came from fossil fuels and 33% from nuclear plants.

The method gives each data center the average fuel mix of its regional power grid. It doesn’t trace which plant physically fed which building.

It also doesn’t count the renewable power contracts some operators sign, unless that power shows up in the regional mix. The authors wrote that the numbers describe the grid, not any company’s performance.

Measured that way, the data centers’ electricity was slightly cleaner than the national average: about 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour against 348 for the country.

About 23% of the demand, though, sat in regions dirtier than that average.

The data also can’t separate AI work from ordinary cloud computing inside a building. And the 272 candidate sites the team couldn’t verify were left out, so the totals likely run low for the industry as a whole.

Guidi said the picture has already moved on.

“The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow,” he said.

The researchers estimated electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions.

The team plans to examine the health effects next, according to study co-author Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

“The fossil fuel power plants in the regional electricity systems associated with this demand also release other pollutants, such as fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, that are directly linked to heart and lung disease and premature death,” Dominici said.

The people who breathe those pollutants live near the power plants, which may be far from any data center.

Earth.com has covered the industry’s other local footprints, from heat zones around server farms to the one in four data centers in water-stressed regions.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Sustainability.

#6329. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

Z. Yu et al. High fiber diet mitigates exposure risk of nanoplastics in male mice. Nature Communications. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-78675-7

#6328. Unusual warmth has reached the seafloor off Canada’s Pacific coast – and scientists may know why

A seafloor sensor off Vancouver Island logged its highest temperature since monitoring began in 2009, and researchers say El Niño may be behind the spike.

El Niño is usually described as a warming of the surface waters in the tropical Pacific.

This fall, sensors off Canada’s west coast recorded unusually warm water hundreds of feet below the surface.

One seafloor sensor logged its highest temperature since monitoring began there in 2009. The scientists who operate the sensor said the warm pulse is consistent with a strong El Niño.

The sensors are operated by Ocean Networks Canada, an ocean-monitoring initiative of the University of Victoria.

The readings were announced by the organization itself this week. They have not yet been published as a study.

The record was set at a site called Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, off Vancouver Island. A sensor rests on the seafloor there, about 1,300 feet (400 meters) down. That depth is roughly a quarter of a mile.

On November 8, the water at this site reached 46.8°F (8.21°C).

Jay Cullen is the interim president and chief executive of Ocean Networks Canada.

“We’re seeing significant warming not just at the surface, but hundreds of meters below it,” Cullen said.

The November 8 reading was 4.5°F (2.49°C) above the long-term average for the site. It was also 1.6°F (0.89°C) warmer than the previous record, which was set in 2019.

The water has cooled since then, but normal temperatures have not returned. In mid-November, it was still about 2.9°F (1.6°C) warmer than average.

Warm water has been found at other sites too. The Barkley Canyon sensor is one part of a much larger network. Roughly 530 miles (850 kilometers) of seafloor cable connect its five main research sites.

One of those sites is Clayoquot Slope, which lies more than 3,900 feet (1,200 meters) down. Temperatures well above average are being recorded there as well.

Since late summer, sites between 1,300 and 4,100 feet (400 and 1,250 meters) deep have logged record seasonal temperatures.

The deepest site is the exception. At Cascadia Basin, about 8,700 feet (2,650 meters) down, temperatures remain within their usual range.

El Niño was declared by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in June.

On November 12, the agency’s Climate Prediction Center said El Niño was still strengthening.

A strong or very strong event was judged likely to continue into early 2027. The chance of that was put at more than 79%.

How can El Niño affect waters off Canada’s Pacific coast?

Steve Mihaly is a senior scientist at Ocean Networks Canada. According to Mihaly, the energy of a strong El Niño travels north from the equatorial Pacific.

It moves as waves that follow the coastline, and oceanographers call them coastal trapped waves.

Sea level has also been above normal since the warm water arrived. The rise was recorded by tide gauges at Bamfield and Tofino, two communities on Vancouver Island.

Pressure recorders on the seafloor picked it up as well. By mid-November, sea level was about 10 inches (25 centimeters) above normal. Local wind and atmospheric effects were accounted for first.

The scientists then attributed about 6 inches (15 centimeters) of the rise to the waves.

At Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, the water temperature began climbing sharply in late October and reached a record on November 8.

Mihaly said northwest winds persisted into the fall, pushing warmer surface water offshore and drawing colder water upward.

This process, known as upwelling, helped mask the warming at depth.

A second network, called VENUS, is run by Ocean Networks Canada in the Salish Sea.

These sheltered waters are shared by British Columbia and Washington State. The VENUS sensors reach depths of about 980 feet (300 meters).

Temperatures in the Strait of Georgia, which is part of that sea, have been above average throughout 2026.

Jordan Watson is the science director of Ocean Networks Canada.

“Since the start of 2026, the VENUS observatory has shown temperatures consistently higher than we’ve previously observed,” Watson said. “And this was before any El Niño effects started to appear.”

Watson described the area as known for migrating salmon, spawning herring, and marine mammals.

Warming from El Niño could add to the already high temperatures there. That would put more stress on marine ecosystems, the organization said.

So far, only temperatures and sea levels have been reported by the scientists. No effects on marine life have been reported yet.

The record is also a short one. Monitoring at Barkley Canyon began in 2009, so it covers less than two decades.

The scientists were not certain about the cause either. They said the warming likely marks the arrival of El Niño’s effects on Canada’s Pacific coast.

Cullen noted that conditions will be monitored closely over the coming months.

A new tool is also being planned by Ocean Networks Canada and CIOOS Pacific, a regional ocean-data group. It will track ocean conditions across the region.

The seafloor data will be combined with measurements from other groups around the Salish Sea.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the University of Washington are among them. More details will be shared later this year, the partners said.

Live and long-term readings can be viewed on Ocean Networks Canada’s data dashboard.

#6326. Howler monkey droppings hold clues about the fragmented forests they live in

In southern Mexico, the mix of gut bacteria in howler monkeys varied with forest patch size, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Howler monkeys can survive in small patches of forest.

A study in southern Mexico found that the mix of bacteria in their guts varied with the size of those patches, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Researchers found these patterns in droppings from adult male mantled howler monkeys.

Repeating that sampling could help conservationists track changes over time without capturing the animals.

The study was led by Tabor Whitney while she was a doctoral student at Northwestern University. She worked with primate researchers at Universidad Veracruzana in Mexico.

The work was carried out in the Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve in the state of Veracruz. About 60% of the original forest cover in the reserve has been lost. The remaining forest is broken into patches among pastures, farm fields, and towns.

The 10 study patches ranged from about 5 acres to nearly 500 acres (2 to 199 hectares). Farmland or pasture bordered every one of them.

Whitney and field assistants followed adult male howlers in October and November, during the 2022 rainy season. When a male defecated, the fresh droppings were collected from the ground with sterile sticks.

The team tested the droppings for three things. The first was the bacteria in them. The second was the fatty acids that those bacteria produce. The third was the breakdown products of stress hormones.

The trees in every patch were also measured. Across patches, average trunk width ranged from about 10 to 16 inches (25 to 42 centimeters).

Biologists call the community of microbes in an animal’s gut its microbiome.

“An awesome takeaway of the study is the knowledge the gut microbiome is the most sensitive to ecological change,” Whitney said.

Gut bacteria were analyzed in 41 samples from 32 males. Monkeys from different patches carried different mixes of bacteria.

These differences were linked to all four measures of a patch’s size and layout. Its area and its distance from other forest were among those measures. All seven measures of the trees growing in the patch were linked to the differences too.

Plant fiber is digested by some of the bacteria involved. One such group is Prevotella, and monkeys in larger patches carried more of it.

A different group of bacteria was most common where trees were small. The same was true where few rows of trees linked a patch to other forest.

Only one forest measure predicted the diversity of bacteria carried by a monkey. That measure was trunk thickness. Less variety was found in monkeys from patches with thicker-trunked trees.

The authors suggested that monkeys in mature forest may eat a narrower diet. Fewer kinds of microbes may be taken in as a result.

The team also tested distances to the nearest houses and roads. Neither distance predicted any of the three health measures in the main analysis.

Stress hormone levels were measured in 36 males. They didn’t differ clearly from patch to patch. One pattern, however, was the reverse of what the team had predicted.

Males in larger patches tended to have higher hormone levels, not lower ones.

Higher levels were also found in patches with more fig trees. Figs are a central part of the howler diet.

The authors explained the result in social terms. Several howler groups are supported by larger patches. More than one group may be attracted to the same place by fig trees.

Hormone levels could be raised by competition during encounters with rival groups, not by food shortage. Ordinary demands such as reproduction and fighting infection are also known to raise these hormones.

A monkey with a high level is therefore not necessarily in trouble.

Plant fiber is fermented by gut bacteria, and small fatty acids are released in the process.

Those acids are used by the animal for energy. These acids also help maintain the gut lining and the immune system.

No difference between patches was found in the amounts of these acids. Instead, the team’s attention was drawn to the balance between propionate and butyrate, two of the acids.

A surplus of propionate over butyrate has been proposed as a sign of an unbalanced gut. That pattern has been documented both in people and in wild primates that are short of food.

More propionate than butyrate was present in the droppings from all 10 patches.

In four of the 10 forest patches, the ratio of propionate to butyrate was about 2.6 or higher.

Human studies have linked that threshold to gut disorders. Whether it signals a health problem in howler monkeys remains unknown.

The authors wrote that a reduction in butyrate-producing bacteria may be indicated by the pattern. The reduction may extend across the whole landscape.

The researchers also raised the possibility of long-term effects on the monkeys’ gut lining and immune function.

Howlers in southern Mexico suffered a mass die-off in 2024. Up to 31% of some local populations died from the combined effects of extreme heat, drought, and habitat degradation.

Baseline health records are needed if early warning signs of decline are to be detected, the authors wrote.

Two conservation priorities were recommended by the authors. Patches of mature, varied forest should be protected and enlarged. Rows of trees and wooded strips along rivers should keep those patches connected.

The researchers also suggested that a wider variety of trees be planted, including fruiting species. Howlers would then be able to move through the canopy in search of food and mates.

Permission from local landowners was needed before the team could reach the monkeys.

“Landowners we’ve spoken with are really open to these conversations,” Whitney said.

“They’ve said they love seeing the monkeys, and if they can help them travel on the trees, they’re very interested in it.”

She said the same sampling could be repeated every five or 10 years. Changes could then be compared over time, and the effect of conservation work could be checked.

Every sample came from an adult male. All of the samples were collected in a single rainy season.

Female and young howlers have different energy and hormone demands. The results therefore can’t be assumed to apply to them.

The gut bacteria samples were also limited and unevenly distributed across patches. Some patches supplied one sample, while others supplied as many as 12.

The team identified which bacteria were present. What those bacteria were doing inside the monkeys was not measured.

The study found links between forest features and gut bacteria.

Further research could test whether changes to the forest lead to changes in the monkeys’ gut bacteria.

The authors also noted that forests across Los Tuxtlas may be too uniformly degraded.

That could explain why the fatty acids varied so little. Comparisons with other landscapes are needed, they wrote.

Future research could pair repeated sampling with long-term records of the monkeys’ behavior. Such work could test whether these signals change as the forest does.

The team is now preparing a study comparing the gut bacteria of male and female howlers.

The full study was published in the journal Animal Conservation.
