In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.

But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

The Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, 1919.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

Prince Philip's DNA was eventually used to confirm the identities of the lost Romanov family.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.

#6324. Wildfire smoke is making two kinds of air pollution spike together

As wildfire smoke travels across the U.S., fine particle pollution and ground-level ozone are more often spiking on the same day.

Two air pollutants are reaching unusually high levels on the same days more often across the contiguous United States. A new study links that rise to wildfire smoke.

The research comes from a team at the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences. Researchers in the Department of Geography looked at public data from 48 states.

They studied the co-occurrence of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and ground-level ozone.

PM2.5 includes microscopic soot, ash, and other inhalable particles.

Ground-level ozone forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.

Intensified by wildfires, vehicle emissions, and other sources, the pollutants are often evaluated separately.

Exposure to both pollutants at once may increase risks to the heart and lungs.

Starting in 2011, wildfire smoke was more often present on days when both pollutants spiked across large parts of the country.

During many of these widespread pollution episodes, both PM2.5 and ground-level ozone exceeded U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) thresholds.

The study did not evaluate individual health impacts. But researchers assessed high-level regional and national pollutant patterns known to affect health.

Increases in the combined pollutant levels appeared alongside steady growth in summertime wildfire smoke. They were most dramatic in the eastern half of the country.

The analysis incorporated observations from 2004 to 2023.

The researchers merged EPA monitoring data, satellite smoke mapping from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and a blend of weather information.

“We’ve been experiencing many summertime instances when wildfire smoke from the western U.S. or Canada has traveled into large parts of the eastern U.S., especially the Northeast,” said lead author Manzhu Yu from Penn State.

Researchers found growing odds of combined pollution hazards across the continental U.S.

In the West, the likelihood of both pollutants spiking on the same day during summer wildfire smoke events roughly doubled over the study period.

Those risks may move progressively eastward.

The paper’s overall findings may help public health researchers and clinicians study, evaluate, and prevent emerging health risks through a regional lens.

Yu said she is especially interested in the eastern U.S. Its smoke comes from several sources, not only the large wildfires in the West.

Regional smoke sources include prescribed burns, such as those to clear acreage for agriculture or general land management. Local wildfires are another source.

The distinct smoke types occasionally overlap, deepening health concerns.

Different smoke carries distinct components. These range from inorganic and organic carbon to heavy metals and influence PM2.5 co-occurrence with ozone.

“We are particularly curious about the links among smoke composition and cardiorespiratory ailments, which involve the heart, blood vessels, and lungs,” Yu said.

A larger goal at Penn State is to understand future wildfire risks and impacts in the eastern U.S.

“I can’t say we’re excited about the work – it’s not good news,” said co-author Erica Smithwick from Penn State.

“People have underestimated the effect of wildfire smoke in this region. But we are pleased to see progress in mapping out and estimating risk factors because of the impact on human health.”

The analysis should help local and regional decisionmakers plan for hazardous smoke conditions. That includes risk-reducing steps at public schools, in older buildings, and for people with medical vulnerabilities.

“In ongoing research elsewhere, we’re learning more about longer-term exposures to air pollution,”  Smithwick said.

“It may affect everything from acute stressors such as sore throats and eye irritation to longer-term effects like mental health and dementia.”

“We’re hoping that evidence-based information about the increase in compound pollutant exposures will help prioritize decision-making around mitigation and resilience to those stressors.”

Air pollution from wildfires historically centered in the western U.S. But longer-range distribution of western and Canadian smoke from bigger fires is posing sharply higher co-occurrence risks.

That now includes the Midwest and Ohio Valley, in addition to the Northeast.

During the study period, researchers found 2012, 2018, 2021, and 2023 were peak years for co-occurrence of the pollutants nationally.

They also determined that widespread co-occurrence days became more frequent, persistent, and intense.

A widespread day is when both pollutants exceed local 90th percentiles over more than 10% of the country.

For each pollutant, the local 90th percentile is the concentration that about 90% of daily values in that area fall below.

Light to moderate smoke raises co-occurrence risks. It introduces particulate organic compounds and nitrogen oxides that promote ozone production.

At the same time, more dense smoke can limit ozone production by blocking sunlight.

To predict the likelihood of combined pollution extremes, the researchers created a machine-learning model. They call it the Spatiotemporal Bayesian Neural Field.

Their model combines the effects of smoke, ground-level pollution, and weather patterns to establish risk.

Parts of the West have fire seasons more than a month longer than they were 35 years ago.

Estimated carbon emissions from forest fires grew 60% globally from 2001 to 2023, according to NASA.

Researchers attributed the changing fire conditions largely to global warming and a drier climate.

“We need to think about community awareness and community perception around smoke and have people be aware of the ecosystems they’re living in,” Smithwick said.

“There should be a general awareness of when not to burn a debris pile in your backyard, or when to be more careful with a campfire because of heightened risks.”

“We want to work with municipalities and communities to think about the educational backbone of this work.”

The study is published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology.

#6323. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

#6322. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

#6321. Lucid Dreaming Was Once a Rare Gift. Now Scientists Say They Can Help You Learn It.

Researchers built dreamlike virtual worlds to teach people how to realize they’re dreaming—and it worked.

Some people don’t just dream. They often realize they’re dreaming and can even control the dreamworld, from giving themselves powers that defy the laws of physics to escaping a nightmare by waking themselves up. Lucid dreamers can go on adventures most of us can only dream about (pun intended). But is it possible to train yourself to do the same?

Dreams can happen during any stage of sleep, but they usually occur during REM sleep. When dreamers suddenly become aware that they’re dreaming, they’re in a lucid state. However, people who frequently have lucid dreams are rare. Researchers from the University of Trento in Rovereto, Italy, wanted to find out whether standard exercises, meditation, and virtual reality could teach people to have lucid dreams. Participants in the experimental group practiced open monitoring meditation, which is meant to sharpen sensory awareness and perception through nonjudgmental observation. They then did VR training that took them into virtual worlds full of bizarre, dreamlike scenarios. For comparison, a control group used VR that had nothing to do with dreaming, while a third group did only the standard training, without VR.

All participants started with the same baseline training, which they did while awake to practice dream recall and reality checks. They were told to keep a dream diary, noting each morning whether they remembered any dreams and, if so, what the dreams were about. Participants were also told to do reality checks, such as pinching themselves, to test whether they were awake or dreaming. They did these checks whenever they ran into something strange or simply thought of something strange. On top of that, phone alarms went off every hour for 12 hours each day to prompt more checks. The idea was that the habit would eventually carry over into their dreams. On top of this training, the experimental group did open monitoring meditation sessions in the lab to prepare for their VR training. During these sessions, participants observed their breathing, bodily sensations, thoughts, and emotions without reacting to them. Each session also included a guided exploration of an environment designed to look like a scene from a dream.

“Through repetition, [reality checks] are intended to become habitual and to transfer into dreams via ‘dream residue,’ where they may be triggered by dream signs that are unusual, surprising, or incongruent events, and thereby precipitate insight into the dream state,” the researchers wrote in their study, recently published in Frontiers in Psychology.

To build these scenes, the researchers created LucidDreamingVR, a program inspired by Tibetan dream yoga. Unlike the VR control group, whose content had nothing to do with dreaming, the experimental group completed eight sessions that grew steadily more elaborate, taking participants from recognizing a dream to controlling one. The early tasks taught them to spot dream signs: the virtual surroundings would suddenly shift, cueing a reality check, much as an odd detail might inside a dream. Later sessions drew on dream yoga techniques to let participants rehearse what they might do once they became lucid. With a single spoken command, they could fly, leap to incredible heights or, like Alice after tumbling down the rabbit hole, grow and shrink at will.

The researchers counted both lucid and semi-lucid dreams as “lucid-like” dreams. By the end of the experiment, 11 of the 13 participants who had trained with LucidDreamingVR had reported at least one lucid-like dream. By contrast, eight of 13 people in the control group without VR and only four of 12 in the VR control group reported one. Nearly 12% of the dreams the experimental group remembered were lucid-like, compared with about 3% for the control group without VR and about 1% for the VR control group. Surprisingly, the LucidDreamingVR group remembered the fewest dreams overall, so they also reported the fewest ordinary, non-lucid dreams. These results suggest that combining open monitoring meditation with dream-themed VR may increase lucid dreaming. However, because neither control group meditated, the study can’t show which part of the training mattered more.

“[Our] findings support the use of immersive environments as…cognitive-enhancement tools,” the researchers said. “Future work should combine VR-based rehearsal with objective sleep verification, factorial designs, and waking cognitive measures to clarify mechanism, specificity, and transfer.”

#6320. What happened when scientists kept birds and bats away from cocoa trees?

An experiment on cocoa farms in the Peruvian Amazon reveals how nearby trees, birds, and bats can help protect the harvest.

In the Peruvian Amazon, the trees beyond a cocoa farm can help determine how much cocoa it produces.

Farms surrounded by forests, orchards, and other tree crops had some of the highest yields in a new study, and an experiment pointed to an unlikely pair of allies: birds and bats.

To find out how much those animals mattered, researchers put nets around some cocoa trees and left others open.

Where forests covered 30–35% of the surrounding landscape, the cocoa trees that birds and bats could reach produced nearly twice as much as the netted trees.

An international team led by the University of Vienna mapped the connections between shade trees, wildlife, and cocoa productivity across 28 organic agroforests in the northern Peruvian Amazon.

The researchers estimated that cocoa trees accessible to birds and bats would yield about 265 kilograms per hectare per year where trees covered roughly 20% of the surrounding landscape.

Where surrounding tree cover reached 70–80%, the estimated yield was nearly four times as high, at about 1,000 kilograms per hectare per year.

At 2023 cocoa prices, the researchers valued the extra cocoa associated with bird and bat activity at about US$1,640 per hectare per year.

For smallholder farmers in a region where average incomes are modest, that’s not a rounding error. It’s the difference between scraping by and building something.

“Birds and bats can be powerful allies for cacao farmers, but only if the surrounding landscape provides enough habitat. If these landscapes become large monocultures, much of this natural pest-control benefit is lost,” said senior author Bea Maas from the University of Vienna.

The intuitive assumption – more shade trees, more biodiversity, better farm – doesn’t hold up cleanly.

Shade-tree cover benefitted wildlife, improved soils, and buffered temperature extremes. But very dense shade starved the cocoa of light and substantially cut yields.

On farms in tree-rich landscapes, a mix of tall and short shade trees helped support biodiversity.

Dense shade, meanwhile, reduced cocoa yields by limiting sunlight.

“Our data show that cacao farms do not need uniform shade to support biodiversity. A mosaic of tall and short trees, tree clusters and open patches can create habitat for wildlife while maintaining production,” said lead author Aycart-Lazo from the University of Vienna.

The researchers surveyed birds, bats, and arthropods. They measured cocoa yield, natural pest control, pollination rates, pest and disease incidence, soil fertility, and microclimate.

Then they used drone imagery and remote-sensing data to connect what was happening inside each farm to what the surrounding landscape looked like.

The finding that probably matters most for policy is this: what’s outside the farm fence may be more important than what’s inside it.

A farmer can do everything right on their own plot and still lose most of the pest-control benefit if the surrounding land has been stripped bare.

This is an uncomfortable truth for programs that focus exclusively on farm-level certification.

A certified organic plot in a deforested landscape doesn’t get the same ecosystem services as one embedded in a matrix of forests and orchards.

“Our results show that these benefits depend strongly on how trees are managed both within farms and across the surrounding landscape,” Aycart-Lazo said.

The team proposes a landscape-level formula for the region: roughly 30–35% forest cover, another 40–45% in tree-based habitats like agroforests or orchards, and 20–30% in open areas for annual crops.

That mix, they argue, could create multifunctional landscapes that sustain both high biodiversity and strong cocoa production.

This is a recommendation though, not a decree. Different regions have different land pressures, different communities, and different histories.

“This is not a one-size-fits-all blueprint. Landscape strategies need to be adapted to local land availability and developed together with local communities,” Ocampo-Ariza said.

The study was conducted in one of the world’s most biodiverse regions. The specifics belong to the northern Peruvian Amazon.

But the underlying logic is portable. Wherever crops depend on natural pest control, the surrounding habitat either supports or undermines it.

The study cuts against a stubborn narrative in tropical agriculture – that farmers must choose between productivity and conservation. The data from these 28 Peruvian farms suggest the opposite.

Biodiversity didn’t just coexist with cocoa production. It actively drove it.

The ecosystem services provided by wildlife – pest control above all – were the mechanism converting habitat into yield.

That doesn’t mean conservation is free. Managing a structurally varied canopy takes skill.

Maintaining landscape-level forest cover requires coordination across farms, communities, and governments. But the economic argument is now harder to wave away.

For cocoa growers, keeping forests nearby can help protect the harvest.

The study is published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Flatology, the study of flatulence, sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion.

We know that a host of creatures ‪—​​ from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind.

"Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '"Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence'' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email.

What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.

Researchers measure the methane animals produce by placing them inside respiration chambers, then inserting a capsule into the stomach that releases a tracer gas while strapping them with a harness that samples their breath. Alternatively, they capture their breath at stations where they feed or are milked.

Research points to livestock, especially cows, as major methane emitters. A recent report puts their total methane emissions at 117 teragrams per year. (One teragram is equal to 1 billion kilograms, or 2.2 billion pounds.) A buildup of cow-generated methane gas even caused a dairy shed in Germany to explode. However, contrary to what many people believe, the "overwhelming majority" of methane emissions from livestock is released through burping, not flatulence, Ermias Kebreab, a professor of animal science at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science in an email.

The reason comes down to where in the gut the gas is made. Herbivores can't break down plant material on their own; they rely on microbes in their guts to ferment it, and that fermentation releases gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, Dr. Marcus Clauss, head of research and co-director of the Clinic for Zoo Animals, Exotic Pets and Wildlife at the University of Zurich, told Live Science in an email. Some of this gas is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled. The rest tends to leave by the nearest exit ‪—‬ animals that ferment their food toward the front of the digestive tract mostly burp it out, while those that ferment it toward the back mostly pass it as wind, Clauss explained.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Cows and other ruminants ‪(such as buffalo, sheep, goats and camels)‬ ferment their food in a chamber called the rumen, located near the front of the digestive system, so most of the methane they produce is through belching, Matthew Hayek, an associate professor of environmental studies at New York University, told Live Science in an email.

So if it's not cows, which animal is the top farter based on their methane emissions? The best candidates are hindgut fermenters ‪—‬ herbivores that digest plant matter in the large intestine (the hindgut). Meat eaters, by contrast, typically produce far less methane than herbivores do, Clauss said.

Are cows really the top contender for animal farts?

One possible contender are termites, which break down wood and grass in their hindguts. Their global population is estimated to be around 27 quadrillion (that's 15 zeros) individuals, and they collectively emit 10 teragrams of methane per year.

But, per individual, the title might go to horses. According to a 2019 report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, horses have the highest methane emissions among hindgut fermenters — around 40 pounds (18 kg) of methane per horse each year.

However, Clauss is skeptical. "The ranking of horse as highest is only because it has been measured," he told Live Science in an email. "But there are so many hindgut fermenters not measured, like rhino ... Who knows?"

If we consider methane emissions per unit of bodyweight, the nutria (Myocastor coypus) ‪—‬ an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent ‪—‬ would have higher methane emissions than the horse, Clauss said.

Clauss also questioned the accuracy of using methane emissions data as an indicator of flatulence. "There is some methane in flatulence, but most likely the majority of methane produced by an animal is exhaled, i.e. it goes via blood to the lungs," he said.

So until scientists figure out how to measure animal farts, any ranking remains speculative. For now, scientists have developed ways to track intestinal gas in people, including swallowable electronic capsules that measure gases inside the gut and clip-on underwear sensors that detect hydrogen in farts.

Methane is a particularly potent greenhouse gas when released into the atmosphere, and the quantities that large herds of cows and other ruminants emit through burping are enough to contribute to climate change. Indeed, scientists are experimenting with ways to reduce methane emissions from cattle — for example, by adding seaweed to their diet.

But animal flatulence is not a major contributor to global methane increases, Hayek said.

Even methane emissions from termite flatulence, while large, do not have an impact, Stefan Arndt, a professor of physiological and ecosystem ecology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "A large proportion of that methane is then consumed by methanotrophic bacteria in the soil," he said. These bacteria use methane as an energy source, thereby reducing the net methane emissions from termites substantially.

"Their emissions are part of the natural cycle of methane that has always been there for millennia," Arndt added. "The increasing methane concentrations in the atmosphere that are leading to climate change are caused by humans."

#6318. One November storm changed how California’s Sierra Nevada looked from orbit

An early storm brought nearly a foot of snow to Donner Pass, offering a first look at the snowpack that helps supply California with water.

Fresh snow stretches across California’s Sierra Nevada in a satellite image taken on the morning of November 14.

Around Lake Tahoe and farther south, white covers much of the high country.

Along part of the range’s western side, green slopes still show through, making it easy to see where the storm left its mark.

A Pacific storm swept through the previous day, bringing heavy rain to the Sacramento area and close to a foot of snow to some mountain locations.

A break between weather systems gave NASA’s Terra satellite a clear look at the mountains after one of the season’s first major snowfalls.

The instrument that captured the view, the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer, or MODIS, takes in long stretches of the mountain range at once.

From that vantage point, the snow that fell on individual peaks and mountain passes comes into view as a broad band of white.

NASA Earth Observatory paired the November 14 view with an image from two days earlier, when snow was largely confined to the highest ridges southeast of Lake Tahoe.

The earlier view gives a sense of how much changed in the time it took for one storm to cross California.

A separate regional analysis from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) estimated that snow covered about 43 percent of its Sierra Nevada analysis area on November 14.

A month earlier, the estimate was less than 1 percent. The comparison shows how quickly snow can spread across terrain that was largely bare in mid-October.

At Donner Pass, northwest of Lake Tahoe, the Central Sierra Snow Laboratory recorded nearly 12 inches of snow on November 13.

Officials closed Interstate 80 in both directions over Donner Summit that evening.

Farther south, Mammoth Mountain reported 9 to 13 inches of fresh snow. In Yosemite National Park, officials closed several roads ahead of the storm.

The reports from Donner Pass and Mammoth give a sense of how much snow fell at specific locations across the long stretch of mountains visible from above.

The storm also brought heavy rain to the Sacramento area, west of the Sierra Nevada.

Elevation helped determine what reached the ground. Where the air was warm enough, precipitation fell as rain.

Higher in the mountains, colder conditions allowed snow to accumulate.

The green slopes along the western side of the range are a reminder that a storm can bring very different weather to places only a short distance apart.

The broad cover visible on November 14 raises a question that matters well beyond the mountains.

How much water is in all that snow? Hydrologists answer it by measuring snow water equivalent, the depth of water that would remain if the snow at a given spot melted.

A foot of light, powdery snow can hold less water than a shallower layer of dense, wet snow.

California’s Department of Water Resources uses that measurement to help forecast how much water could flow out of the mountains as the snow melts.

Some of that runoff reaches major reservoirs in spring and early summer, helping supply water during the state’s dry months.

Timing matters because California receives much of its precipitation during the cooler part of the year.

Rain can reach streams and reservoirs soon after a storm.

Snow can stay in the mountains for months before melting, releasing some of that water later, when storms are less frequent.

The November storm arrived about six weeks into the water year, the 12-month period hydrologists use to track precipitation and runoff beginning October 1.

The Sierra Nevada snowpack generally peaks around April 1, leaving several months for new storms to add to it or for warm spells to melt some of what has already accumulated.

More snow was already in the forecast when NASA released the image on November 18.

The National Weather Service had issued a winter storm warning for parts of the Sierra Nevada through November 20, with around four feet of snow possible at some locations above 8,000 feet.

The November 14 image captures the mountains at the start of that longer process.

In a single day, snow spread across enough of the Sierra Nevada to change how the range looked from orbit.

Over the coming months, the same slopes will collect or lose snow with each shift in the weather.

By spring, what remains will help determine how much meltwater reaches California’s reservoirs as the state heads into its dry season.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview

#6316. Office light may throw off the body’s daily rhythm

In a study of day-active rats, an hour of simulated daylight at noon helped restore activity rhythms weakened by fluorescent office lighting.

People spend about 90% of their time indoors, under ceiling lights that are a small fraction as bright as the sky outside. The body reads that light as a biological signal.

In a rodent that keeps human hours, living under standard fluorescent office light weakened the animal’s daily rhythm of activity.

An hour of simulated daylight at noon each day, roughly analogous to a lunchtime walk outdoors, partly restored the rats’ daily activity rhythm.

In a second experiment, more of the male rats that spent six weeks under fluorescent light showed diabetic-range blood sugar than rats under daylight-strength light.

A smaller share of sperm were moving in the fluorescent-light group, about 19% compared with 45% under simulated daylight.

The study is small, with eight animals in the first experiment and 20 in the second, and all of them were male.

Lily Yan, a professor in the Department of Psychology at Michigan State University, led the work. The lead author is Antony Bum Kim of the Department of Architecture at the University of California, Berkeley.

“It is a biological signal that influences circadian organization and, potentially, a range of downstream health outcomes,” Yan said of light.

The body’s internal clock helps regulate daily patterns, known as circadian rhythms, in sleep, appetite, and much else.

Nearly every lab rodent is awake at night, which makes it a poor stand-in for a person whose body clock runs on daylight.

The Nile grass rat, a small African rodent, is active in the daytime, and Yan’s lab has used it for years to study how light affects the brain.

Over each cage, the team installed a programmable light that can imitate the color mix of many sources. Its daylight setting ran at about 5,600 lux, roughly the level that building designers treat as true daylight.

The office setting imitated a standard fluorescent tube at about 150 lux, the brightness of a typical indoor workspace.

Eight male grass rats lived under four lighting schedules in turn, two weeks each. Sensors logged their movement day and night.

The first schedule was steady daylight from dawn to dusk. The second was daylight that brightened to the same midday peak and faded again, which delivered about half the total light.

The third was fluorescent office light all day. The fourth was office light with one hour of full daylight at noon.

The rats were most active, and most sharply divided between a busy day and a quiet night, under steady daylight.

Under fluorescent light their activity was lower and their rhythm flatter, with its peak shifted later in the day.

The ramped daylight did not match the steady version even though it reached the same peak.

The authors wrote that the total amount of light over the day, more than its brightest moment, seems to set the strength of the rhythm.

Adding the noon hour of daylight to the office schedule raised the strength of the rhythm again, though only partly.

All eight animals showed a burst of activity during that hour. The authors called it a partial rescue.

A separate group of 20 male grass rats lived for six weeks under either steady daylight or fluorescent light, 10 in each group.

The rats’ body weight, belly fat, and average blood sugar did not differ between the groups.

But five of the 20 animals had blood sugar in a range the lab treats as diabetic, and four of the five had lived under fluorescent light.

In a follow-up with a different way of drawing blood, the pattern held. Four of eight rats under fluorescent light crossed that line, compared with one of seven under daylight.

The two groups produced the same number of sperm. Under daylight, about 45% of those sperm were moving. Under fluorescent light, about 19% were.

“Factors affecting health are not limited to drugs, diet and exercise,” Kim said. “The light environments we create in our homes, schools and workplaces are also biological exposures.”

Ten animals per group is a small sample. More rats under fluorescent light crossed the study’s threshold for diabetic-range blood sugar, while average blood sugar was similar in the two groups.

The authors also wrote that blood drawn after euthanasia can read differently, which is why they ran the follow-up.

Every animal was male, so the study says nothing about females. And a grass rat under a programmable lamp is not an office worker with windows, a commute, and a phone.

The authors wrote that the findings support daylight deficiency as a risk factor for diabetes in this animal.

The sperm result is new, they wrote, since earlier work on light and sperm looked at day length rather than light quality.

What remains untested is whether the same shifts happen in people. The authors wrote that the next step is for other groups to repeat the work in grass rats or other day-active animals.

The next question is whether an hour of brighter light at midday could help people who work far from a window maintain a stronger daily rhythm.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Biological Rhythms.

#6315. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6314. The fight to save one of Australia’s rarest frogs has taken a cue from farmers

Selective breeding could help Australia’s southern corroboree frog survive longer after exposure to the deadly chytrid fungus.

A breeding technique from agriculture might help one of Australia’s most threatened frogs.

Researchers found that southern corroboree frogs can inherit traits that help them survive longer after exposure to a deadly fungus. That means selective breeding could make the species more resilient.

The frog is functionally extinct in the wild. The culprit is chytridiomycosis, an infectious disease caused by the amphibian chytrid fungus.

Captive breeding has kept the species alive. But returning frogs to the wild is hard because the fungus persists in the environment.

Lead author Mikaeylah Davidson completed the work as part of her PhD at the University of Melbourne.

The study tested whether genomic selection could guide conservation breeding for the frog.

Davidson and her colleagues combined laboratory experiments with genome-wide genetic information. That included a custom genotyping array built for the frog.

The team found that southern corroboree frogs differ in how long they survive after exposure to chytrid fungus. Some of that variation is inherited.

“Using genomic data, we were able to show that survival following chytrid infection is a heritable trait, meaning some of the differences in survival are due to genetic differences that can be passed on to the next generation,” Davidson said.

“This means there is genetic variation we could potentially use to improve survival through selective breeding.”

“Excitingly, this approach is a potential way to move beyond simply keeping endangered frogs alive in captivity, towards actively improving their ability to cope with the threats preventing their recovery in the wild.”

Modeling suggested genomic information could guide breeding decisions.

It could potentially increase average survival time after exposure to chytrid fungus by around nine percent in the next generation.

The model projected that gain while accounting for inbreeding and genetic diversity.

An established captive breeding program offered a chance to test the idea in practice. Zoos Victoria and the Taronga Conservation Society support that program through partnerships.

The research suggests improved disease resilience doesn’t need to come at the expense of genetic diversity. That is especially significant for small, critically endangered populations.

In such groups, maintaining diversity and limiting inbreeding are central to long-term population health and evolutionary potential.

Senior author Lee Skerratt from the University of Melbourne argued the approach may also have potential for other threatened wildlife affected by persistent disease.

That is particularly true for species already managed through captive breeding.

“Amphibians are an important focus, with hundreds of species now maintained in captivity for conservation as chytrid fungus continues to threaten populations globally,” he said.

“Genomic selection could help conservation breeding programs move beyond preventing extinction by moving animals into captivity towards actively supporting animals’ ability to survive threats in the wild.”

First, researchers developed the genomic tools and disease datasets needed to explore new strategies for the frog. They then combined a newly mapped genome and a custom genotyping array with extensive disease-resilience data.

That let them investigate selective breeding as a proactive approach to species recovery.

The next stage is to improve and validate the predictions.

The team will use genomic information from more of the breeding population. They will also explore other genetic approaches to improve disease resistance.

Researchers will also test whether the predicted improvements show up in later generations. And critically, they will check whether greater survival in the lab translates into better outcomes in the wild.

Amphibians are in deep trouble worldwide. The chytrid fungus has caused catastrophic declines and extinctions.

More than 200 threatened frog species are now kept in captivity. These colonies have prevented immediate extinctions.

But they are temporary refuges, meant to hold the line until threats can be mitigated.

Selective breeding offers a different path. Instead of just keeping animals alive, it can improve their ability to cope. That could raise the odds of successful reintroduction.

While genomic selection has transformed plant and animal breeding, it has rarely been applied to wildlife. The main barriers have been missing datasets and a lack of structured breeding programs.

This frog had both, which made it an ideal test case.

The species produces fewer than 30 eggs per year and reaches sexual maturity at 2 to 5 years of age. Those traits slow generational turnover.

The trait is also polygenic. No single gene has a large effect. Resistance is shaped by many loci, each contributing a little.

Because many genes contribute to survival, the team used genomic selection, which draws on information from across the genome.

And the modelling covers only part of the breeding population. Future work could capture more genetic variation.

First, refine the breeding value predictions with more parental genotyping. Second, test realized responses in controlled and semi-natural conditions. Third, run multi-generational selective breeding alongside ongoing diversity management.

Data from each phase would feed back into the program. That supports adaptive management and continuous improvement.

For now, the result is a proof of concept. It shows that captive populations can become more than passive safeguards. For a frog on the brink, that shift could matter a great deal.

The study is published in the journal npj Biodiversity.

After nine days in space, the Artemis II crewmembers faced their final and riskiest challenge: splashdown. In this excerpt from the book "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space," astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes the moment from his chair.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nine days in space, the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission looked out their capsule window on April 10, 2026, and saw the bright-blue Earth below them. The crew had traveled more than 250,000 miles (400,000 kilometers) from our planet — farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone — and now, home was just a few hundred miles straight down.

Only one milestone remained: splashdown, a fast and fiery plunge into the Pacific Ocean that would mark the end of humanity's first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years.Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian Space Agency astronaut on the crew, had every reason to be confident that the team's Orion crew capsule would hold up just fine. But this was Hansen's first time in space, and his first time dropping through the sky like a fireball at 24,600 mph (39,600 kmh).

It wasn't that he was afraid for himself, Hansen explains in "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space" (Hanover Square Press, 2026), which he co-wrote with John Larsen). Rather, he knew that his wife Catherine and three children would be among the millions of Earthlings watching the most dangerous moment of his mission from below.

In this excerpt from the book, Hansen describes the thrilling intensity of splashdown and the euphoria of knowing that he and his crewmates were going to make it back safely — and make history.

CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen smiles inside the Orion crew capsule during the Artemis II lunar flyby.

Immediately after jettisoning the European Service Module, and exactly half an hour before we were due to splashdown, Mission Control initiated the crew module raise burn. This nineteen-second burn was the first and only burn using the small thrusters built into our Orion capsule. It slightly shallowed our entry trajectory to put us right in the sweet spot while also providing some added distance from the service module, as we'd be hitting the atmosphere in near succession. It, too, went flawlessly. I tightened my straps; it was time for the fireworks.

A re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere is absolutely on the short list of the most incredible experiences of my life. We slammed into it at 7:53 p.m., thundering down at over 10 kilometres [6.2 miles] per second. Per second.

The thrusters fired almost constantly to stabilize the capsule: loud thuds, as if Thor himself were hammering on our spacecraft, as the G-forces quickly began to build, aggressively scrubbing off the velocity we had added to our rocket nine days earlier. Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us. It started red and transformed into a bright, bluish-green, pulsating light. It was breathtaking, the bright colors igniting our senses.

It was insane to think about what we were doing. We all knew how this worked; we all knew the science. But deep inside, I also recognized that astronauts must have a screw loose to do this. Nobody in their right mind would strap themselves inside a metal canister that itself was sitting inside a giant fireball. But there was no other way down, and I had accepted the realities of this journey long in advance.

Although I was at peace, I felt guilty for the stress I was putting on my family. I had talked to them openly about the mission's risks, and this was the highest-risk moment. I tried to send my love telepathically, telling them it was going great.

The Orion capsule drops toward the Pacific Ocean with all parachutes successfully deployed.

As we continued our freefall, it looked like a thousand camera flashes were exploding inside Integrity. I lowered the sun visor on my helmet. There were only centimeters of heatshield and aluminum separating me from the more than 2500°C heat outside. Almost instantly, the heat inside our cramped home also began to rise, an increase that engineers refer to as "thermally benign." All I know is that I couldn't feel it, blissfully wrapped in my thermally controlled garments.

As we continued to fall, the G-forces built up to nearly four times the pressure we feel on Earth. I wasn't too worried, having endured more than five minutes of the same G-force, or more, in the NASA centrifuge trainer. I had half-expected the freefall back to Earth to seem short, but it was a long six minutes before the flames finally ceased and we re-established communications with Mission Control.

It had already been a wild ride, but I also knew another crazy part — parachute deployment and the actual splashdown — lay ahead. My adrenalin kept pumping.

Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us.

"Integrity, Houston. Comms check, post-blackout," we heard from Mission Control. It was music to our ears. It was exactly 8:00 p.m.

"Houston, Integrity," Reid [Wiseman, mission commander], replied. "We have you loud and clear."

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried. For the folks at NASA, it was clear that all had gone well during the descent — a small fleet of NASA and Air Force planes had captured it on high-resolution cameras. But, for me, it wasn't over yet. I wouldn't truly feel safe until our three main parachutes successfully deployed. If they didn't, we'd be a chunk of metal slamming into the ocean at incredibly high speed, and the chances of surviving that would be somewhere between minimal and non-existent.

I've watched many of my close friends return from space, and I find the minutes after surviving the re-entry heat until the parachutes deploy to be the hardest part to watch. When I see a capsule plunge through the clouds with no chutes, I always worry they might not appear at all. That's completely terrifying.

Jeremy Hansen arrives on the deck of the USS John P. Murtha after being recovered from the Orion capsule. All four crewmembers were in perfect health after splashdown.

I thought of Catherine and the kids, sending them a "don't worry, gang" message in my mind. Catherine later told me that she had a very bad feeling about the heatshield, so when we emerged from blackout, she began crying and didn't even focus on the parachutes.

Three minutes later, at an altitude of 7,100 metres, timed explosions released small chutes that pulled off the cover for two larger chutes, called drogues because they are intended to slow our acceleration to a speed that would allow our main parachutes to open without ripping. They did their job perfectly, but it was wild inside the capsule, jerking us back and forth like a ride at the fair.

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried.

One minute later, at only 1,500 metres above the ocean, the drogue chutes cut loose, and, for a few moments, we felt like we were falling backward. Then, in succession, the three main parachutes began deploying, blossoming slowly so they wouldn't tear apart. The rate of our fall slowed as the red-and-white nylon canopies, each 35 metres in diameter, filled with air. The thrusters kept firing, aiming the capsule's base directly toward the point of impact.

"Integrity, we see three good-looking parachutes," we heard from our CAPCOM. Within seconds, our splashdown speed had reduced to 27 kilometres per hour.

That's it, I said to myself. I'm pretty sure we can survive whatever else could be thrown at us now.

Christina [Koch, mission specialist] seemed to agree. We grabbed one another's hands in a moment of celebration.

Excerpted from "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, The Groundbreaking Human Mission Into Deep Space" by John Larsen with Jeremy Hansen. © 2026 by John Larsen, used with permission by HarperCollins/Hanover Square Press.

#6311. New Congress will still be filled with losers

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.
