#6192. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real company.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

You may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car company, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

First, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

#6191. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6190. Walking the Peaks of the Balkans, a Trekking Route With Community At Its Core

I'm awoken by the sound of cowbells clanging outside my bare-boned wood cabin in Dobërdol, a high mountain settlement in northern Albania. Through the window, slightly fogged from the chilly morning air at 5,700 feet, I see the culprits: five chestnut-colored cows munching on grass just feet from my bedside, their bells and tails swinging away.

The Albanian Alps are one of our Best Places to Go in 2027.

I make the short and frigid walk across the guesthouse lawn to the breakfast room, maneuvering around a dozen or so hikers' tents pitched in the grass. Yesterday’s 10-mile trek from Çerem to Dobërdol is still fresh in my mind: dusty dirt trails edged with wild blueberries I couldn’t resist picking and patches of willow gentian, their petals so intensely purple they matched the berry stains on my fingers. The forests of pine, beech, and spruce in these parts are thick enough that the daylight dims inside of them; the valleys dizzyingly deep as they fold in on themselves.

The Peaks of the Balkans trek is a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro.

Local-owned guesthouses welcome trekkers with included meals, like fresh vegetables, homemade dairy, and cured sausages and meats.

It’s mid-September, and only 7 a.m., but breakfast is already in full swing, not an empty seat left at the tables squeezed into the cozy timber-framed room. The Kurmekaj brothers, our hosts, are frantically grabbing four plates apiece from the kitchen, loaded with fried eggs, sausage, fresh sheep cheese, and cucumber-and-tomato salad, a fixture on the Balkan plate. I do my best to duck out of their way as the door behind me swings open and more trekkers pile in.

This is my fourth day of ten on the Peaks of the Balkans trek, a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro, through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask. Conceived in the early 2010s as a cross-border peace and tourism project, this trail was meant to reconnect mountain communities that had been splintered by war, create livelihoods, and give residents a reason to remain—or return—to villages hollowed out by conflict and emigration.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail offers both busy sections and quiet side trails where your only companions may be a single hiker or group of grazing cattle.

By those measures, it has been remarkably successful. A late 2025 study published in the Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism estimated that roughly 43,000 hikers now walk the trail each year—up from regional estimates of roughly 20,000 in the pre-pandemic era—injecting more than €25 million ($27.7 million USD) annually into mountain regions where family homes, shepherd settlements, and seasonal villages have increasingly become guesthouses for trekkers. But that success is also beginning to crowd some of the places that the trail was created to support, as a growing number of travelers takes interest.

Ricardo Fahrig of the Albania-based adventure travel company Zbulo, which has been running Peaks trips since the trail’s early years, helped me piece together my own self-guided route on these trails. He says the contrast between busy Dobërdol and the quieter terrain I’m soon to enter after breakfast gets to the heart of the issue. “It’s not the number of travelers on the Peaks of the Balkans trail,” he tells me, “but rather the distribution. Some sections remain sparsely visited, while others, like Dobërdol, struggle with volume during a relatively short season”, a period from roughly June through September, with some hikers continuing into early October.

After breakfast, just a few steps down the trail from the guesthouse in Dobërdol, the clatter and congestion of the morning fade immediately. So do the other trekkers, flowing like a stream up the steep green lip of the expansive bowl-shaped valley we all woke up in, then onward to Milishevc, Montenegro, the usual stop after Dobërdol.

Stepping off the primary Peak of the Balkans trail—which the writer did with a self-guided itinerary from Zbulo—allows for quieter moments and a greater sense of solitude.

All except two. Stef Van Dam, a seasoned Dutch thru-hiker I’d met on my second day on the trail, falls into step beside me on the cattle-worn traces of the route we've chosen to take instead. He, too, is detouring off the official trail. Whereas I’m headed for the heart-shaped lake below Gjeravica, Kosovo’s highest peak, he will peel off later to summit it—“the peak of the Peaks of the Balkans,” he calls the mountain.

At the empty pass marking the Albania-Kosovo border, 1,600 feet of ascent later, we collapse onto the same rock—for all we know, Van Dam is munching his apple in Albania while I air my blisters in Kosovo just next to him. From up here, this border is steeped in irony—a line so invisible we have to guess at where exactly it’s drawn, yet a matter that has been fought over, fortified, closed, and redrawn for more than a century.

Ahead, a narrow dirt track just below the Kosovo side of the pass continues along the contour line, snaking through the treeless and boulder-strewn landscape. To our left and many mountain miles away, we spot the village of Junik where we’re both planning to sleep that night, me in a gueshouse and Van Dam in his tent somewhere nearby. As if marking the spot, a golden eagle circles in the unblemished autumn sky above it.

“This is exactly what I came to this trail to find,” Van Dam says, the first to interrupt the silence. “I wanted something quiet, more remote than other trails in Europe. I’ve found it here.”

Having myself walked a few of the more notably crowded European trails, including the Camino de Santiago, I know what he means. Besides the two of us and the eagle riding the thermals overhead, there isn’t another soul in sight.

Along the route, small guesthouses warmly welcome trekkers, who have created a reason to stay—or return—to communities once disrupted by conflict and emagration.

By late afternoon, after Van Dam and I part ways below Gjeravica. What appeared as a scattering of rooftops no bigger than a thumbnail now reveals itself in the distinct forms of summer homes and traditional katuns, seasonal shepherd settlements composed of simple huts and stone-walled livestock pens.

The family has only recently begun welcoming trekkers into their home, and they radiate the kind of excitement that comes from still being delighted by every single arrival. Renaja leads me to my room for the night, tucked on the third floor beneath the A-frame eaves. Downstairs, pizza bakes in an old wood-burning stove while Renaja's mother and grandmother set a long table for the dozen or so guests still dribbling in.

The old highland idea of besa—that a house belongs not only to its owner, but to God and to the guest—is coming to life before my eyes. Or, as Fahrig, who first came to these mountains in 2012, later puts it: bukë, kripë, zemër, an Albanian expression meaning “bread, salt, and heart.” “The material offering may be simple,” he says. “The welcome is what makes it memorable.”

The following morning, I continue deeper into Kosovo, eventually rejoining the main Peaks of the Balkans route. Now, it’s Montenegro on the other side of the invisible line I keep crossing. Over the coming days, the trail shifts between empty mountain passes and occasional stretches of asphalt—the latter one being a reason, Fahrig says, that many trekkers truncate this section entirely. He estimates that places such as the Rugova Gorge—a river-carved passage whose 2-3,000-foot-deep limestone walls bear stone-blasted tunnels, a frothy emerald river, and viewpoints at every turn—currently receive around 30 percent or less of the traffic funneled through Dobërdol.

The Peaks of the Balkans stitches together sections that include dirt paths, country roads, and sometimes asphalt—but even the less photogenic portions lead to impactful destinations.

In Drelaj, where this dramatic gorge opens into a wider pastoral valley, skipping Kosovo begins to feel like missing the point. This quiet highland hamlet is embraced on all sides by forested mountains. Across its green curves and garden plots are chalet-like summer homes built out of wood and stone, each boasting a balcony or porch turned toward the mountains and the mosque whose slender minaret rises at the center of it all.

After a day of sharing the trail with more cows than people, passing by deserted villages, and hugging a gully’s edge on a heavily eroded and unpaved fire road, I eventually spill out of the forest onto asphalt that ends in Drelaj. My guesthouse, Konaku i Malsorit, is tucked just to the right of the minaret. An Albanian flag (this part of Kosovo is majority ethnic Albanian) whips in the breeze above the two-story home and its garden, ripe with peppers, tomatoes, onions, and maize.

Minarets dot the skyline in even small villages in Kosovo and Albania.

My host Blendi Lajqi tells me his family fled Drelaj during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War after their home was burned by Yugoslav and Serbian forces. He was six years old. After the war, the family moved to Peja, the nearest major city, and for around two decades, he says, the house and the land they left behind here were “dead, no longer a home.” The creation of the trail gave his family—and others in the village—a reason to return and reinvest in what they left behind. Looking around at it now, “dead” is hard to imagine.

The room I’m sleeping in, now completely redone into what could easily be a fully functioning apartment, once served as a makeshift hospital for the Kosovo Liberation Army (UÇK), the ethnic Albanian guerrilla force that fought the Yugoslav and Serbian forces during the war. Here, he tells me, Lajqi’s mother and aunt cared for the wounded.

Many hikers arrive knowing almost nothing about what happened here, he says. But for those who make a point to learn about it, the history of this region gives different weight to this trail—and the intention behind it. The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Lajqi tells me. “When we opened the guesthouse, our home became a place where people from all over the world could come, stay, eat, talk with us, and experience our way of life. For me, there’s something special about that.”

Trails in this region include a great deal of altitude change—and the views that come with that.

The writer gathers around the dinner table with fellow trekkers at a local guesthouse.

Few people, however, have watched tourism reshape these mountains as long as Skender Selimaj of Hotel Rezidenca Quku i Valbones in Valbona, Albania. When he and his brother Alfred returned from the United Kingdom in the early 2000s, after leaving Albania during the period of communism, the high-walled valley hemmed in by jagged limestone peaks still revolved largely around subsistence farming. In 2004, they opened Restaurant Rilindja—meaning “rebirth” in Albanian—without knowing whether enough travelers would come to sustain it. Then, in 2009, Selimaj helped clear the passes toward Theth and Çerem and carried some of the first wooden trail signs into the mountains himself.

As in many locations along the Peaks of the Balkans route, the influx of tourism has since reshaped the Valbona Valley. The single-day hike over Valbona Pass to Theth has become one of Albania’s most popular mountain routes, which is also why my self-guided Zbulo itinerary intentionally bypassed it. Even with the trade-offs, Valbona has benefited. Farmers can now sell cheese, meat, eggs, and milk locally at better prices. Families have new income, while local children, Selimaj says, sometimes grow up speaking English simply from meeting travelers from around the world.

Selimaj, who spent years working as a mountain guide and in mountain rescue, still spends his free time exploring the terrain he grew up in, though he’s faced the fact that solitude is increasingly difficult to find. Where he once expected wild goats and empty mountains, “everywhere you go, you see somebody,” he says. He doesn’t wish tourism away; he has seen too clearly what it has done for local livelihoods. What he does want is a Valbona that remains clean, green, and recognizably local, where old stone houses and family-run businesses aren’t crowded out by large-scale outside development.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail passes through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask.

For Fahrig of Zbulo, the answer to the newfound business isn’t necessarily fewer trekkers. What he hopes to preserve on this trail are “living communities rather than places shaped entirely around visitors.” Doing that, he argues, means spreading trekkers more evenly: encouraging hikers to continue through Kosovo, directing some traffic toward quieter alternatives just beyond the busiest passes, and steering repeat or more adventurous trekkers toward newer alternative long-distance routes like the 225-mile High Scardus Trail that traverses the remote and mountainous borderlands of North Macedonia, Kosovo, and Albania.

In Kosovo, some of that work is already underway. Lajqi is part of a volunteer effort with other guesthouse owners and tourism businesses to create more natural alternatives around paved sections of the original route without cutting the villages themselves out of the trail—the other risk of making changes. “The best solution is not to completely change the original trail,” Lajqi says, “but to offer more choices, preserving the connection between the villages while also giving hikers the kind of mountain experience they came for.”

Over the days that follow, I keep moving west, circling back towards Theth. Each day brings with it another 3,000-foot pass to scale, another cucumber-and-tomato sandwich to enjoy once I get there, along with a steady mix of surprise, (some) stress, and plenty of solitude. Occasionally, I get lost when my GPS stops working or the orange dots and red-and-white striped trail markers disappear, and yet I always find my way. I walk, at times, with no one, and in other moments with dozens of travelers. Sometimes, it's just me and cowbell-clanging bovine. I keep going like this, collecting these little moments and memories, until, on the 10th day, I pass a bunker, the crumbling Cold War-era concrete mushrooms built by communist dictator Enver Hoxha, and realize I must be back in Albania.

By the time I approach Theth—the end of my route—I feel like I’ve walked through both versions of the Peaks: the one overwhelmed by its own success and the quieter version still there available alongside it.

The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Blendi Lajqi of Konaku i Malsorit says.

For my final night on the trails, I hike into Bujtina Kometa, a guesthouse in the quiet hamlet of Okol situated roughly a mile-and-a-half from central Theth. A mezze spread of marinated chicken, seasoned potatoes, olives, tomatoes, soft cheese, and tzatziki for dipping lands on the table, all prepared by our host Ermira and her family. The thing about these trails is that even if you go your own way by day, you'll find yourself breaking bread with familiar faces by night. Every person around the table, I realize, is someone I've met somewhere along the trail—people I’ve shared miles with over the last 10 days as our paths kept crossing.

Ermira’s father tops up our water and hints at honey-soaked fruit for dessert; woodsmoke from a neighbor distilling homemade raki drifts through the low-lit dining room. Van Dam, seated across the table from me now, reaches for another forkful of potato dripping with tzatziki. The busy center of Theth, with its tour buses and day-trippers, still feels worlds away.

For one more night, these Accursed Mountains and all they carry—the besa, the borders, the beauty, and the stories etched into them—envelop us, proving that wide-open spaces and quiet still have their place in these mountains.

Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full Peaks of the Balkans route.

The complete Peaks of the Balkans circuit covers roughly 119 miles (192 km) across Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro. Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full route, though shorter itineraries of 5 to 8 days often cut or bypass certain stages. Most routes involve 5 to 8 hours of hiking per day, typically covering 8 to 17 miles with significant elevation gain and loss.

Getting there: Fly into Podgorica in Montenegro or Tirana in Albania, transferring via shuttle or 4x4 to trailheads in Theth, Valbona, or Plav.

When to go: The core trekking season runs from June through September, but is increasingly stretching into October. Late June through August generally offers more reliable pass conditions, though the trail can get busy. Early June can still mean snow lingering on the highest passes, while September is the sweet spot for favorable hiking weather (peak traffic proves that everyone knows this). Early-to-mid October can be beautiful for experienced hikers willing to gamble on shorter days, colder nights, and the occasional burst of snow; later in the month, high-altitude guesthouses begin winding down, and do not reopen again until early May or June.

Who to go with: Albania-based Zbulo offers guided and self-guided trips (with logistics arranged, but no guide) ranging from 8 to 12 days. These include cross-border permits, guesthouse reservations, meals, luggage transfers, and route planning. If you're traveling independently, be sure to secure your date-locked cross-border permits at least two weeks before hiking, or have an agency like Zbulo secure them for you.

Where to stay: Accommodation ranges from family-run guesthouses and homestays to simple mountain huts, cabins, and small hotels. In remote sections, expect basic rooms—sometimes shared—along with hearty home-cooked dinners, breakfasts, and often a packed lunch for the following day. Budget roughly $25-55 USD per person per night depending on the room and whether meals are included. Book ahead in high season, and carry plenty of cash in Albanian lek or Euros in small denominations; card payments and ATMs are scarce in the mountains. In May and other shoulder-season periods, it is possible to arrange rooms on the fly, but from June through September—especially in bottlenecks like Dobërdol and popular stops such as Theth and Valbona—it’s smarter to book several weeks ahead. Camping is also possible on parts of the route, including at some guesthouses that allow trekkers to pitch a tent for a small fee and use facilities or buy meals. You can arrange your accommodations directly with hosts over WhatsApp using contacts found through Google Maps, social media, or the official Peaks of the Balkans App; many are now available on platforms like Booking.com as well.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6189. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6188. Dreaming of Country Living? These Renovated Barn Airbnbs Got You Covered

Country living, with its beautiful nature, relaxing atmosphere, and stunning wildlife, makes it incredibly easy to forget your day-to-day stressors and embrace the slower path. And where better to enjoy this peace and quiet than from an Airbnb converted from a barn—provided, of course, you’re not actually sleeping next to a pitchfork and a pile of hay? Across the US, old dairy barns, horse stables, haylofts, and grain silos that once kept America’s farms running are finding dreamy second lives as vacation rentals. These sturdy structures are getting some very glamorous redesigns, but keeping the soaring ceilings, original timber beams, weathered wood, and old architectural details that no new build can quite replicate.

From sprawling farmhouses with enough room for the whole gang, to intimate hayloft hideaways made for a national park trip, to old grain silos that are surprisingly stylish places to sleep, there’s something interesting in every corner of the country. Expect modern interiors tucked behind century-old barn doors, outdoor soaking tubs overlooking rolling pastures, and properties where the resident animals are still very much part of the picture (morning coffee with a few curious goats, anyone?).

Whether you’re after a little farmyard nostalgia, a design-forward country escape, or simply a storied home just steps away from the wild, these barn Airbnbs make a pretty compelling case to trade your average stay for something with a little more hay-day history.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to Nashville, floor-to-ceiling windows, fully equipped kitchen, optional farm tours and event bookings

Bloomsbury Farm is a family-owned and -operated organic farm just outside Nashville. The 400-acre retreat is pastorally posh—the kind of place where wild turkeys and deer roam free, hawks swoop overhead, and coyotes howl in the night. The one-bedroom, one-bath rental is tastefully decorated: It’s where Martha Stewart meets Modern Farmer. That said, intentionality permeates every design choice, from the handsome leather headboard to the subway-tiled bath with Aesop hand soap. Guests are given farm-fresh eggs and a box of fruits and vegetables that are grown on-site; these come in handy when preparing meals on the kitchen’s professional gas range or grilling over the outdoor firepit.

City: Smyrna, TennesseeThings to do nearby: Brewer Farms, Cedar Stone Park, The Barn at Sycamore Farms, Arrington Vineyards

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Proximity to NYC, wood-burning fireplace, reading nooks, meadow and valley views, vintage arcade and board games

Just around a two-hour drive from NYC, this charmingly restored barn cottage awaits in the Hudson Valley. The space pairs a cozy wood-burning fireplace with expansive windows overlooking a meadow—one that the host notes becomes a “veritable bird sanctuary for most of the year.” It’s a harbor of hidden nooks made for cozying up with a book, and features a well-stocked kitchen and dining space for cooking, as well as a vintage arcade and board games for fun nights in with your crew. Previous guests have raved about its proximity to Hudson Valley hot spots: There’s no shortage of places to hike, ski, see art, or dine, as well as some fun local breweries and wineries. The property is within a 10- to 25-minute drive of six quaint Hudson Valley towns. (You can also request bikes from the hosts if you’re inclined to venture out on two wheels.)

City: Red Hook, New YorkThings to do nearby: Pine Plains, Stissing Mountain (and iconic restaurant Stissing House), Thompson Pond

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Desert views, on-site animals, proximity to Zion National Park, fully equipped kitchen, firepit, sauna

With a classic red-barn build, friendly farm animals, and a sauna practically made for stargazing, this dreamy Airbnb is an oasis—especially if Zion National Park is on your itinerary. Just one hour from the park, you’ll find this whimsical base for two set between Utah’s red rock cliffs, sweeping canyons, and heaps of local hiking paths. Inside, enjoy tasteful touches everywhere. Sunlight pours through the studio; a vintage-style soaking tub sits on black-and-white checkered flooring, and the kitchenette has modern appliances as well as some plants and pastel green cabinets. You’ll have some company when walking outside, too: This farm stay comes with two adorable Highland cows as well as a chicken coop. There’s also a sauna and firepit, just in case you need another reason to visit.

City: Hildale, UtahThings to do nearby: Water Canyon Winery, Squirrel Canyon Trailhead, Coral Pink Sand Dunes, Zion National Park

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Outdoor firepit, central location, private stargazing deck, wood-burning fireplace, vinyl player

A silo in the Catskills? Now that's a fun place to spend a weekend. From the outside, this three-story converted tower is fairly understated, but step inside, and you'll find a surprisingly airy, thoughtfully designed little escape that makes every inch count. There's an open living room that flows into a stocked kitchen, two spacious (and stunningly modern) bathrooms, and a private deck for soaking up the quiet. The interiors have a cool, pared-back feel, with just the right amount of personality to make it feel like somewhere you'd actually want to hang out (board games and a puzzle marathon are very much encouraged). And while it feels nicely tucked away, Woodstock's galleries, shops, and restaurants are just 10 minutes down the road.

City: Willow, New YorkThings to do nearby: Mount Tremper, Emerson Kaleidoscope, Phoenicia Diner, Overlook Mountain

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ocean views, stereo system, heated floors, wood-burning stove, open and modern kitchen

What could be better—or more endearing—than this modern Northern California barn in a forest clearing? Renovated by San Francisco architect David Crimmins, this gem leans into its sleek agrarian style, with airy, open-beam ceilings, heated concrete floors, a redwood slab dining table, and windows on all sides, bringing the outside in. The house sits along a rocky coastline, primed for whale watching and trips to coastal wineries between the Redwoods and the Pacific. The high-design stay stands tall on Anchor Bay along the Mendocino Coast; you’ll have your very own one-acre yard amid the state’s dreamy Redwoods, and it’s just a 20-minute walk to the beach.

City: Gualala, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Whale Watch Point, Gualala Arts Center, Point Arena Lighthouse, Bonham Trail to Cooks Beach

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, firepit, outdoor shower, proximity to Lake Michigan

Not every barn stay comes with Lake Michigan practically in its backyard. Tucked among 12 wooded acres in Leelanau County, this country base holds its former farm structure while offering its guests a fresh and pretty new lease. Once part of a 30-acre farm that stretched across both sides of the road, you can still appreciate a little of that history in its beautifully restored bones. These days, it's a two-bedroom hideaway that makes a wonderful home base for exploring Northern Michigan's wine country, with Northport's small-town charm and the peninsula's wineries and breweries just a hop and a skip away. There’s no need to leave your Airbnb for a fun day out: Spend the afternoon wandering out in nature, then make your way to the nearby secluded Lake Michigan beach. Peruse the guest reviews, and you’ll notice a telling pattern: Most travelers don't just stay once or twice—they return time and time again.

City: Northport, MichiganThings to do nearby: Cherry Basket Farm, Onomonee Road Beach, Fischer’s Happy Hour Tavern, Bay Front Park

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Silo design, mountain views, fully equipped kitchenette, private patio, firepit, proximity to Glacier National Park

On an 80-acre family farm in Montana’s Flathead Valley, this converted grain silo is truly one of a kind. Alongside jaw-dropping mountain views, the structure itself is a treat—and happens to be more homey than one might think at first glance. Inside, the lofted king bedroom is spacious and comfy, the kitchenette is stocked with all you might need for a long weekend, and kid-friendly amenities are at your ready, from a pack-and-play to a portable high chair. That said, it’s best for one or two, or a couple traveling with a little one, since there aren’t full walls between the sleeping area.

Embrace the outdoors as much as you can here: According to previous guests, this barn puts you in a prime spot for stargazing around the firepit, jumping in the glittering Flathead Lake, and taking advantage of Glacier National Park—only 30 minutes away.

City: Kalispell, MontanaThings to do nearby: Glacier National Park, Conrad Mansion Museum, Flathead Lake, Wild Horse Island

#6187. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

#6186. What to Pack for a Stay at the Hotel Sacher, Vienna’s Grandest Grand Dame

This grande dame has long held the title of society hot spot: Everyone from King Charles to Grace Kelly has passed through its damask suites. In honor of its 150th anniversary, however, Hotel Sacher Vienna is celebrating its rich tradition of fostering the arts by commissioning Austrian artist Erwin Wurm to create two surreal anthropomorphic sculptures of bright pink handbags to flank its doors. Earlier this year American artist Kaws also designed a limited edition box for its famed Sacher torte cake, as did tastemaker Aerin Lauder on another occasion, adorning hers with golden flowers inspired by Viennese decorative arts. Join the festivities by channeling the aesthetics of former regular Gustave Klimt—think jewel tones and sequins that will shimmer below the chandeliers of the ruby-red Rote Bar.

#6185. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6184. Air India Cuts Up To Five Hours From New York Flights By Flying Over Iraq

Air India has eliminated fuel stops in Rome on its flights from Delhi and Mumbai to New York, cutting some journeys by five hours. The surprising key to restoring nonstop service was not Russian airspace, but the reopening of a shorter corridor over Iraq.

Air India has restored nonstop service on all four of its routes linking Delhi and Mumbai with New York JFK and Newark.

Flights that had taken approximately 22 hours with a technical stop in Rome are once again operating in about 17 hours.

The Delhi flights are operated with Airbus A350-900 aircraft featuring business class suites, premium economy, and economy class. The Mumbai routes use refurbished Boeing 777-300ERs with first class, business class, premium economy, and economy class.

Removing five hours from an already very long journey represents the difference between a difficult nonstop flight and a 22-hour saga involving an annoying fuel stop.

Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian-operated aircraft, eliminating the most direct westbound corridor from India toward Europe and North America.

The conflict involving Iran then created further restrictions across the Middle East. Air India was forced to operate a much longer route through Jordan and Egypt before continuing across Europe and the Atlantic. That routing pushed the limits of what the aircraft could operate with a commercially useful payload. Air India consequently added a technical stop in Rome to refuel before continuing to New York.

The reopening of Iraqi airspace changed the calculation. Air India can now fly a shorter route across Iraq and Turkey before continuing through Europe and across the Atlantic.

The airline says this has reduced total journey time by as much as five hours. Additionally, the shorter route will reduce fuel consumption by approximately 10% and also ease crew scheduling pressures associated with flight-duty limits. Considering the cost of operating a fully loaded Airbus A350 or Boeing 777 for several additional hours, this is a substantial operational improvement for Air India as well as a welcome one for passengers.

Air India remains permitted to use Russian airspace and has done so on certain North American routes, particularly services connecting India with the West Coast of the United States.

That has given Air India an advantage over U.S. and European airlines that avoid or are prohibited from using Russian airspace. But it would be incorrect to assume that Air India routinely flies over Russia when traveling between India and New York.

The available flight-tracking data suggests otherwise.

Recorded routes displayed by FlightPaths.com for Delhi–JFK show no use of Russian airspace in its sample of 20 flights. Among seven recorded Mumbai–JFK flights, just one crossed Russia. The pattern is even clearer in the opposite direction. Russia did not appear in the displayed samples of 20 JFK–Delhi flights or 10 JFK–Mumbai flights.

(Those samples are not a comprehensive record of every Air India flight, and routings can change based on winds, restrictions, and operational requirements. But they demonstrate that Russian airspace is not the normal solution for Air India’s New York service).

These flights generally travel westward through the Middle East and Europe, which why access to Iraqi airspace has such a large effect.

Air India has restored nonstop flights from Delhi and Mumbai to New York JFK and Newark, cutting journey times by as much as five hours.

The change was made possible by renewed access to Iraqi airspace, not by shifting these flights over Russia. Although Air India uses Russian airspace on some routes, flight-tracking data indicates that it is not routinely used for New York service.

A 17-hour flight remains very long, but it is much better than a 22-hour journey with an unwanted fuel stop in Rome. For passengers traveling between India and the New York area, this is a genuine and substantial improvement…and ironically might allow Air India to charge a higher premium for its nonstop service, despite the fuel and labor savings this shorter flight time will produce.

#6183. Planning a Nashville Bachelorette? These Airbnbs Offer Rooftop Views, Hot Tubs, and Beauty Bars

There’s a reason Nashville is known as the bachelorette capital of the world, and it has everything to do with the city’s Southern charm, group-friendly accommodations, and choose-your-own-adventure approach towards night life. No two bachelorette parties are the same, and Nashville gets that more than most cities, where a mix of high-energy Honky Tonks, crave-worthy restaurants, and quaint shopping streets round out its nightly lineup of live music across the city. There are even customizable tours for bachelorettes that celebrate the city’s biggest claims to fame (ahem, Taylor Swift, whiskey, and hot chicken).

Nashville just does bachelorettes right, especially when it comes to places to stay. There’s an Airbnb in Nashville for every group size and vibe, from a spacious loft just off Broadway to a storybook cottage in the trendy 12 South neighborhood. Plus, many of Nashville’s Airbnbs were designed specifically with bachelorette parties in mind, offering spacious rooftops, beauty bars, and plenty of party decor. Read on for 12 of the best Airbnbs in Nashville for a bachelorette trip.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, willingness to host bachelorette groups, and decor.

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, infrared sauna, firepits, outdoor TV, karaoke

This four-level condo is just across the Cumberland River and a 10-minute drive from Nashville’s best bars and restaurants. Each floor is a new adventure, with a dive-bar lounge and karaoke stage on the bottom level, and a vibey rooftop with an outdoor kitchen and a private hot tub on top. There’s even an infrared sauna with a Bluetooth speaker somewhere in between. No fighting over where to sleep here, either, since there are 11 comfy beds to choose from across the four floors.

Neighborhood: Trinity HillsThings to do nearby: Nissan Stadium, Grand Ole Opry, Germantown

In my humble opinion, the best bachelorette parties are a balance of memorable experiences and total relaxation. This City Heights rental nails the combination: There are plenty of spaces for chilling out, like in front of the rose wall or on the private rooftop with gas firepits. The location is pretty great, too—the heart of Broadway is only a short Uber ride from this West Nashville Airbnb. Previous guests rave about the host and his response time, but also about the cute coffee shop just across the street, and the endless photo opportunities inside this thoughtfully decorated home.

Neighborhood: Charlotte CorridorThings to do nearby: Centennial Park, Parthenon, Taylor Swift’s Bench, Broadway

Within walking distance to Broadway and some of downtown Nashville’s top bars, like Tootsie’s and the Twelve Thirty Club, this perfectly pink crash pad comes with all the condo perks. There’s a social lounge, a heated courtyard pool with firepits and grills, and even a gym. The details are everything inside this two-bedroom condo, where the pink glasses match the pink slushy machine and the pink pots and pans, cloud sofa bed, shot glasses, utensils, and more. Sensing a theme? For an additional fee, the host will happily add on some festive decor or local beauty services, if desired.

#6182. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

#6181. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6180. Guide: United Airlines Has Starlink On More Than Half Its Flights, But These Aircraft Offer The Best Odds

United Airlines has reached an impressive milestone: Starlink is now available on more than half of its daily flights. I increasingly choose United when I know Starlink will be onboard, but customers generally cannot determine that when booking. Here is what United should change and which aircraft currently offer your best chance of getting Starlink.

United announced last week that Starlink had crossed the 50% threshold across its daily schedule. The airline expects that number to approach 64% by the end of 2026 and plans to complete fleetwide installations by the end of 2027.

That is an extraordinarily fast rollout for an airline with more than 1,000 mainline aircraft plus a large regional fleet.

The announcement was packaged around Thanksgiving travel, with United expecting to carry more than 6.6 million passengers between November 19 and December 1. But the more consequential development is that Starlink is no longer a novelty you might encounter on a regional jet. Instead, it is becoming a defining part of the United experience.

I have used just about every major inflight internet system, and Starlink is clearly the best.

The connection is fast, latency is low, and it works well enough that I can complete almost everything onboard that I would ordinarily do from my office. Large files load quickly, video calls are possible (but thankfully not allowed on United), and the service supports multiple devices. It is also free for MileagePlus members.

If two departures are similarly priced and one has Starlink, I will choose the Starlink flight. I may even accept a slightly less convenient departure time because several productive hours in the air are worth far more to me than leaving an hour earlier.

That is precisely the sort of customer behavior United wants. Scott Kirby has repeatedly suggested that Starlink will persuade customers loyal to other airlines to try United, after which the rest of the experience will convince them to stay.

I understand his confidence. Once you experience internet that works almost like it does on the ground, returning to a slow or unreliable connection is painful.

Here is the problem: United generally does not confirm Starlink availability until three days before departure.

The airline offers a useful Starlink tracker, but it is designed to check an upcoming flight rather than help someone choose among flights several weeks or months in advance. By the time the tracker confirms the aircraft, most passengers have already purchased their tickets.

Aircraft substitutions will always occur, and no airline can guarantee that a particular tail number will operate a flight. But that does not prevent United from displaying the expected connectivity during booking.

United already identifies many onboard features in the reservation process. It could add a Starlink indicator based on the scheduled aircraft, accompanied by a clear disclaimer that equipment may change. Even an imperfect forecast would be useful.

United carefully says Starlink is available on more than half of its daily flights, which is not the same as saying more than half of its aircraft or passenger seats have Starlink. Regional jets and narrowbody aircraft generally operate more flights per day than widebody aircraft, allowing each installation to influence a larger number of departures.

United’s entire two-cabin regional fleet now has Starlink. If you want the best chance of getting it, book a flight operated by a Bombardier CRJ-550 or Embraer E175.

If you are traveling on a mainline aircraft, the Airbus A321neo is most likely to have Starlink, with 88% of that fleet equipped. The Boeing 737-800 follows at 77%, while 67% of the Boeing 737-900 fleet has it.

Avoid the Airbus A319, Airbus A320, and Boeing 757-300 if connectivity is important to you. None currently have Starlink, and the aging Panasonic systems installed on some of those aircraft are most likely not to work at all.

Personally, I avoid 757-300s and go out of my way to fly on A321neos. You should too if onboard connectivity is important to you.

Progress on the widebody fleet remains slow. Only 2% of United’s Boeing 787 fleet and 5% of its Boeing 777 fleet currently have Starlink, while none of its Boeing 767s are equipped.

Delta Air Lines has selected Amazon Leo for its next-generation internet, with installations scheduled to begin in 2028. As I discussed yesterday, a rocket failure that destroyed 40 Amazon satellites illustrates the risk of selecting a network that is still being constructed.

Delta already offers free Wi-Fi on most of its fleet, and I have found it perfectly usable on many flights. This is not a choice between internet and no internet. But in terms of functionality, Starlink is better. It is not even a contest.

United may complete its fleetwide rollout before Delta installs Amazon Leo on its first aircraft. That gives United time to turn a technical advantage into a behavioral one: customers try Starlink, discover they can be more productive in the air, and begin considering connectivity when selecting future flights.

That is why displaying Starlink during booking would be valuable. If the product is strong enough to influence purchasing decisions, United should make it easier for customers to find before purchasing.

It would also help reduce disappointments. I was recently on a Boeing 777-200 with old-school Panasonic Wi-Fi, and a business class passenger across the aisle from me was fuming that there was no Starlink. Better to underpromise and overdeliver than the other way around.

Starlink is now available on more than half of United Airlines flights and should reach nearly 64% by the end of the year. That is impressive progress and gives United a genuine advantage over its domestic competitors.

I increasingly choose flights based on whether Starlink will be onboard. The frustration is that United generally cannot confirm it until three days before departure, long after the booking decision has been made.

A Starlink indicator during booking would not need to be a guarantee. It could simply tell customers what United reasonably expects to offer. In the meantime, regional jets, Airbus A321neos, and Boeing 737-800s give you the best shot at Starlink on United.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.
