#6179. The Best Airbnbs in Amsterdam, From Canal Houses to a Boat on the Amstel River

Amsterdam today looks remarkably similar to how it did on my first visit as a high schooler over a decade ago, with its maze of canals, steady flow of bikes, and gabled façades—many of which have stood there since the 17th century. To a history-loving teenager visiting Europe for the first time, the Dutch capital was a wonderland of Van Goghs. It felt so different from my hometown, yet still approachable, and sparked my lifelong love of travel.

What has changed since then is the crowds. Amsterdam is now one of Europe's most visited cities, so you'll need to book tickets to the major sites well in advance, especially during summer. The same goes for accommodations. On more than a dozen return trips (many by train from Belgium, where I used to live), I have stayed everywhere from youth hostels to boutique hotels to Airbnbs. And over the years, I've learned that renting an Airbnb offers a completely different way to experience the city.

Whether you're looking for a classic canal house in the Jordaan, a design-forward houseboat along the Amstel, or a multi-level family home near Vondelpark, the rentals on this list can help you settle into the city in your own way. Read on for a few of my favorite Airbnbs in Amsterdam, whether you're here for the art, the nightlife, or to explore by bike.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canalside location, separate kitchen, quiet street

Couples or small families who want to stay in the heart of old Amsterdam will adore this renovated one-bedroom inside a historic canal house on one of the city's widest canals. The roughly 650-square-foot space sleeps up to three, and the separate kitchen has a large dining table. Step outside and you're around the corner from lively Nieuwmarkt, where cafés line the market square. Or, check out the dim sum spots in nearby Chinatown. Despite the proximity to so much activity, previous guests say the street itself stays peaceful at night. Just be prepared to haul your luggage up a steep staircase, as is expected for most Amsterdam buildings.

Neighborhood: Centrum (Nieuwmarkt)Things to do nearby: Rembrandt House Museum, De Oude Kerk

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private garden, dedicated playroom, fireplace

As in most big European cities, space is at a premium in Amsterdam, which makes this industrial-style town house a real find for families. It even has a dedicated playroom packed with toys and books. It sits in Oud-West, a grid-like neighborhood just outside the central canal ring, steps from the daily Ten Kate Market. When the weather cooperates, fire up the Weber grill in the private garden out back. Inside, a gas fireplace warms the light-filled living room and kitchen. But you may not find yourself cooking much, since the home's location puts you right near the Foodhallen. Three bedrooms sleep up to four, with a king bed, a double bed, and a toddler bed.

Neighborhood: Oud-WestThings to do nearby: Foodhallen, Ten Kate Market, Vondelpark

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Heated pool, private garden, Nintendo Wii

Groups who want to dip in and out of city life should take a look at this detached four-bedroom house in a tranquil, residential corner of Amsterdam Noord. The nearby metro reaches Central Station in about five minutes (or you can bike there in 15), and the countryside is close by too. The highlight, however, is the large private garden, where you'll find a heated pool (open roughly April through October) and a sauna. There's also a grill and space to dine outdoors. During the colder months, your crew will probably prefer curling up on the cozy couch for a movie or a round of games on the Nintendo Wii. Practical perks include a washer and dryer, a dedicated workspace, and four bedrooms.

Neighborhood: Amsterdam NoordThings to do nearby: Eye Filmmuseum, A'DAM Lookout, NDSM Wharf

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: King-size bed, canal views, amenities for kids

If your image of the perfect trip to Amsterdam includes staying in an authentic canal house, then consider this character-filled apartment in the leafy Jordaan neighborhood. Guests enter through the roomy breakfast area on the ground floor, and upstairs, you'll find a living area filled with plush furniture, jewel-toned accents, and views of the canal, Anne Frank House, and Westerkerk (Western Church). There's one true bedroom with a king bed and a pull-out couch in the living room. The hosts, who warmly welcome families with little ones, provide lots of kid-friendly necessities, like a high chair.

Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: The 9 Streets, Anne Frank House, Dam Square

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Piano, record player with vinyl collection, fireplace

If you're looking to house a group, this rental might be the perfect fit. The three bedrooms (a king, a double, and a single) and one-and-a-half bathrooms are scattered across multiple floors. Gather in the dining area (there's also a full kitchen) or around the fireplace in the cozy living room stocked with board games, a vinyl collection, and even a piano. Stained-glass windows and art-covered walls are fitting for the prime location near the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh Museum. However, be prepared to carry your luggage up some steep and narrow steps.

Neighborhood: VondelparkThings to do nearby: Stedelijk Museum, Van Gogh Museum, Rijksmuseum

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Air-conditioning, sparkling water on tap, large garden patio

This spacious luxury apartment in a historic building offers some perks that can be hard to come by in Amsterdam: air-conditioning (in the living room and one bedroom), no stairs to climb, sparkling water on tap, and a living room that opens onto a garden patio with a lovely view of the Rijksmuseum. Families with small kids can also request a travel crib, high chair, and other gear. Plus, there isn't much for little hands to grab onto thanks to the minimalist decor. The two bedrooms each feature plush king beds.

Neighborhood: MuseumpleinThings to do nearby: Stedelijk Museum, Van Gogh Museum, Rijksmuseum

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fitness equipment, chef's kitchen, dedicated workspace with printer

Want to feel really at home for an extended stay? Save this open-plan loft housed inside a converted 19th-century police station, which stands out with a dedicated workspace (desk, monitor, printer) and fitness equipment (kettlebells, dumbbells, rowing machine). There's also a chef's kitchen and an Art Deco–style bathroom. It’s wonderful for those looking to take a step back from the hustle and bustle—not the best pick for all-night partiers. The living space blends modern and vintage flourishes, featuring French paintings that are part of the owner's personal art collection and front windows overlooking a canal. Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: Leidseplein, Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Amsterdam?

Book a stay in the Grachtengordel (canal ring) for the quintessential Amsterdam experience. The Jordaan has a similarly atmospheric feel with slightly quieter surroundings, while the Museum District puts the city's famous art museums right at your doorstep.

When is the best season to visit Amsterdam?

Spring is one of the best times to visit. It's when the city wakes up from the long winter and the Netherlands's colorful tulips burst into bloom (plan a day trip to the famous Keukenhof Gardens, about 40 minutes away). Come for King's Day on April 27, when the entire city turns bright orange with street parties and canal boat parades, or visit on the brink of summertime, in late May or June, and you'll enjoy much longer days, with daylight sometimes lasting past 9 p.m.

#6178. United CEO Still Keen on Merger Prospects

Months after American Airlines rejected his pitch for a merger, United CEO Scott Kirby remains convinced that U.S. carriers will have to consolidate to thrive.

“I think the biggest impediment is having a willing partner,” Kirby said at the Yahoo Finance Invest conference on Nov. 12. “I am more convinced today than I was when I wrote my note six months ago that it could get approval. It could get approval because it is good for customers.”

Kirby’s original pitch to American shocked the aviation industry, as it would have brought together two of the country’s largest commercial airlines and given the combined company a market share of just over 34%, a level of dominance not seen by any U.S. carrier in years. Analysts predicated that the Justice Department would reject the tie-up as anticompetitive, citing regulators’ decisions on much smaller attempted mergers over the past several years.

The speculation ended when American released a public statement saying it had no interest in a merger, and would stick to its existing turnaround plan.

But Kirby has continued to defend his proposal and the logic behind it, arguing that a consolidated United-American would deliver a better experience for customers, create more high-paying unionized jobs, and make the U.S. more competitive in international travel.

The CEO acknowledged Thursday that such a large deal would face obstacles but insisted they could be overcome.

“It wouldn’t be easy,” he said. “We’d have to do some divestitures, but I 100% think it could get approved.”

Airlines around the world are facing new pressure to cut costs or consolidate as jet fuel prices rise. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in April that he believes there is “room for some mergers” in the airline industry, but did not mention United or American by name.

Neither the Justice Department nor the Transportation Department ever formally weighed in on the potential United-American merger, as a final deal was never filed. President Donald Trump said he would not support it, and cited competition and consumer prices as the reason.

#6177. Lufthansa Unveils Spacious Business Class Seats And Starlink For Select A320 Flights

Lufthansa is finally adding proper business class recliners to a small portion of its Airbus A320 fleet. The new seats will cost extra, even for passengers already booked in business class, but I welcome the option. After years of selling an economy seat with a blocked middle as business class, this is an upgrade worth getting excited about. It is a welcome change for an airline more accustomed to following competitors than setting the standard.

Lufthansa has opened bookings for its new “Premium Business Seat,” which will initially be installed on six Airbus A320ceo aircraft.

Each aircraft will receive eight recliners in the first two rows, arranged 2-2. Features include:

The six aircraft will also receive Starlink Wi-Fi during the retrofit.

These are recliners rather than flat beds, but they will represent a substantial improvement over the standard European business class seat, particularly on longer flights, which for those unaware is simply a regular economy class seat with the adjacent seat blocked.

The first modified aircraft is scheduled to enter service on December 16, 2026, initially operating various routes.

Dedicated deployment begins in February 2027, with seat reservations now available for flights from March 1, 2027:

Look for the Premium Business Seat designation when booking:

Lufthansa is retaining its standard business class offering behind the recliners. Business class passengers can select the larger seat during booking or subsequently through seat reservations, subject to the buy-up price: buying business class will not automatically get you a business class recliner on these routes.

I can already hear the objections: passengers are paying a premium for business class and then being asked to pay again for a better seat. But this is quite different than what intra-Europe business class has been for as long as I can remember on Lufthansa (except for the old A300s) and I would still rather have this option than continue with the blocked-middle arrangement as the only choice.

Lufthansa calls this a “commercial test.” Demand and the response to its booking options will determine whether the concept expands, but I think this concept is going to do great.

I wrote about the Eurowings Premium BIZ concept when it was announced last year. It was rather amusing that the budget carrier would introduce proper narrowbody business class seating before its “full service” Lufthansa Group siblings.

That project was intended to test the concept for other airlines within the group. Now we are seeing a similar approach at Lufthansa itself. The conventional European model has an operational advantage: airlines can move the curtain to adjust the size of business class. Dedicated recliners make that space less flexible.

Installing a small permanent cabin while retaining conventional business class behind it strikes me as a reasonable compromise. Lufthansa can sell the larger seats to passengers willing to pay for them and still expand the rest of business class when demand warrants. I would particularly like to see this spread to longer routes across the group. An empty middle seat is welcome, but it becomes a rather thin comfort proposition when you are spending several hours onboard, especially with those uncomfortable Recaro slimline seats.

One Mile At A Time suggests that Air France should introduce proper business class seats throughout its Airbus A220 fleet. I love that idea…SWISS should do the same.

The A220 offers an especially compelling opportunity because its economy cabin is arranged 2-3. With adjacent seats blocked in business class, Air France sells only three seats per row.

A proper 2-2 business class cabin would allow it to sell four seats across while giving passengers a wider seat. Additional legroom would consume more cabin length, of course, so the calculation is not quite as simple as adding another paying passenger in every existing row, but I think the math would work.

For illustration, replacing three conventional business class rows with two recliner rows would reduce capacity from nine passengers to eight. That is a modest reduction in exchange for a much better product, though the actual economics would depend on the seat dimensions and final layout.

I have already experienced what this could look like on my Bulgaria Air A220-300 flight from Sofia to Amsterdam. The airline offered proper recliners in a 2-2 layout, with leg rests and power outlets. I found it an excellent way to spend three hours flying within Europe.

Air France and SWISS have invested heavily in its premium reputation. A small recliner cabin on the A220 would extend that investment to the European flights that often begin or end a longhaul business class journey.

We do not need a flat bed from Paris to Amsterdam or Zurich to London, but on longer European routes, a comfortable recliner would give me another reason to choose one carrier over another.

Lufthansa will install eight Premium Business Seats on each of six Airbus A320s, with bookings now open for select Frankfurt flights to Athens, Nice, and Cairo from March 2027.

The surcharge will bother some passengers, understandably, but I think it makes sense and am pleased to see Lufthansa offer a better seat and hope the test succeeds.

Eurowings demonstrated a willingness to try something different. Lufthansa is following. Perhaps Air France, SWISS, and others will see an opportunity too. European business class has room to improve, and a seat that is actually different from economy is a very good place to start.

#6176. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#6175. The Best Aluminum Luggage for Travelers, From Iconic Rimowa Suitcases to Sleek Tumi Trunks

The first time I traveled with an aluminum suitcase, I emerged into the airport with a whole new energy. There’s an undeniable allure to rolling through a terminal with a gleaming statement piece, shimmering as it does against a sea of boring black suitcases. There’s no way to travel more smugly.

Commerce writer Charley Ward testing Rimowa's iconic aluminum carry-on in Mallorca

But while the style is an undeniable draw, beyond the immediate hit of glamour, aluminum luggage offers some practical perks too. It offers greater structural protection than polycarbonate and soft-shell options—you can’t really argue with that, given it’s the type of material they make planes out of. And these durable suitcases are typically fitted with secure latch locking mechanisms over temperamental zippers, with steel corners and frames designed to comfortably absorb bumps, drops, and scrapes on the go.

Investing in high-end aluminum luggage is a serious price commitment—especially when considering that there are plenty of excellent soft-sided and hard-shell suitcases on the market. It’s why putting these more expensive suitcases through their paces in real-world scenarios is essential for our testing.

Our editors and contributors took the market's leading aluminum suitcases with us near and far, from long weekends in Milan and Mallorca to extended three-week international journeys, considering wheel smoothness, internal compression systems, weight-to-capacity ratios, and overall durability. Below, the select few of our editors’ favorite aluminum suitcase to travel with for every type of trip.

Carl Friedrik has built a cult following across the globe for its elevated, leather-trimmed luggage. Its venture into all-aluminum suitcases is nothing short of exceptional, with all the same careful design details we know and love from its original Carry-On. This new iteration retains the brand’s signature understated ridged design, super-secure dual lock (no zips to bust here), steel-reinforced corners, leather detailing, and smooth, 360-degree spinner wheels.

I packed comfortably for three nights in Milan and Paris: a couple of outfit changes, pajamas, gym clothes, a toiletry bag, and a spare pair of shoes. For warmer destinations where you'd prioritize packing lighter fabrics, you could likely stretch this to four or five- days’ worth of clothing. I also lent the suitcase to a colleague for a trip to Lisbon, who managed five-days’ worth of packing with ease—and said she could have got in more. Ultimately, capacity will depend on how heavy a packer you are, but it’s ideal for a long weekend during the winter at minimum.

Dimensions: 9" x 15" x 21.7"Weight: 10.8 lb.Capacity: 41LWarranty: Lifetime guarantee

Rimowa remains the gold standard for luxury travel gear, and its Classic Cabin carry-on is possibly the most famous suitcase on the planet. It combines high-grade anodized aluminum with high-gloss aluminum corners and that iconic ridged design, offering timeless heritage design and equally great functionality for short getaways. I took this suitcase on a long weekend to Mallorca and immediately understood the hype. Simply put, I’ve never felt so glamorous in an airport—it has that ability to make you feel put together even when you’re sprinting through the terminal; and when you’re a frequent traveler who’s often dipping in and out of airports at odd hours, it’s these little things that really count.

I couldn’t stop looking at it. While the aesthetics are the real draw here, this hard-shell aluminum carry-on doesn’t scrimp on technical details, gliding smoothly across airport floors and cobbled streets alike, thanks to buttery-smooth wheels and a sturdy handle. Inside, everything stayed neatly in place thanks to the clever compression system, and it was easy to get closed, despite my notorious overpacking tendencies. Any Rimowa suitcase is an investment, yes, but one that delivers on both style and substance.

What are the benefits of aluminum luggage?

Aluminum luggage offers superior durability and protection compared to fabric or plastic alternatives. Its rigid, crush-proof shell and heavy-duty frame safeguard fragile contents against rough handling and impact during transit. Aluminum suitcases come finished with latches instead of vulnerable zippers, creating an airtight, water-resistant seal that deters theft. Aluminum is built to last a lifetime, developing a distinctive, travel-worn patina over time rather than tearing or cracking. Then there’s that effortlessly sleek aesthetic at the airport, which is another fun perk.

Our editors have personally tested a wide range of bags from leading luggage brands, carefully selecting their favorites based on function, innovation, and design. Each suitcase was thoroughly tested in-office by our editors before being taken on trips by members of the wider team for real-world use. During testing, we assess overall build quality, wheel performance, TSA-approved locks, design features such as external pockets and laptop compartments, and overall value. Weight, size, usability, and visual appeal are also carefully considered.

#6174. Trump Blames Buttigieg For FAA Meltdown While Elon Musk Blames Sean Duffy

President Donald Trump blames Pete Buttigieg for the nationwide FAA meltdown. Elon Musk, meanwhile, is pointing at the tTransportation Secretary Trump appointed, claiming Sean Duffy rejected an offer of free Starlink service. The finger-pointing continues, but neither accusation tells stranded passengers exactly why a router installation brought the system down.

Speaking to reporters on November 16, Trump singled out his predecessor’s transportation secretary for the failure that halted departures across the United States:

“Buttigieg ruined the system. He totally ruined it.”

When asked what personal responsibility he accepted, Trump responded:

He also praised Duffy and attributed the disruption to aging equipment. I have already addressed the problem with blaming the previous administration. America’s air traffic control infrastructure has suffered from decades of deferred investment. That includes the Biden administration, but also Trump’s first term and the administrations before it.

Friday’s failure, however, occurred during work performed under the current administration. An explanation of what Buttigieg allegedly did wrong would be useful, but of course Buttigieg is just the whipping boy for an administration that shows no personal responsibly for any of its deleterious actions.

Musk has offered a different accusation. In a post on X, he wrote:

“Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were.”

Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were. https://t.co/OZwDeiXOAr

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 16, 2026

That is a pointed criticism of the same official Trump says handled the situation well, but Musk does not explain when the offer was made, what equipment or service was included, where it would have been deployed, or how it would have prevented this particular failure…what a surprise.

I would like Duffy to answer the allegation directly. Was there an offer? What did it cover? Why was it declined? If the proposal was unsuitable, explain why.

Musk should also substantiate his assertion that the service would have been needed here. Being able to offer satellite internet does not establish that his proposed “gift” would have kept this particular network operating.

I love Starlink as an airline passenger. It is easily the best inflight internet service available now, and it increasingly influences which flights I book. But that does not mean it is or would have been a solution to an air traffic control network failure.

According to the FAA’s explanation, excessive connection attempts flooded its telecommunications network, destabilizing aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in El Dorado, Arkansas, and Amarillo, Texas. L3Harris had been working at El Dorado, including installing a new router. Blocking those locations apparently stabilized the network. The broadcasting function on the new routers was also disabled as a precaution.

To support Musk’s claim, we would need to know whether his proposed Starlink connections would have bypassed the affected equipment and preserved the necessary communications.  Perhaps Starlink could have provided useful redundancy…but maybe the proposed installation would have had no bearing on this failure.

Buttigieg has defended his record, pointing to improvements in controller staffing, runway safety, and flight cancellations during his tenure.

He also says he launched the communications modernization project that the current administration is continuing. His response asks for an accounting of the money already authorized and an explanation of why the execution of that work triggered such a widespread failure.

As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived. We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in… https://t.co/68KleIhFEc

— Pete Buttigieg (@PeteButtigieg) November 16, 2026

They do not mean Buttigieg’s tenure should escape scrutiny. The January 2023 nationwide ground stop occurred on his watch, and the system still required enormous investment when he left office while his boss prioritized student loan forgiveness and federal mask mandates instead of accelerating infrastructure programs like Air Traffic Control modernization.

But acknowledging those shortcomings does not relieve the current administration of responsibility for its own decisions. Duffy has been Transportation Secretary for nearly two years. He oversees the department responsible for explaining this failure and should be held accountable for the actions under his watch.

There is an obvious temptation to enjoy the spectacle: Trump blames Buttigieg while Musk suggests Trump’s own transportation secretary rejected help. I find the contradiction revealing, but passengers deserve something more useful than competing accusations.

The investigation must establish what changed in the network, why that change caused such a widespread disruption, and whether the safeguards surrounding the work were adequate. Congress should examine the Starlink allegation too, if Musk can provide a concrete proposal and evidence supporting his account.

Duffy may have had reasonable grounds to decline whatever Musk offered, but he should be able to articulate them. Likewise, Musk may have identified a missed opportunity, but he should be able to demonstrate his rather glaring accusation.

And Trump should stop treating an investigation as unnecessary because he has already identified a political opponent to blame. The age of the equipment was known. The difficult task was upgrading it while maintaining reliable service. That is the work his administration undertook, and that is the work it must explain to a weary public.

Trump says Buttigieg ruined the system and accepts no personal responsibility. Musk says Duffy rejected free Starlink service that was needed. Both claims deserve scrutiny and neither establishes the technical cause of Friday’s meltdown.

I would be far more receptive to an administration that acknowledged a failure during a difficult modernization project and explained how it would improve the process. Instead, we keep receiving accusations, praise for the response, and demands for more money.

The passengers who lost days getting home deserve a candid explanation of what went wrong. So do the taxpayers being asked to fund the repair. Is this really a political issue that should divide us?

Situated halfway between San Francisco and the Oregon border, California's Mendocino Coast has managed to remain a relatively hidden gem, of sorts. While it's certainly not a secret, its remote location has kept it from getting overrun with tourists — but new direct flights and millions of dollars in roadwork funding are making it more accessible than ever. And that's just one reason the coastal town of Mendocino made our list of top destinations to visit in 2027.

Nestled between rugged cliffs, redwood forests and rich wine terroirs, Mendocino has it all. No matter what you get up to out here — and there’s more to do than you might expect — it’s virtually impossible not to feel your blood pressure drop. The area’s relaxed pace of life is infectious, and during a recent two-day trip, this type-A traveler found herself hopping on the slow travel train.

From how to get there and where to stay to the best things to do and eat, here’s how to spend a long weekend (or longer!) on the Mendocino Coast. I dare you not to fall in love.

Travelers have several airports to choose from when flying to Mendocino.

The closest, albeit smallest, option is Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (STS), which puts you only a two-to-three-hour drive from Mendocino. Alaska Airlines, Delta and Southwest have all launched new routes to STS this year from Austin, Phoenix, Salt Lake City and more.

You’ll have more options if you fly into San Francisco International Airport (SFO), Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) or Sacramento International Airport (SAC). All are roughly the same distance from Mendocino — three to four hours depending on traffic — and offer plenty of direct flights from around the country through various airlines. A local I spoke to recommended SAC, saying that the drive is less stressful because it doesn’t go through a city.

No matter where your flight lands, you’ll need to rent a car. The drive can be tiring, especially as the roads get windier approaching the coast. Thankfully, there are plenty of wineries and cideries along the way where you can stop for a restroom break (and maybe a drink or two, if you’re not the driver).

One of the many facets of Mendocino’s appeal is the charming, walkable downtown — complete with views of Mendocino Bay.

You’ll find no shortage of souvenirs here, from bookshops and toy stores to clothing and home decor. Art lovers will enjoy perusing the handful of galleries. Coffeeshops, bakeries and chocolate shops abound, so you needn't worry about finding caffeine or snacks to sustain you during your wanderings.

If you wear jewelry (or are in the market for a unique gift that will fit in your suitcase), you won’t want to miss Mendocino Sandpiper, which offers a wide variety of work by local artists.

And that’s just the town of Mendocino. Its slightly larger neighbor, Fort Bragg, located about a 15-minute drive north along the coast, has even more boutiques to browse.

Related: 9 tertiary cities in the US that are both charming and affordable

You will need a car to get around the Mendocino Coast area, but you won’t have to spend much time in the car once you arrive. That’s because the area’s best outdoors activities are within easy reach of Mendocino and Fort Bragg.

The expansive Mendocino Coast Botanical Gardens were a highlight for me, and would probably be stunning in the spring and summer when most of the flowers are in bloom.

Mendocino Headlands State Park is literally steps from downtown, and there are several other state parks under 20 minutes away, including Jug Handle State Natural Reserve and Russian Gulch State Park. To commune with the area’s famous redwoods, head to Otis R. Johnson Wilderness Park, a glorious corner of green tucked away on the edge of Fort Bragg. Or head to MacKerricher State Park for a stroll along a black-sand beach and views of the aptly named Seal Rocks.

February to March is peak whale-watching season due to the gray whale migration, but this area gets visits from various whale species year-round, so keep your eyes peeled. I didn’t spot any whales, but I did see some seals and sea lions bobbing in the waves, as well as flocks of pelicans and other waterbirds.

You may also hear about a place called Glass Beach, which served as a community garbage dump at the beginning of the 20th century; over several decades, the waves tumbled some of the debris into colorful sea glass. Locals warned me that most of the glass is gone now, snatched up by tourists over the years. You’re better off going to the International Sea Glass Museum in Fort Bragg — with over 3,000 pieces on display, it boasts the world’s largest permanent sea glass exhibit.

Related: 7 warm-weather expedition cruises that will wow nature and adventure lovers

Both Mendocino and Fort Bragg have surprisingly varied food scenes, from the casual organic Good Life Cafe & Bakery and elevated all-vegan Fog Eater to the Irish-inspired Patterson’s Pub and Asian fusion Gnar Bar. And foodies won’t want to miss the local farmers’ markets, held on summer Fridays in Mendocino and Wednesdays year-round in Fort Bragg.

However, the main draws for foodies are, of course, the seafood — I heard Fort Bragg’s Sea Pals described as “the best fish ‘n’ chips outside of the U.K.” — and the thriving beverage scene.

Oenophiles will want to take the Highway 128 Wine Road to sample the fruits of the nearby Anderson Valley and Yorkville Highlands wine regions. But you’ll get plenty of opportunities to sample local wines in town as well. My hotel even offered a lobby wine machine where you can get wine samples with the press a button and tap of a keycard.

If wine isn’t your thing, don’t worry, there are plenty more local beverages to try. Gowan’s Cider Garden, which brews both alcoholic and non-alcoholic varieties, bills itself as California's first-ever cider tasting orchard. Meanwhile, the zero-waste, solar-powered North Coast Brewing Co. has been brewing unique beers (and winning awards for them) since 1988.

Related: The best credit cards for dining

The Mendocino Coast is also home to some fascinating history, and it has an array of museums and other attractions where visitors can learn more.

Fort Bragg’s Guest House Museum is a great starting point to learn about local history, from the logging industry to the Great 1906 Earthquake. Or visit during Labor Day weekend to experience lumberjack games at the annual Paul Bunyan Days festival.

If you have young travelers in tow, check out Fort Bragg’s Noyo Center for Marine Science, which offers interactive exhibits like tide pools and a full orca skeleton. Or climb to the top of a lighthouse and see a real Fresnel lens at either Point Cabrillo Light Station State Historic Park or the 156-year-old Point Arena Lighthouse.

Train enthusiasts won’t want to miss the historic Skunk Train, which started carrying timber in the late 1800s and now carries passengers through scenic redwood forests. While the train’s traditional 35-mile route has a reputation for jaw-dropping scenery, a tunnel collapse in recent years has shortened the route to a sliver of its former glory. However, I still enjoyed the nostalgic vibes of the Redwood Presidential Class, which made me feel like I had been dropped into one of my favorite Agatha Christie murder mysteries.

Related: The world's most scenic train rides

The Mendocino Coast has been leaning into slow and wellness travel, and for obvious reasons. With ancient redwoods on one side and windswept cliffs on the other — and blessedly few tourists crowding the trails — the landscape itself is therapeutic.

If you want something more structured, there are plenty of wellness activities if you know where to look. Many are offered by locals hotels but open to the public.

A few examples include yoga classes at Stanford Inn by the Sea, redwood hot tub and sauna sessions at Sweet Water Inn & Spa, sound healing in a geodesic dome at Mendocino Grove, and guided shinrin-yoku (forest bathing) walks at Brewery Gulch Inn & Spa.

Related: 9 wellness trends and where to experience them

Summer is Mendocino’s most popular season. It will also be the most expensive and busiest time to go — though I don’t expect the area to get too packed at any time of year, given its remoteness.

For adventure seekers looking to make the most of the area’s hiking, water sports and more, it’s probably worth planning your trip in summer for longer days and maximum sunshine. And with average highs topping out in the mid-70s Fahrenheit, Mendo could make a nice coolcation spot.

However, you can save money and all but guarantee a quiet vacation by traveling in the shoulder seasons from mid-October to November and April to early June. During these times, you can still expect warm enough weather for outdoor exploits, though temperatures will drop at night and more frequent rains may wash out hiking trails occasionally.

The hotel scene in Mendocino is characterized by quiet luxury. Its neighbor, Fort Bragg, has more variety and more budget-friendly options.

I spent three nights in the new Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino, a half-century-old property that was recently renovated before joining the Trailborn nature lodge collection and Marriott Bonvoy program. Other points options include Holiday Inn Express Fort Bragg by IHG and Baymont by Wyndham Fort Bragg.

If, like me, you love a good independent or boutique hotel, Mendocino is full of them. For instance, you could book a seaside cottage at Agate Cove Inn through Amex Travel or Capital One Travel, earning 5 points per dollar with your or 10 miles per dollar with your Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, respectively.

Or consider staying at SCP Mendocino Inn and Farm, a 19th-century manor turned B&B where guests can enjoy complimentary breakfast sourced from the onsite farm. Even better, you can redeem your points for more than 1 cent apiece via Chase Points Boost.

Overall, one of the things I loved most about the Mendocino Coast was its manageable size. From the downtown areas to the state parks, everything I visited was small but high-quality.

So instead of running around a city trying to cram in as much as possible, you can spend a leisurely weekend (or longer) exploring charming boutiques, quirky museums, local dining or natural wonders. You won’t run out of things to do, but the close proximity between attractions and “island time” mentality will help you savor the activities you choose.

That’s what slow travel is all about, right?

#6172. Inside the 2026 Condé Nast Traveler Points of View Summit

On November 12, our ninth annual Points of View Summit brought together trip designers, luxury planners, and on-the-ground experts in New York City for a day exploring the latest in travel. While unrelenting rain poured outside, the atmosphere inside was anything but dreary and gray.

Global editorial director Divia Thani kicked things off with opening remarks on big-picture trends: how American travelers are driving luxury travel; the transfer of wealth to a younger generation; and a shift from spending on products to lived experiences. These overarching themes gave the audience a preview of what would come later in the day on panels and in breakout sessions. From a talk about Hilton Head’s Gullah culture and a run-through of reasons to visit Morocco—yes, this bit was accompanied by a post-lunch tea ceremony—to an exchange on all-inclusives with Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and a sit-down unpacking food and memory with Antoni Porowski, the day was full of thoughtful exchanges that reminded us why we journey in the first place. After much applause, the summit concluded with a cocktail party featuring wines from San Miguel de Allende and a taste of Lowcountry South Carolina by way of shrimp, grits, and fried green tomatoes—there was lots to celebrate, with a decade of Hilton Head being on our Readers' Choice Awards and its Savannah/Hilton Head International Airport drawing visitors from all over. Below, explore all that went down at our 2026 Points of View Summit.

Our editors discuss next year's editorial coverage themes, including spotlight destinations and how we're tapping into pop culture.

The day kicked off with a roundtable over what’s been on our minds and what'll be on our editorial calendar next year, just in time for our 40th anniversary. Our features director Rebecca Misner led the conversation with Thani, global features director Erin Florio, global executive director of video Dana Kravis, senior features editor Megan Spurrell, and associate editor Charlie Hobbs, who all agreed that a demand for substantive, long-form storytelling is back (though did it ever truly leave?). Spurrell shared an early preview of the now-live Best Places to Go in 2027, including destinations like the Albanian Alps for hiking, Memphis for museum openings, Yunnan for a slew of new restaurants, and more. Kravis spoke about cross-platform stories such as our new video series Made In, exploring craft in a particular destination, and upcoming video iterations of series like On Location, which unpacks beloved film and show locations. On the topic of pop culture, Hobbs highlighted a continued focus on cultural happenings, sporting events, and festivals that we're keeping on our radar as reasons to travel. Ultimately, going into 2027, Florio said, our coverage will explore “what it is that drives us to travel, as opposed to where it is we want to go"—not only the destination for destination's sake, but the experiences and impulses underlying travelers' choices.

Eduardo Schutte and Madison Flager discuss the future of the all-inclusive stay and Hyatt's rapidly growing portfolio.

Next up, commerce director Madison Flager spoke with Eduardo Schutte, Hyatt Inclusive Collection’s commercial SVP, on how all-inclusive stays have evolved and expanded far beyond your typical beachside bubbles to meet globetrotters of all kinds. In an age of optimization, it's only natural that travelers would value the ease and confidence of a bundled vacation, with less time spent planning so that they can enjoy their destination sans stress. Schutte observed that Hyatt Inclusive Collection has grown from two properties in 2013 to over 120 today, with expansion well underway in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. “You're going to know exactly how much your vacation is, so it's much more predictable and easier to plan,” Schutte said. Afterwards, one lucky guest won a trip to a Hyatt Inclusive Resort. Perhaps the all-inclusive is a remedy for the times.

Erin Florio helms the conversation on summer travel, from increasing shoulder season trips to less crowded destinations.

We recently unpacked why it seems everyone took a fallcation this year, and spotlighted the year-round appeal of off-season Greece. Though the once-sweltering days of the summer months might be all you’re yearning for as winter fast approaches, increasingly unpredictable weather and overcrowded destinations are shifting and expanding the typical high season. Florio led this panel with Jack Ezon, founder and managing partner of Embark Beyond; Catherine Heald, CEO and founder of Remote Lands; Jade McBride, president of Ted Turner Reserves; Scott Jordan, vice president of sales–East at Delta Air Lines; and Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina.

To Ezon, it's less about the timing and more about the value of a trip; entry-level Mediterranean rooms can cost $4,000 to $6,000 per night, raising questions about whether the experience delivers value beyond price. Reframing a destination’s appeal beyond one season is key—going to Amalfi in October for wine or December for Christmas markets—as per Jordan, who stressed the value of meeting travelers where they're headed. He noted Delta is extending and adding seasonal service, including earlier flights to Porto and routes to Copenhagen, Sardinia, and Prague. Still, the group wondered whether greater access to Sardinia might relieve pressure on Amalfi and Como or simply congest another destination.

Zhang said her clients aren't choosing between European hotspots at all; they're set on Asia, the choice becoming whether to visit Japan or China. In 2025, China saw sweeping growth in international visitors, which Zhang credited to new visa policies, renewed country perceptions, and a global interest in regional lifestyles. “I just think that's part of wellness. It's drinking hot water, wearing slippers, playing mahjong, being social with family," she said. "A lot of these concepts are promoting China as a way of living, rather than as a destination.”

Katie Mathews and Omolola Campbell on Hilton Head Island's Gullah culture

For a chat presented by Hilton Head Island, senior creative producer Katie Mathews sat down with Omolola Campbell, executive producer of The Spirit We Move With, a short documentary about South Carolina's Gullah community. The Gullah people are the descendants of West Africans who were brought to the Carolinas, Georgia, and Florida, in the 1700s and 1800s for slavery. A sixth-gen Gullah descendant herself, Campbell spoke with Mathews on the importance of leading the narrative and memorializing these stories today. In South Carolina’s case, it’s about hearing from Gullah people themselves. Campbell uses her gift shop on the island, Binya, as a space for educating customers through handwoven sweetgrass baskets, cookbooks, prints, and more. “People say that storytelling is a way of preservation. I like to say conservation, because to preserve something is to put it on a shelf, [but] Gullah culture is still alive and thriving,” Campbell said.

In between panels, Mei Zhang and others tried Moroccan tea.

Hannah Towey and Ms. Siham Fettouhi discuss lesser-known Moroccan cities and itineraries.

After breakout sessions with editors and travel specialists, guests were served Moroccan tea before settling into a chat with news editor Hannah Towey and Ms. Siham Fettouhi, North America executive director of the Moroccan National Tourism Office. Beyond Marrakech and the desert, Fettouhi noted the country's appeal lies in its Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines and can't-miss surfing spots. "We're talking about a country that offers you the possibility to ski literally in the morning and enjoy sunset in the beach in the afternoon," Fettouhi said. “Morocco has never been this accessible from North America," she continued, mentioning nonstop flights now available from North America through Royal Air Maroc, Air Canada, Air Transat, Delta, and United. And domestic travel is also getting an update, as Morocco's high-speed rail network, Al Boraq, has extensions planned toward Marrakech and Agadir ahead of the 2030 World Cup.

An attendee captures Lale Arikoglu and Antoni Porowski's culinary conversation.

We closed out Points of View with a chat between Lale Arikoglu, director of special projects, and Antoni Porowski, Emmy-winning producer, Queer Eye veteran, and host of National Geographic's Best of the World series, which aired in June. While his other Nat Geo series No Taste Like Home traces family histories through food, this more recent show highlights the people behind well-known destinations' institutions and traditions—think a mustachioed clockmaker at Big Ben's Great Clock or a family-run cheese cave in Paris. “There’s always a beautiful nerd that’s behind this larger-than-life thing that millions of us have had a chance to experience,” Porowski said with a laugh, referencing folks not unlike himself, dedicated to that one experience and sharing it with others.

For Porowski, it's food that has offered a way to connect people with their roots and family histories, inspired in large part by his own journey toward embracing his Polish heritage. While planning a retirement trip for his dad several years ago, Porowski said his dad insisted they visit the Polish mountain village Zakopane. “We tried soups that I hadn't had since I was six or seven years old and got to connect through that,” he recalled. Porowski wrapped up the conversation with a handful of anecdotes from filming No Taste Like Home; a particular favorite was being in Senegal with Issa Rae, where he learned about teraanga, or the concept of generosity and sharing so integral to the West African country. Plus, the conversation would not have been complete without a rapid-fire round—see Porowski's answers below.

Delta does Shake Shack, which I’m not opposed to. I would say nine times out of 10—unless I’m sleeping and it's a red-eye—I’ll always have it, even if the chicken’s rubbery.

When the drinks cart goes by, what’s your go-to?

Chamomile tea, typically. This is so random, but it’s something I had as a child: sparkling water with a splash of apple juice. It feels really chic.

Because my parents taught me to arrive for a flight 10 minutes before it takes off when we lived in West Virginia, Jaeger Airport in Charleston, West Virginia. You can show up like 30 minutes before with checked luggage, and they will let you on.

Aisle, because I get to look at the flight attendants and see if they’re nervous during turbulence. But if they’re not, I know I’m fine.

There’s nothing more powerful than grabbing your carry-on.

Tomato bisque with a patty melt on sourdough focaccia from Il Buco Alimentari with sharp Vermont clothbound cheddar. That would be my appetizer, then puntarelle as my salad dish. For a main course, the shrimp from ABC Cocina—they have a lovely chili oil with lime zest and pink peppercorns—with again more bread to sop up all those oils. Since it’s my last meal, we’re doing surf and turf, scalloped potatoes, and a little broccoli rabe for fiber—no, I don’t care about fiber. For dessert, I was thinking about Campo de’ Fiori’s wild strawberries, with whipped cream and crème brûlée. I would finish it off with that Moroccan tea.

#6170. Are US Flight Schedules Returning to Normal? What Thanksgiving Travelers Need to Know

Travel chaos erupted at US airports over the weekend following a historic FAA ground stop that paused all flight takeoffs across the country for nearly five hours.

The ground stop, declared by the FAA amid air traffic control issues on Friday, November 13, stranded millions of fliers nationwide, with tens of thousands of flight delays and cancellations continuing for days. Now, with the busy Thanksgiving travel period fast approaching, travelers are wondering when US air travel system will return to normal.

Fortunately for travelers, both federal officials and airlines are doing everything they can to get flight schedules back on track and have airport operations running smoothly in time for the holiday rush. “Recovery to normal operations will be slow and steady,” says a November 15 statement from the FAA. “We ask for your patience as airlines work to get you to your destination.”

Although the incident is frustrating, experts say that travelers shouldn’t be concerned about the safety of the air traffic control system. “While the disruption was significant, travelers should take confidence in knowing that safety remained the top priority throughout the incident,” says Geoff Freeman, president and CEO of the US Travel Association. “Our aviation professionals deserve tremendous credit for managing the crisis and getting Americans safely back on their way."

If you have Thanksgiving travel plans and you're flying out this week, here's what to know about the current state of air travel in the US.

The ground stop was issued due to air traffic control equipment outages and issues with telecommunications systems that the FAA uses to track and communicate with planes while they’re flying. “The ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution,” says the FAA’s statement. “Safety is, and will always remain, the FAA’s highest priority. We will never compromise the safety of the flying public.”

On Friday afternoon, the FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was updating telecommunications equipment at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the issues began, according to the FAA. The company was deploying a new router that also began to cause system disruptions at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” says an FAA statement. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”

Once the inconsistencies were identified, the FAA says that L3Harris blocked those two locations, and the network stabilized. However, the exact cause of the telecommunications issues are still under investigation.

Regulators are still working to identify the root cause of the issue. “The work that was done on Friday, that's been done thousands of times by L3Harris in our network,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a Sunday interview on ABC’s “This Week.” “It's been done thousands of times by other companies, and these issues haven't arisen, and so that's why we have to figure out what went wrong here.”

Duffy also noted that the equipment in question is several decades old: the router was originally purchased in 2001 and was also part of a system that ran on obsolete copper wiring.

Experts say that the archaic equipment underscores the urgent need to update the nation’s air traffic control system. “While the investigation continues, the incident exposed a troubling reality: America's aviation system remains vulnerable because we have relied on aging infrastructure for far too long,” says Freeman. “Friday's disruption was a wake-up call that Washington cannot afford to ignore.”

Air travel experts say that the ground stop’s effects on Thanksgiving travel plans beginning later this week should be minimal.

As of Monday afternoon, the majority of airline flight schedules were back on track. There were still about 2,800 flight delays within, into, or out of the US on Monday, and nearly 330 flight cancellations, according to FlightAware data. It also helps that fewer travelers are expected to fly this year compared to recent years. According to Mike Arnot, spokesman for Cirium, an aviation analytics company, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is usually the busiest air travel day of the year. But in 2026, it’s not even slated to be in the top 50 busiest days for flying,

American Airlines, the largest carrier at DFW, said its operations were returning to normal on Monday. “American is prepared to operate a largely normal schedule Monday, Nov. 16, following the FAA's nationwide ground stop,” the carrier said in a statement. "With crews and aircraft in position and favorable weather expected across our system, we are set up for a good start to the week and do not anticipate additional broad cancellations related to this incredibly disruptive industry-wide event.”

Delta has also advised its passengers traveling on Monday to continue to allow extra time at the airport for any lingering effects on flight schedules. “While most flights are operating normally, some customers may still experience delays or cancellations,” the carrier said.

Travelers should still continue to check with their airline for the latest travel updates and plan to be at the airport at least two hours before takeoff for a domestic flight.

Operations are largely back on track, so many airlines have ended the flexible rebooking waivers that were issued at the beginning of the ground stop. However, two major carriers still have travel waivers in place.

Delta is still allowing passengers scheduled to fly through Monday, November 16, to make changes to their flights at no extra cost through November 23. Travelers’ new departure dates must be on or before November 23, according to the airline’s rebooking policy.

American Airlines is waiving change fees for passengers booked to travel to or from one of 21 major US airports through Wednesday, November 18. Passengers can choose a new travel date through November 21, but all changes must be made by November 18.

Even if your airline no longer has a travel waiver in place, if you’re flying with a major US carrier, you likely have the ability to change your flight without paying a fee (although a difference in fare may apply). However, these policies usually do not apply to low-cost carriers or tickets booked in basic economy class.

It’s impossible to predict if a nationwide ground stop could happen again, according to Freeman. However, modernizing the air traffic control system should reduce these types of outages over the long run.

“The FAA is making progress, replacing outdated copper communications lines with high-speed fiber, upgrading radar and radio systems, and introducing technology that allows air traffic controllers to manage flights more efficiently,” Freeman says. “For travelers, these investments should mean fewer delays, more reliable flights, and greater confidence that the system can handle disruptions.”

Airline executives echoed a similar sentiment regarding the state of US air traffic control systems. “This moment must be a call to action,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement emailed to media. “It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now.”

#6169. Review: Park Hyatt Vienna, My Favorite Hotel In The Austrian Capital

The Park Hyatt Vienna is not only my favorite hotels in Vienna, but one of my favorite Hyatt properties in the world. With excellent service, nice amenities, delicious breakfast, and central location, our latest stay was another great reminder of what a superb property this is.

Although we could have connected directly to Zürich after landing in Vienna, I was able to force a 23.5-hour layover into the itinerary, which gave us a chance to stay to the Park Hyatt Vienna, a hotel I’ve enjoyed many times over the years but it was the first time my children had come along.

I booked this for 35,000 World of Hyatt points (versus a cash rate of over €700) and applied a “Guest of Honor” to the reservation, which essentially marks me as “Globalist” in the system.

Our Austrian flight landed at 11:30 am into VIE and I had emailed the hotel requesting an early check-in, specifically noting that we would be happy to forgo an upgrade in order to access our room a few hours early. Our request was honored.

The Park Hyatt Vienna is ideally located on Am Hof in the heart of the old town, an easy walk from St. Stephen’s Cathedral and many of the places I most enjoy visiting in Vienna.

Checking in, I was welcomed back to the hotel and the amenities were explained, including breakfast and pool hours (most important to my kids!).

We were assigned room 331, a standard room with two twins beds. While not an upgrade, the room was spacious enough and quite comfortable with a desk, round table, chair, and the two beds.

My daughter jumped right into bed to go to sleep (it was, after all, about 3:15 am in Los Angeles), but I pulled her out: no napping today would hopefully mean no jet lag tomorrow.

The bathroom featured really beautiful stonework behind the bathtub and included two sinks, a separate water closet, and walk-in shower.

The room had a wardrobe that included a coffee machine, hot water kettle, and mini-bar including snacks and drinks.

A welcome amenity was also waiting for us including various chocolates and candies.

The room had plenty of 220-volt outlets and also a safe to lock valuables. Unfortunately, the room did not have any USB-C ports or wireless chargers.

A primary reason I booked this hotel was for the pool and wellness. My kids love to swim and I can’t think of a better hotel pool than this one: we spent a lot of time here in the afternoon and evening.

The entire pool and spa area is posh, with a full-range of treatments available but nice say chairs with fresh peaches and plums, a locker room, and a wellness area with a sauna and steam room available to all guests.

Side note: the hotel has a cryogenic machine in the spa that will let you stand in -110ºC temperatures for three minutes…I was tempted and probably would have tried it had I been alone.

Thankfully, there was no drama this time in the sauna!

> Read More: Accused Of Being A Child Predator at Park Hyatt Vienna!

The fitness center is located in the spa area on the lower level, but accessible 24/7 with your room card and includes TechnoGym equipment. I awoke an hour before the kids and went down to workout…a nice way to start the day and fight jet lag.

You mustn’t skip breakfast here, for it is truly a treat.

The Bank is the most beautiful part of the hotel: an ornate dining room that was once the grand lobby when this hotel was still a bank. Breakfast is served from 7:00 am each morning until 10:30 am (11:00 am on weekends) and includes a delicious buffet plus an additional a la carte menu. If breakfast isn’t clouded in your rate, it is €58 each, which while steep is really worthwhile considering all you get with it.

There’s a bar section in The Bank that includes alcohol, including a large cocktail menu, and lighter food. It’s open from 9:00 am to 1:00 am on Monday – Wednesday, till 2:00 am on Thursday – Saturday, and from 5:00 pm to 1:00 pm on Sunday (good luck finding anything open on Sunday in Vienna…).

The hotel’s Viennese café includes cakes, coffee and chocolates, as well as alcoholic drinks and snacks, with an outdoor terrace. Open each day from 9:00 am to 8:00 pm.

Open from 9:00 am to 6:00 pm daily, the Lounge offers a more informal dining experience where you can enjoy hot and cold drinks plus a variety of food. Menu here.

Finally, 24/7 room service is available. Menu here.

There used to be really posh cigar lounge in this hotel, but now it is a beauty salon (Vienna has banned indoor smoking after being a smoker’s haven for so many years).

Our entire say was marked by one pleasant service encounter after another. I had a nice extended conversation with teh doorman and another great conversation with the agent who checked me in. We had a nice chat with our waitress in The Bank and the spa staff was also very friendly. I do speak German, albeit with an American accent, and appreciated that the staff was willing to engage in my less-than-perfect German as opposed to switching to English.

This was another wonderful stay at the Park Hyatt Vienna and I’ll sum it up by saying simply that I cannot wait to return.

My original review is below, dating all the way back to August 2014. Heidi and I went for my birthday just weeks after we got married…the hotel had recently opened and we had a great stay. It’s nice to see this hotel age so gracefully and what a joy it is to share this property and the lovely city of Vienna with my children.

Vienna is a stately city rich with majestic architecture, an erudite culture, and a regal sense of style. In the center of the old city, replete with cobblestone walkways, horse drawn carriages, and glistening statues of historical luminaries, a new Park Hyatt hotel has opened on the site of a former monarchical bank. My wife and I celebrated my birthday in Vienna last weekend and stayed for two nights at Park Hyatt’s newest property.

A historic property located on Am Hof 2 in the heart of the First District of Vienna, a UNESCO World Heritage site, the hotel’s location cannot be beat. Within a few paces is the Goldenes Quartier shopping district, St. Stephan’s Cathedral, Hofburg Palace, Spanish Riding School, and many museums.

We began the day in Frankfurt with an early flight on Austrian Airlines to Vienna. I sent a note to the main hotel e-mail, park.vienna@hyatt.com, just before takeoff requesting an early check-in and had a response waiting when I landed in Vienna – the room was ready.

From Vienna Airport you have two public transportation options for getting into the city – the City Airport Train (CAT) which travels non-stop to the heart of Vienna or a suburban train (S-Bahn) which calls at several stations on the way into town, taking about 15 minutes longer than the direct service. The CAT is 14EUR one-way while the S-Bahn is 4.40EUR. We took the S-Bahn into town, then connected on the underground train (U-Bahn) to Herrengasse Station, which is just a short walk from the hotel.

A smiling porter greeted us outside the door and took our luggage. Inside, a friendly young man checked us in, speaking first in English when he noticed my American passport but then switching to German upon the request of my wife that I practice my Deutsch! He escorted us upstairs and demonstrated the hi-tech features of our room. Like many Park Hyatt properties, lighting and draperies are electronically controlled by a central push-button unit.

I loved the room – a spacious standard room with tremendous natural light, a great view, and functionality. The room featured copious electrical outlets – an essential amenity when taking my business on the road, as I did here even on my birthday weekend. The layout of the couch in front of the bed in front of the desk nicely utilized the space in the room and the separate entry hall insulated the room from outside noise.

Two doors decorated in geometric art-deco style, closed off the bathroom and entry hall from the bedroom. The bathroom was very large (and well-placed mirrors made it appear even larger) and featured a sizeable bathtub, walk-in rain shower, two sinks, and a separate water closet.

A minibar featured an Illy coffee machine with several packets of complimentary espresso and snack and drink for purchase. The refrigerator did make a rather loud humming sound that could be heard even when the bedroom door was closed. I am a heavy sleeper, but my wife woke me up one night to “turn the climate off” yet it was not the air conditioning, it was the refrigerator! It was not terrible, just noticeable.

It was warm outside and we had a problem getting the air conditioning to activate. Turns out one of the windows was open just ajar – just make sure all your windows are tightly shut and your room key is in the slot by the door or else your air conditioning will not function. Once on, the room cooled down rapidly. Vienna boasts exceptional weather so most of the year there is no need for a/c anyway.

The hotel offers three dining options in addition to 24-hour room service; The Bank, Pearl, and The Lobby Lounge. Pearl bar features an outdoor terrace in addition to a contemporary indoor seating area and specializes in cocktails. A tapas menu is available with food as substantial as Wiener Schnitzel also available.

The Lobby Lounge offers drinks and light meals and sits next to the Living Room, a cigar and whiskey lounge that is one of the hotel’s best features. Admittedly, I see little value in setting fire to and then inhaling a plant that is linked to lung cancer but many of my friends and my brother hold a different opinion, so I find myself in cigar bars quite often. If you are a conneousier of cigars or just enjoy an opulent room to enjoy a drink in with friends, this bar is not to be missed. With plush couches and rich wooden paneling on the walls, I felt like I was part of the gentry mulling over world affairs in the cigar and brandy room onboard the Titanic.

Finally, The Bank is the hotel’s most opulent restaurant and central to the character of the property. Here, on the site of the former cashier’s hall, we had breakfast each morning. Breakfast was 33EUR and the buffet was expansive with all that you would expect in a comprehensive breakfast—fresh squeezed juices, cereals, fruits, breads, cold-cuts, cheeses, breakfast meats, and eggs. Coffee (it was tremendous) as well as pancakes, waffles, French Toast, and eggs are included in the buffet and can be ordered from your server.

We spent hours in here each morning enjoying a leisurely breakfast (breakfast ends at 10:30a during the week and 11:00a on weekends) and found the service to be warm, personal, and punctual. I thought everything was great – my wife had a problem with her eggs on the first morning (soft boiled eggs came out hard-boiled, then an omelet ordered with no cheese was delivered with cheese) but the issues were quickly remedied and did not reoccur the next morning. The juices were remarkably tasty (apple, orange, and even grapefruit were exceptional) and my favorite part of the breakfast was the cheese-covered cooked tomatoes.

Lunch and dinner are also offered each night in The Bank and you will find no menu posted online because the menu, sourced with local ingredients, changes often. Prices were moderate and I was prepared to dine at the restaurant for my birthday, but when mentioning that I was especially looking for fish, the concierge directed me to a restaurant called Kornat about 15 minutes away by foot, which specializes in fish and seafood.

So I missed trying out The Bank for an evening meal, but I did appreciate the restaurant recommendation for the food was amazing and we enjoyed a prime outdoor table thanks to a call ahead from the concierge.

I do have one gripe and only one true gripe about the property: the in-room wireless internet speed was unreliable. The Park Hyatt Vienna offers complimentary wired and wi-fi internet, which is a nice feature, but I found myself on multiple occasions banging my hand on the desk with disgust as poor connectivity led to unacceptably long page load times and the inability to make internet-based telephone calls. Other times, though, the interent worked perfectly well with pages loading fast and no issue with Skype calls or viewing YouTube videos. Admittedly, I did not not bring my ethernet cable converter for my MacBook Air so I was unable to test the wired internet speed.

A large fitness studio with state-of-the-art, brand new equipment was much appreciated. Several bikes, treadmills, and ellipticals filled one side of the room while strength training equipment and free weights filled out the other. The room itself, with brass candelabras and wooden floors was an elegant place to work out and apples, bottled water, refrigerated towels, newspapers, and magazines were available.

The gym overlooks the swimming pool below, which sits on the site of the former bank vault. With an ornate frieze relief and elongated white leather couches, it offers a refreshing antidote to the hot afternoon sun (or cold). Adjacent to the pool is a lounge with chairs to relax and also steam room and sauna facilities. My one regret is that we did not spend an extra day in Vienna just to lounge around the spa. Certainly, seeing Vienna is the priority if your time is limited, but this is a great complimentary benefit of the hotel that seems to go unutilized, as I saw many hotel guests and no one using the pool or spa lounge. Full spa services are available here in the Arany Spa and you can even see the original 3-ton bank vault door.

This hotel is a category six property, meaning it is 25,000 Hyatt Gold Passport points per night or 12,500 points plus a $150 co-pay (my preferred method of payment to help stretch out my points). The daily rate during the summer is about 375EUR or $500. Gold Passport availblity is good.

I can’t tell you how much I enjoyed the city of Vienna and both my wife (who is not usually a city person) and I wish to return soon. When we do, we will definitely choose the Park Hyatt again, allowing an extra day for the spa and enjoying at a more leisurely pace one of Europe’s greatest capital cities.

#6168. Ground Stop Could Cost U.S. Airlines Hundreds of Millions of Dollars

Friday’s mass grounding could cost the four largest U.S. airlines a combined $345 million or more, according to investment firm Bernstein.

The estimate, first reported by Reuters, comes after more than 18,000 flights were canceled on Friday and over the weekend, upending travel plans for hundreds of thousands of people both in and outside the U.S.

Bernstein’s projection includes lost earnings at United, Delta, American Airlines, and Southwest. The financial hit for other U.S. carriers, such as JetBlue, Alaska Airlines, and Frontier, could push the total impact to over half a billion dollars.

More exact information about potential losses will come with the airlines’ fourth-quarter earnings reports.

Flight disruptions eased somewhat Monday, and the FAA expects air traffic to normalize by the evening. But questions remain about the cause of Friday’s ATC outage, and it could take days, weeks, or even longer to get a clear picture of exactly what went wrong.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a router installed by contractor L3Harris as part of a routine copper line-to-fiber optic upgrade “flooded” other routers with data, causing the crash. It was not clear if L3Harris incorrectly installed the router, or if the device itself was faulty, Duffy said.

That explanation has drawn some pushback, most notably from Hewlett Packard, the parent company of Juniper Networks, which makes the routers L3Harris was installing. HP said the Juniper device was “functioning exactly as intended” based on available information.

Additionally, some anonymous air traffic controllers have charged that the secretary’s narrative does not match with what they saw unfold in towers and control rooms during the ground stop.

L3Harris said Saturday that it is working with the FAA to determine why the outage occurred.

Small tips are customary at restaurants and hotels.

Taxis are cheap and plentiful, but public transport within the city is free.

Yes, Serbia is generally considered safe for travelers. The U.S. State Department currently lists it as Level 2, so travelers should exercise increased caution, but no severe threats are present.
