You might have seen Serbia in the news lately. The country’s recent national elections enacted a political sea change spearheaded by student groups seeking greater freedoms and opportunities.

The jubilant energy unleashed, combined with the Serbian capital’s soon-to-shine spotlight as it prepares to host the 2027 World Expo make now the perfect time to plan your visit to Belgrade. That’s why the city made our list of top destinations for next year.

Sleepier than some other European capitals, yet vibrant and buzzing with a construction boom, Belgrade is coming into its own. It’s also easier than ever to get there, thanks to plentiful airline connections not only to other European hubs but also to the U.S. via the country’s national carrier, Air Serbia.

So start your points planning and make Belgrade a part of your next transatlantic trip.

The fastest way to get to Belgrade’s Nikola Tesla Airport (BEG) from the U.S. is aboard Air Serbia from Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport (ORD) or New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). The airline also recently announced that it will launch twice-weekly service to Miami International Airport (MIA) in May 2027.

Air Serbia’s main major airline partner is Etihad, so your best bet for booking award tickets is to use Etihad Guest miles. The program is a transfer partner of:

That said, award availability is hard to come by since these flights only operate a few times a week. Instead, you might want to consider redeeming Flying Blue miles for flights on Air France via Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) or via Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) on KLM.

For Star Alliance flyers, award availability between the U.S. and Belgrade is plentiful on carriers like LOT via Warsaw Chopin Airport (WAW) and Lufthansa via Frankfurt Airport (FRA) or Munich International Airport (MUC) and Swiss via Zurich Airport (ZRH), starting at 42,500 Aeroplan points each way in economy and 75,000 Aeroplan points each way in business class. Taxes and fees range from about $100 to $150 in each direction.

Belgrade is expecting to see its first Intercontinental open in early 2027, just in time for the World Expo. Until then, there are plenty of other hotels where your points will come in handy.

Located in the new riverside Belgrade Waterfront District, which is home to a sprawling luxury mall, a promenade with tons of bars, cafes and restaurants, and more than a few high-rise apartment buildings, the St. Regis Belgrade opened in November 2024 in a striking glass-and-steel tower. The hotel has just 119 spacious rooms and suites with floor-to-ceiling windows, a beautiful spa with an indoor pool, a cafe-patisserie, a continental restaurant and an outpost of the brand’s signature St. Regis Bar. Rates start at $290 or 43,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

The Hyatt Regency Belgrade is a comfortable, modern hotel in Novi Beograd, the city’s main business district, across the Sava River from the historic core, so it’s not the best for leisure travelers. That said, you can’t beat nightly rates that start at $148 or 6,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

The Hilton Belgrade is centrally located near Slavija Square, within walking distance of attractions like the Nikola Tesla Museum and the Church of Saint Sava. It has 242 rooms and suites and a restaurant that serves contemporary Serbian cuisine. Rates start at $170 or 50,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

You won’t find Uber in Serbia, but taxis are plentiful and can be hailed via apps like Yandex, Pink Taxi Nova and Car:Go. The apps make it easy to pay with a credit card. Just be sure to use a credit card that earns bonus points on ride-hailing services or on travel charges in general.

Sometimes drivers will not accept rides unless you are paying cash, though, which you can also book through the app and then take a metered ride. So be sure to pull some cash out at the ATM at the airport before heading into the city.

Once in Belgrade, it’s easy to get around by public trams and buses, which are free to use within the city center.

Related: The best credit cards for commuting expenses

For a city of its size, Belgrade’s restaurant scene is surprisingly diverse. Of course, you should make it a priority to try typical Serbian dishes like grilled cevapi sausages with fluffy bread and ajvar red pepper sauce, and sarma, which is pickled cabbage stuffed with spiced meat and rice, not to mention the plethora of cured meats and mountain cheeses. Bela Reka is a great place to try a smattering of Serbian specialties, many of them sourced from the restaurant’s own farm in the Homolje Mountains.

Perched on the riverbank, Suvenir serves traditional dishes like roasted lamb and bacon-wrapped prunes in a beautiful setting.

For a contemporary take on Balkan cuisine, Iva is a sophisticated hideaway tucked into a courtyard near Saint Sava church where age-old dishes are reinterpreted through a modern lens. The piping-hot burek pastries stuffed with cheese, baked peach, hot pepper and honey are not to miss ($12), as is the confit river pike-perch with gnocchi and charred Swiss chard in a white wine sauce ($20). A glass of crisp Deuric Severna Morava white wine from the Fruska Gora region is the perfect accompaniment ($7).

Be sure to book ahead for a table at S5 by Angie, a fine-dining bolthole hidden in an otherwise unremarkable apartment building in the city’s quiet Zemun district. Spend a while enjoying a cocktail in the living-room-like parlor, complete with a vinyl record collection, then settle in for a multicourse feast prepared by chef "Angie" Risimic that might include dishes like creamy labneh with tart tomatoes, fluffy ravioli with mild ricotta-style cheese doused in a green herb and blackberry sauce with trout roe, and tender pork in a rosehip demi-glace with end-of-summer morels. Prix-fixe menu prices vary but range from $75-$150, though a la carte ordering is also possible.

For something more casual, spend an evening strolling cobblestones of Skadarska Street in the bohemian neighborhood of Skadarlija, just a short walk from Republic Square, where you will find over a dozen traditional kafane, or taverns, serving similar menus of hearty dishes along with plenty of plum-flavored rakija spirits.

Tri Sesira, or the Three Hats, was a favorite of the Serbian Romantic poet and painter Dura Jaksic, a statue of whom sits outside his humble former house nearby.

Belgrade has a handful of worthwhile museums, but not so many as to commandeer your entire timeline.

The National Museum has exhibits ranging from prehistoric artifacts to medieval Balkan icons, Italian Renaissance and Flemish masters, French Impressionists and modern artists, including pieces by well-known Yugoslav painters like Sava Sumanovic. Entrance is $3 for adults.

It’s free to stroll the grounds of Belgrade Fortress and Kalemegdan Park, which overlook the confluence of the Danube and Sava Rivers and are popular places for sunset meetups.

Some of the museums at the fortress have their own entrance fees and operating hours. The citadel dates to the third century B.C.E., though it has seen hundreds of battles and been destroyed, rebuilt and expanded dozens of times in the ensuing millennia.

Even if churches aren’t your thing, no visit to Belgrade would be complete without a stop at the brilliant white, copper-domed Church of Saint Sava, which is one of the largest Eastern Orthodox churches in the world.

The interior mosaics gleam with gold and are utterly breathtaking. Entrance is free.

Nearby the Nikola Tesla Museum is a fun, interactive affair. It offers guided tours every 45 minutes, but they fill up fast, so get there at least half an hour before the next one to line up. Entrance costs $7.50 and includes a short film, then demonstrations using Tesla coils before a small exhibit spanning the inventor’s life and some of his personal effects.

Sitting in a small park of its own, the Museum of Yugoslavia is a memorial to the former country’s late strongman, Josip Broz Tito, who rose to prominence in the resistance to the Nazi occupation of World War II and eventually oversaw every aspect of life in Yugoslavia until his death in 1980.

The complex includes his mausoleum — the so-called “House of Flowers” — an older building with some of his personal belongings and displays about daily life in Yugoslavia and a larger wing with temporary exhibits including a recent one on themes of propaganda in wartime. Admission is $7.50 for adults.

The pedestrian shopping street of Knez Mihailova is also well worth a wander, if only for unique souvenirs produced by Serbian craftspeople at the Belgrade Window boutique.

It might not have been on your radar before, but Belgrade is well worth a visit, especially with all the events on the calendar for 2027, including hosting the World Expo. Along with some luxurious new hotels and a growing crop of exciting new restaurants, plus a small but impressive cadre of museums and galleries, it might just become one of your favorite European capitals.

#6166. Well-Traveled Women on Where They Plan to Visit in 2027

A bucket list item is one thing—turning it into an itinerary is another. The difference often lies in deciding that the places we dream about are worth pursuing amid limited vacation days and financial constraints. It’s a sentiment captured by avid traveler and content creator, Lucrenzia Worthington: “If there's one thing I've learned, it's that it’s never the right time, only the time you finally decide to go.”

With 2027 in sight, we’re taking inspiration from well-traveled women who are already thinking about the possibilities of the fresh, new year ahead and the trips they hope to pull off. Spanning photographers, artisans, interior designers, rock climbers, divers, and cookbook authors, their wanderlust is as varied as it is far-reaching. Read on for how they plan to travel next, from diving Antarctica’s crystalline waters to cooking in the fertile valleys of the Peloponnese Peninsula.

“For as long as I can remember, I’ve dreamed of diving in Antarctica. Maybe it’s growing up in Bangkok’s tropical heat, but the polar regions endlessly fascinate me: the icebergs, the seals, and penguins. I’ve visited the White Continent before, but seeing it underwater is something else entirely. In 2027, I’m joining Aurora Expeditions, a pioneer in polar diving for over 20 years. Even as an experienced diver and underwater photographer, it takes serious preparation: I’m logging drysuit dives off [the coast of] Cape Town with specialized gear to get ready for one of the most extraordinary dive sites on earth.” —Pier Nirandara, travel writer, underwater photographer, and founder of Immersiv Expeditions

“You know, I've been lucky enough to see some extraordinary corners of the world, yet one place keeps slipping down my list. It's always ’not the right time,’ always ’too complicated to book.’ But 2027 is the year: Lapland, in February. There are direct flights from Milan to Rovaniemi, Finland, and I would plan two nights there and two in Levi. I'm dreaming of a night in those super cool glass cabins where you fall asleep under the northern lights and endless starry skies, and booking experiences like visiting a reindeer farm, husky sledding, and snowshoe hikes through frosted pines—but also cozy up indoors by a crackling fire, with a warm blanket, and soak up the winter wonderland around me. If there's one thing I've learned, it's that it’s never the right time, only the time you finally decide to go.” —Lucrezia Worthington, content creator and freelance journalist

“I've always wanted to visit Morocco, and I think 2027 is the year. My dream is to stay in a riad in Marrakech with however many friends I can persuade to join me. I want to find tagine and wander through the [medina]. I also hope to venture out to the Atlas Mountains for a weekend.” —Ríoghnach Robinson, author of Bad Words

“In 2027, I'm planning to return to Antalya, Turkey. I spent a week there this year and fell in love with the food, the people, and the climbing. I'll be based around Geyikbayırı and Çitdibi, where there are limestone crags in the hills with views out to the sea. I usually find a place to stay on Airbnb and lean on local recommendations for where to eat. One spot I'm definitely returning to is Coffee Roaster 404.” —Sasha DiGiulian, professional climber and founder of SEND Bars

“Most flock to Greece for the idyllic beaches and all things Mediterranean, and while I completely understand that desire, my curiosity has landed me in the Peloponnese Peninsula, in particular the central region of Arcadia. Its fertile valleys are known for strong culinary and agricultural traditions; apples, sour cherries, slender eggplants, cheeses from mountain sheep and goats, walnuts, chestnuts, and mushroom foraging. I have been obsessing over a beautiful hotel that caught my eye: Manna, located on Mount Mainalo among hiking trails and dense forests. The mountain is also known for a very special high altitude honey cultivated from fir trees. Honestly, the honey alone is enough to get me on a plane.” —Noreen Wasti, cook, food creative, and author of Feast Your Eyes: Beautiful Recipes to Garnish, Share, and Savor

“In 2027, I’d love to finally visit Peru and see Machu Picchu. South America is completely new territory for me, and the landscapes, craftsmanship, and food are all calling. I’m imagining local guides, time in the Sacred Valley, and plenty of exploring. I’d also love to go home to Mauritius, but this time be a tourist. A beautiful hotel, all the food I miss, and time to enjoy the island and its lovely hospitality. Usually, my visits revolve around family and catching up. In 2027, for once, I’d like my biggest responsibility to be deciding what to have for lunch.” —Nashmita Rajiah, interior designer

“I’m perpetually scouting [destinations] for In Hand’s newsletter and group trips by exploring culturally rich regions through the lens of traditional craft. I'm looking forward to an upcoming trip to the Atlas Mountains to visit the female Amazigh weavers in their homes, and learning about the by-hand process of weaving Berber rugs at the source rather than the point of sale, focusing on the culture and traditions around this generation-to-generation craft. I’m staying at Kasbah du Toubkal in Imlil, a small mountain town grounded in real Amazigh village life. It’s a trip I’ve wanted to take for years. ” —Meghan McEwen, writer and founder of group trip planner In Hand

“What I look forward to most is traveling with friends and family. Mornings in the sea, a simple lunch in the hot sun. Afternoons are for slow wandering, and at night we'll cook big meals from our market finds. In 2027, my family is heading to Sicily for two weeks in shoulder season, before the [summer] tourist wave. The first half we'll explore the main island, from the salt flats of Trapani to the bone white cliffs of Scala dei Turchi on the south coast. Then Favignana in the Egadi Islands, off Sicily's west coast, will hopefully be home for a week or so. The water is crystal blue, the coves are plentiful, and you can bike around the entire island easily. Tuna is still king there, though the old canning factory has long since closed. I'm dreaming of spaghetti with bottarga. At the moment I have my eyes on Villa Zu Nillu from The Thinking Traveller, perched above its own labyrinthine Roman stone quarry, into which a beautiful pool and a Mediterranean garden have been set. And I will document it all.” —Andrea Gentl, photographer and author of Cooking with Mushrooms

“After last summer’s European heatwave, we’re planning a cooler 2027 Finnish escape with my decorative arts grad school friend and her family. We always mix design with fun for the kids, so we’ll visit Helsinki’s Aalto House, the design district, and Hvitträsk museum before renting a lakeside mökki for swimming, hiking, and archipelago adventures. I want to experience the “midnight sun,” but I might regret it if the kids never sleep. Truthfully, I’m more of a lazy reptile than an outdoor adventurer, so afterward, our family of four will retreat to a less popular Italian beach for pasta, sunshine, and absolutely no obligation to do anything adventurous at all.” —Ajiri Aki, author of JOIE: A Parisian’s Guide to Celebrating The Good Life and The Joie Journal

“Long the secret destination of all the chic Italians I know, the low-key vibe of Maremma [in Tuscany and Lazio] is starting to also draw an international crowd looking for relaxed summers featuring all the best of Italy—raw nature, excellent food—minus the crowds and bling. For families, the Terre di Sacra Estate is on my wish list, either “glamping” on the beach or in one of their villas. And speaking of villas, Maremma doyenne Amanda Sposito is behind one of the most beautiful private rentals, the Villa Tre Querce, in town.” —Philomena Schurer Merckoll, founder of Riad Mena and hospitality group Egypt Beyond

“I would love to visit Japan. Surprisingly, I have never been to Asia before, so it feels like a whole new world waiting to be explored. As a designer working with raffia and traditional weaving techniques, I am fascinated by Japan’s appreciation for craftsmanship and handmade objects. I would love to explore Kyoto’s historic temples, meet local artisans, and learn about their weaving traditions and use of natural materials. Seeing Mount Fuji in person would also be incredible: I find so much inspiration in the colors, textures, and everyday details of a place, and I would love to bring those experiences into my designs.” —Akosua Afriyie-Kumi, founder of AAKS

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6165. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

#6164. Delta Air Lines Cuts JFK–Dulles Route After More Than 30 Years

Delta Air Lines will end nonstop service between Washington Dulles and New York JFK in February, leaving the two airports without a direct link. The cut removes another connection to Delta’s JFK hub and follows similar exits by United and JetBlue.

Delta will operate its final flight between Washington Dulles (IAD) and New York Kennedy (JFK) on February 10, 2027. The move eliminates the only nonstop link between the two airports (JetBlue cut the route in 2019 and United in 2014). Delta is not leaving Dulles, nor will this route cut eliminate flights between Dulles and the New York metropolitan area. United serves Newark and LaGuardia from its Washington hub.

But passengers who specifically want to connect at JFK on Delta or its partners will lose an option.

This route has run for over 30 years, so the route cut is certainly newsworthy. Without seeing Delta’s route economics, I’m not going to speculate how much money this service made or lost. But I struggle to see a large number of passengers who need this particular connection and cannot reasonably be accommodated elsewhere. I’m frankly surprised Delta operated a route like this for so long, which sounds like the sort of slot-squatting United does by scheulding so many flights between Washington National and Newark.

The case for this route has always been onward connections at JFK, particularly to international flights. But even there, Delta has alternatives. Washington-area passengers can begin at Reagan National (DCA), while travelers who prefer Dulles can connect through another Delta hub, such as Atlanta or Detroit, depending on their destination. I cannot imagine that there is so connecting traffic from Northern Virginia and the broader Washington area that Delta cannot handle it through DCA or another hub.

While I’m sure there will be “regulars” who are greatly inconvenienced by this route cut, that’s no justification to keep any route going and we do know the load factor was lower on this route than its network average.

This brought back memories of my coverage of United ending JFK–Dulles service in October 2014.

“Two-thirds of traffic on the route is connecting traffic that does not generate sufficient yields.”

United’s circumstances were somewhat similar. Dulles was its hub, while JFK had become a small station focused on flights to Los Angeles and San Francisco. Today, Delta operates a substantial hub at JFK, but it only flies to its hubs, now less JFK, from IAD.

In both cases the underlying question is similar: does the connecting revenue justify using an aircraft and scarce airport access on a short route when passengers have other ways to reach the network?

United decided it did not. Delta is now removing the same airport pair from its schedule.

More than 12 years later, I still find United’s explanation brutally honest as to why it cut that route (and eventually pulled out of JFK altogether).

I have written about Delta becoming more selective at JFK, including cuts to domestic feeder routes and international destinations. With air traffic control congestion and slot restrictions still in place, it makes sense to me that Delta would want to funnel less travel through JFK and more throughout other hubs: the focus must be on local traffic or at least costal traffic that can command a higher premium.

Meanwhile, United is preparing to return to JFK through its partnership with JetBlue. Does this create an opening for United to restore Dulles service? Perhaps, but I would think it would be difficult to work now just like it was then and has been for Delta. United already has extensive Washington–New York connectivity through Newark, and its initial JFK access will be limited. Each available slot will have more compelling uses via transcon traffic.

I do not think the disappearance of Delta from this route will make starting that route attractive to United, especially since United previously abandoned it.

Delta will end JFK–Dulles flights after February 10, 2027, removing a useful option for some Washington-area passengers connecting through Kennedy. Even so, the decision makes sense to me. Delta can accommodate much of that traffic through Reagan National or other hubs, and local Washington–New York travelers have several alternatives…so no, this isn’t a sign that Delta is continuing to lose ground in New York.

United cut this route in 2014 because connecting traffic did not produce sufficient revenue. Delta has not publicly supplied the same explanation, but the commercial question remains much the same. A “useful connection” for many passengers does not necessarily mean a profitable or smart one for the airline.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Back when I worked in Washington and flew to and from DCA weekly, I used to take advantage of Delta’s duplicative flights at IAD. That was also when a Sky Club membership granted you access to the Air France/KLM lounge at IAD even when flying Delta on a domestic trip.

For starters, IAD and DCA (along with BWI) were considered the same airport (coterminous) for purposes of same-day change.

Second, in the event of an IROP at DCA, you could easily switch over to IAD.

Third, upgrades in or out of IAD were marginally easier to obtain than upgrades in or out of DCA.

With all of that said, I do wonder about the impact on connections at Dulles since there are several SkyTeam carriers or Delta partners who fly into Dulles. Presumably, some of those passengers have onward connections within the US.

There’s very little if any “sky team” connectivity behind Dulles. Dulles and the region can support AF/KL/KE nonstops to their markets because the DC region is a huge wealthy region that generates lots of traffic. It doesnt rely on “sky team” connectivity to make those work.

The DL lounge at DCA and faster drop off-to-gate time probably attract many people who could fly DL out of IAD. But also, I suspect there are far more people flying out of the national capitol area to JFK to make Skyteam connections in JFK than there are people flying DL to IAD to make a Skyteam connection out of IAD.

I’m just going to respectfully disagree with you, Jason. I hear you and don’t mind at all that you point out the errors, which I always correct. But I think you may underestimate how long this blog takes to update 4-5 times each day and this is a hobby, not a career (I practice law as a full-time job and cannot afford to be sloppy in that practice). So as much as I’d love my writing to be error free, it’s really me that you’re reading, I do this for fun, and I thank you for reading this blog for so many years.

I’m surprised delta still had the route but it is a reflection and problem of routes to jfk in delta’s split hub operation — outside lga perimeter, few want or need to connect at jfk. Inside the perimeter, you’re mostly going for connections and some airports like iAd just don’t make a lot of sense when their destinations are nearly as good and they probably aren’t delta flyers anyway — in dc it’s AA or united, not delta.

Yup. Sorry, Frank. (He’s a nice guy. He’ll get over it.)

DCA is still the preferred airport for domestic Washington DC traffic and DL has the 2nd largest number of flights from DCA after AA and the same #2 ranking is DL’s at BWI.

DL is still well-positioned in the Baltimore/Washington area even as the only big 4 airline w/o a hub in the metro area.

#6163. How to Decide Which Ski Pass Is Best For Your Winter Travel Plans

With snow already falling in the Rockies and a strong El Niño weather pattern expected to benefit certain US mountain regions, skiers and riders are already dusting off their gear and booking their winter trips.

Of course, skiing and snowboarding aren’t typically budget-friendly sports. Once you factor in meals, lodging, and transportation in addition to a lift ticket (which costs well over $300 per day at several US resorts), it’s almost worth taking out a loan to pay for a one-week family ski trip.

But in recent years, the industry has moved away from one-day lift tickets in favor of multi-mountain ski passes with heavily discounted rates and additional perks, like Epic’s “Pay Over Time” or Ikon’s deals on friends and family tickets.

The dreamy Big Bear Resort is included on Ikon Pass.

"For those who ski or ride more than six to eight days a season, multi-mountain passes have reshaped the [ski] resort industry,” says Olivia Rowan, publisher of trade magazine Ski Area Management. “The multi-mountain pass opened up new possibilities for snow sports travel and tourism beyond your home hill. They're a great deal for an in-the-know skier or rider.”

Before choosing a pass, determine your skiing goals for the season. If you’re looking to check out a handful of new resorts for a day or two each, the Indy Pass might be your best option. But if you’re hoping to spend a week at a more popular resort like Park City, the Epic or Ikon passes are the way to go. To figure out which pass is best for you and your travel plans, here's a breakdown of the major players.

Best for: Individuals and families who want unlimited access to some of the world's largest and most popular ski areas

When the Vail-owned Epic Pass debuted in 2008, it was the first of its kind and set the stage for the multi-mountain passes that followed in the coming years. Today, it remains one of the biggest players in the industry, offering access to over 90 resorts in North America, Europe, Japan, and Australia.

Pricing: The standard Epic Pass, which offers unlimited access to all its resorts, costs $1,169. But if you don’t plan to ski during holiday weeks and weekends, consider the Epic Local Pass, which excludes peak dates at certain resorts. Epic also offers a customizable pass that lets skiers choose up to 7 days across different resort tiers. The cheapest option, at $337, gives skiers 7 days at 22 resorts in the Midwest, Northeast, and Mid-Atlantic.

Epic Pass offers access to over 90 resorts in North America, Europe, Japan, and Australia.

Vail, Colorado, one of the most popular mountains included with Epic Pass.

Traveler-approved ski resorts near Epic Pass mountains:

Best for: Skiers and riders who want to check out several uncrowded, under-the-radar ski resorts

The Indy Pass, which is the antithesis of larger passes like Epic and Ikon, offers two days of skiing at each of its over 300 partner resorts across four continents. The pass partners with smaller, independently owned resorts that are typically uncrowded and have deeply rooted local vibes. This season, Indy is rolling out an upgrade that lets passholders ski up to five days at 13 resorts, starting at $199. The pass sells out quickly and is already off sale for the 2026-27 ski season, but now is the time to get on the waiting list for next season (sales sometimes reopen mid-season, too).

Pricing: The Indy+ Pass, which doesn’t have blackout dates, costs $469 for adults and $299 for kids 12 and under.

Jay Peak mountain resort in Vermont, which saw record snowfall last winter.

Traveler-approved ski resorts near Indy Pass mountains:

Best for: Skiers who live near one of Ikon’s premier destinations, or families with children who want to take advantage of Ikon’s discounted kids passes

Like the Epic Pass, the Ikon Pass offers unlimited access to some of the world’s most popular ski resorts. The pass includes access to over 70 resorts across 13 countries, including some bigger US destinations like Jackson Hole, Deer Valley, and Aspen Snowmass.

Pricing: Like Epic, Ikon offers tiered passes, with its unlimited pass starting at $1,529 (or $1,129 for young adults ages 13-22 and $499 for children ages 5-12). The base pass, which has some blackout dates, starts at $1,099 for adults over 23. Skiers and riders who want to dip their toes into the sport or who may not have time to get out much during the season should consider a personalized pass that allows two, three, or four days at partner resorts.

Fresh powder at Big Bear Mountain Resort, a gem of a mountain on the Ikon Pass.

Traveler-approved ski resorts near Ikon Pass mountains:

Best for: East Coast skiers and riders who mostly plan on skiing in the Mid-Atlantic, Northeast, or eastern Canada, or individuals looking to supplement another multi-mountain pass; It includes two mountains in Colorado and Wyoming, but they are on the smaller side.

New for the 2026-27 ski season, the Snow Pass is the newest player in the game. Like Indy, the Snow Pass offers two days at each partner resort, but so far it has only 14 resorts to choose from, most of which are in the Northeast. You can buy additional days for 30% off the retail price. Snow Pass offers an alternate three-day pass—Snow Triple Play—that includes three days total at 23 partner resorts.

Pricing: The Snow Pass costs $379.99, and the Snow Triple Play costs $189.99.

Whiteface Mountain Ski Resort is a haven of varied terrain for skiers and snowboarders alike.

Traveler-approved ski resorts near Snow Pass mountains:

Best for: Skiers and riders who want to check some big-name resorts off their list but aren’t looking to ski for an extended period at one ski area, or those looking to supplement another multi-mountain or season pass.

The Mountain Collective Pass offers passholders two days each at its 27 resorts in the US, Canada, Japan, Europe, South America, Australia, and New Zealand. It’s a slightly more affordable alternative to the Epic and Ikon, yet it still gives skiers access to big-name resorts like Jackson Hole and Big Sky.

Pricing: The Mountain Collective Pass goes for $729 for adults, $594 for teens, and $304 for kids 6-12. Skiers and riders who want to ski more than their allotted 2 days at a specific resort can purchase day tickets at half off.

A sprawling mountain view at Jackson Hole, included on the Mountain Collective pass.

Where to visit with the Mountain Collective Pass:

#6162. Aer Lingus Unveils Business Class Suites With Doors And Its First Premium Economy Cabin On A330s

Aer Lingus has announced a cabin overhaul for 10 Airbus A330 aircraft, with the first refurbished jet scheduled to enter service on October 1, 2027. The initial route will be Dublin–New York JFK, on select EI104/EI105 services. Additional North American routes will follow as more aircraft are refurbished.

This is an A330-only project for now: there will be no corresponding cabin overhaul for the Airbus A321LR or A321XLR.

The refurbished aircraft will feature 28 Collins Elevation business class suites in a 1-2-1 layout. Every passenger will have direct aisle access and a closing door, with each seat converting into a 78-inch flat bed. Improved bedding and amenity kits are also planned.

The renderings look attractive to me. Green upholstery and lighter finishes give the cabin an Irish identity and a premium feel (hello Singapore Airlines). More importantly, the layout addresses a weakness I encountered on my Aer Lingus A330-200 flight from Dublin to Los Angeles. I had a window seat with a passenger beside me and no direct aisle access. Storage was limited too.

I slept well, but the seat was behind what many competitors offered. The lovely crew helped redeem that flight, though warm service should complement a competitive seat rather than compensate for one. Doors are fine, but giving every passenger access to the aisle is the more consequential improvement.

Aer Lingus also plans refreshed dining and a self-service business class snack and refreshment bar, much like SAS offers its on its A330 aircraft:

The new premium economy cabin will have four rows of Recaro R4 seats:

Passengers will receive an upgraded three-course meal, complimentary drinks, bedding, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing headphones. It’s a hardly a unique or transformative hard product compared to its peers, but it’s an increasingly important middle way providing a noticeably more comfortable seat at a price that makes sense relative to economy and business class.

This fills an obvious gap for Aer Lingus. Someone who wants more room than economy offers but cannot justify a business class fare currently has limited options within the airline’s own cabin lineup. A genuine premium economy product gives that passenger another reason to stay with Aer Lingus.

Economy will retain the A330’s appealing 2-4-2 layout, with new seats and adjustable headrests. A self-service snack station is coming to this cabin too.

If I fly economy class, I prefer the A330 or 767. Two seats together by the window remain a compelling reason to choose an A330 when traveling as a couple, especially compared with being part of a block of three on most other widebody aircraft.

Aer Lingus promises more personal space, but we will wait for the final seat pitch and total economy seat count before drawing conclusions about legroom. A redesigned seatback can improve knee clearance without increasing the distance between rows, but padding is also essential.

The refurbished A330s will receive Panasonic Astrova entertainment systems, with 4K screens, Bluetooth headphone pairing, and USB-C charging.

Free Starlink Wi-Fi will also be available, though Aer Lingus says that service is already offered across its transatlantic routes. Passengers do not need to wait for the new cabins to benefit from it. My previous A330 flight featured an entertainment system with missing graphics and internet that was slow but stable. Working screens and fast connectivity would improve the experience considerably.

For a daytime transatlantic flight, I place enormous value on reliable internet. A better seat may help me sleep on the overnight journey to Dublin, but Starlink makes the flight home a far more useful part of my day.

The first aircraft is still almost a year away, and the announcement does not provide a completion date for all 10 retrofits.

An October 1 launch on select JFK flights should not be confused with every Aer Lingus A330 having the new cabins from that date, even to JFK. During the transition, you’ll be able to tell which aircraft have the new business class because that aircraft will also be selling premium economy seats.

I hope Aer Lingus makes the differences clear during booking and handles aircraft substitutions sensibly…

Aer Lingus is giving 10 A330s new business class suites, adding premium economy, and refreshing economy class, with the first aircraft scheduled to debut between Dublin and New York JFK in October 2027.

My last longhaul flight on Aer Lingus left me impressed by the crew but disappointed by parts of the onboard product. This overhaul addresses the seat and technology shortcomings that made me reluctant to seek out the airline. I look forward to trying it. Aer Lingus already showed me how pleasant its service can be. Pair that with a competitive seat and better catering, and I might go out of my way to book it again.

#6160. Update: United Resolves System Outage

United said it has resolved a system outage that delayed flights across its network late Monday afternoon.

“We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures,” the airline said in a statement. “While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights. There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”

Between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m. Eastern time, crews at multiple airports reported they could not get the final weight-and-balance figures required for departure.

United acknowledged a “widespread system outage” in a post on X. In a separate statement, the carrier said it was “troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights.”

The first report identified in radio audio captured by the ATC App came at about 4:02 p.m. ET, when the crew of United flight 2787 in Denver reported trouble getting its final weights. At Chicago O’Hare, the system used to request pushbacks also went down. At Newark, a ramp controller said the outage affected how ramp crews received gate changes.

“We are having an extreme system-wide outage… which is preventing us from closing out flights, which is affecting pretty much all of our mainline departures at this point,” an O’Hare ramp controller said.

Radio reports named at least 30 United flights across 12 airports. Some crews at O’Hare and Los Angeles reported receiving final weights between 4:40 and 5:09 p.m. ET. At 5:11 p.m., an O’Hare ramp controller canceled a United flight’s pushback after it had waited about 20 minutes.

#6159. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

You'll need a valid passport to enter the Cayman Islands. U.S. citizens do not need a visa for stays of up to 30 days, though you'll receive a tourist entry stamp on arrival. Make sure your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond your travel dates to be safe.

Yes, many restaurants automatically add a 15% gratuity to your bill, so check before tipping on top of that for exceptional service. Cash tips are fine, but many places also take cards.

English is the official language and is widely spoken everywhere you'll go as a visitor. You won't need a translation app.

Grand Cayman is compact and manageable by taxi, rental car, or ride-sharing services. Taxis are metered and reliable; rides typically start at  $8–15, depending on distance. If you rent a car, remember to drive on the left side of the road. Uber does not operate here, but other services are available.

The Cayman Islands are generally safe for tourists, with a strong police presence and low rates of violent crime. Standard travel precautions apply: don't leave valuables unattended, be aware of your surroundings at night, and keep a copy of your important documents separate from the originals.

November through April offers the best weather, warm and comfortable. In peak season, expect higher prices and more crowds. May through October is hurricane season, so be aware that even though direct hits are rare. If you're flexible, September and October can offer lower rates and fewer tourists, with the tradeoff of higher humidity and occasional afternoon storms.

Top-tier resorts, nature excursions and seven-mile stretches of clear water — there's much worth experiencing when visiting the Cayman Islands.

The Cayman Islands’ luxury boom in hotels, restaurants and experiences made it an easy pick for our 2027 Where to Go list. But building the right itinerary can be a challenge when there’s so much to enjoy — especially when you're trying to maximize your point earnings and fit everything into a long weekend.

What really makes the Cayman Islands work as a points destination is how every part of your trip, from flights and hotels to dining and activities, can help you earn.

That's why TPG and Chase are teaming up to bring travelers everything they need to know to make the most of their trip to the Cayman Islands. Planning and earning are easier with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), thanks to its recently refreshed benefits, including the annual $100 Chase Travel℠ Hotel Credit, a statement credit of up to $120 back every four years for a TSA PreCheck®, Global Entry or Nexus application fee charged to the card. Cardmembers also enjoy long-standing benefits, including no foreign transaction fees and a comprehensive suite of built-in travel protections.

Here's how I spent four unforgettable days on the islands, and how you can use your Chase Sapphire Preferred card to do the same.

Getting to the Cayman Islands is easy, as there are plenty of nonstop flight options to Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) year-round from major U.S. hubs, including:

All three airlines are Chase transfer partners, meaning you can book through the Chase Travel or transfer points to any of these airline loyalty programs.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Getting to and from the airport is one of my favorite ways to earn some extra points on a trip. With the Chase Sapphire Preferred, you can earn 5 points per dollar on Lyft* if you opt for a ride, or 3 points per dollar on gas station purchases and EV charging if you decide to drive yourself, as I did.

Either way, don't forget that your Chase Sapphire Preferred card offers a statement credit of up to $120 every four years toward a Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus application fee. If you choose Global Entry, membership also includes TSA PreCheck, making it easier to breeze through airport security.

Once you land in Grand Cayman, you will need to take a taxi or book private transportation to your resort. Hotels, resorts and condo properties are not permitted to offer complimentary or in-house airport shuttle services to arriving and departing guests to protect the local taxi and licensed public transit trade. When exiting the airport, simply locate the taxi stand directly outside the main arrivals greeting area for a ride to your hotel.

The best part of staying in Grand Cayman is that the island has no shortage of luxury hotel options in the Seven Mile Beach area, the ideal home base for island activities and excursions.

I stayed at the Kimpton Seafire Resort + Spa, which has three on-site restaurants and bars, a Forbes Five-Star spa (trust me, book the massage) and daily yoga and fitness classes overlooking the ocean. The sprawling pool connects directly to Seven Mile Beach, and the hotel regularly hosts events ranging from mixology classes to live Caribbean music, so there is always something to do.

Other TPG-recommended properties include:

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Cardmembers can book hotels through Chase Travel and receive up to $100 in statement credits each account anniversary year on eligible hotel stays. The cherry on top? After the first $100 in hotel purchases that qualify for the credit, you'll earn 5 points per dollar on additional hotel purchases made through Chase Travel with your Sapphire Preferred card.

All these recommended properties are part of a wave of luxury hotels elevating the Caribbean escape. Keep an eye out for additional resorts opening in 2027 and beyond, including the highly anticipated Grand Hyatt Grand Cayman Resort & Spa.

Once you check in and freshen up, head downstairs at Kimpton Seafire to dine at Ave. The Mediterranean-inspired menu has plenty to choose from, and I can say the local snapper ($38) and the Mediterranean orzo salad ($22) were excellent — and don’t skip the creamy mashed potatoes ($9).

The cocktails were as beautiful as the sunset you'll watch from their outdoor patio. I sipped a colorful mocktail called the Butterfly Lemonade ($12), made with butterfly pea flower, ginger, rosemary, orange, cinnamon, lemon and soda, while my husband enjoyed the Ponoma, which features Beefeater gin, Dolin dry, grapefruit and hibiscus cordial, lemon and ginger ale. It was a perfect ending to day one.

Spend day two on one of Cayman Island’s most popular and iconic excursions: a boat tour to Stingray City. The famous shallow sandbars on the North Sound sit in water that can only be described as Gatorade blue, where visitors can stand, swim and interact with dozens of friendly, wild southern stingrays. If you don’t feel like getting up close and personal with the rays, you are welcome to soak up the sun and enjoy the views from the boat.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Activities and tours booked through Chase Travel, such as a boat excursion to Stingray City, earn 5 points per dollar when you pay with your Preferred Card.

For a rooftop sunset dinner, make a reservation at Pom Pom at the neighboring Hotel Indigo, where you can enjoy Caribbean small plates and cocktails with some of the best views Grand Cayman has to offer. Since Hotel Indigo and the Kimpton Seafire are IHG sister properties, you can just take a quick three-minute golf cart ride to get there, no taxi required.

After a long day in the sun, I sipped on the Raspberry & Chicha Tereré ($13), an alcohol-free refresher that blends yerba mate, raspberry, and purple corn. For food, our server recommended the Picanha ($39), a 10-oz. sirloin cap with a Brazilian vinaigrette and lava salt, and Pollo Anticuchos ($30), chicken skewers with Peruvian chilies puré and chimichurri that had a little kick without being too spicy. For dessert, do not skip the Quatro Leches ($15) cake; it was sweet, light and absolutely delicious. Needless to say, it was one of my favorite meals of the whole trip.

Wake up bright and early and take a taxi to Cayman Crystal Caves, an underground cave system that's part geology lesson, part adventure, and it’s safe for all ages. The caves are accessible through guided tours that last about an hour and a half, and take you through chambers filled with stalactites and stalagmites that formed over millennia.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Transportation expenses such as taxi rides can earn 2 points per dollar with the Chase Sapphire Preferred card, helping you earn bonus points even when you're exploring beyond your hotel or resort.

If you have time, visit the Queen Elizabeth II Botanical Gardens before heading back to the resort. It has 65 acres of maintained grounds with orchid gardens and woodland trails. You'll wind through native plant collections, endemic species and tropical pathways, home to endangered Grand Cayman Blue Iguanas and other Caribbean-native animals. I’d budget about 90 minutes to wander.

For sunset dinner on the beach, head over to Bonny Moon Beach Club. It’s a two-minute walk from the Kimpton, and the restaurant offers seating under their outdoor canopy or directly on the sand. You can’t go wrong with anything on the menu either: flatbreads, ceviches and hummus will all make for delicious accompaniments to another perfect view of the sun setting over the water.

After a few days full of adventure and sightseeing, I prefer to slow it down on my last full day with a little R&R, and that, of course, includes a trip to the spa. Book a morning treatment at The Spa at Seafire, as I did, and enjoy the Artisan’s Touch massage ($250) or a facial that incorporates locally inspired ingredients and techniques to really lean into the Caribbean vibes. (Ask for Donna if she is available!)

And of course, take advantage of the included amenities, such as the spa garden, steam room, cold plunge and hot tub.

In the afternoon, take it easy with a poolside lunch, then head on over to the beach to unwind on a lounger and go for a calming swim in the Caribbean's clear waters.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: One of my favorite multipliers on the card focuses on dining. You’ll earn 3 points per dollar on dining, whether it’s happy hour at Tillie's or breakfast at Ave.

For your final night, make your last dinner count at Cocoloba. The beachfront Mexican-inspired restaurant is elevated enough to feel like a celebration, but since it's located at the Kimpton Seafire, you can enjoy the meal and easily head back up to your room to pack and get proper rest before your flight home the next day.

After four days spent swimming with stingrays, exploring underground crystal caves and enjoying the Caribbean, leaving was definitely the hardest part. Thankfully, my Chase Sapphire Preferred card helped make the trip home easier. The card's application fee credit for Global Entry helped cover the cost of enrollment, and the program's expedited arrival process meant minimal wait times when we landed. Instead of standing in long lines, we had extra time to enjoy our layover before the final leg of our journey.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Back home, my grocery delivery was waiting for me. The Chase Sapphire Preferred can earn 3 points per dollar on online grocery purchases to help make the reset from vacation a little easier.

The growing number of hotels bookable with points in the Cayman Islands means your points stretch further when you visit. Plus, when you're making the most of everything the islands have to offer, the Chase Sapphire Preferred card makes it easy to earn along the way so you can easily redeem when you’re ready to come back and visit again.

#6157. Hyatt Adds Stackable Awards, But Globalists Lose Free Parking Benefit

World of Hyatt is adding new Milestone Rewards and allowing members to combine awards starting in 2027. There is plenty to like, particularly the ability to apply a suite upgrade to a free night certificate. But Globalists will lose automatic free parking on award stays, and a uniform one-year expiration will make some awards harder to use.

Hyatt has announced changes beginning January 1, 2027, that will give members more ways to earn and redeem rewards. But there are concessions here too, especially for frequent guests who already make good use of the existing benefits.

Globalists currently receive complimentary parking on eligible award nights at participating hotels where parking can be charged to the room. That can be a substantial benefit, particularly at city hotels and resorts with expensive parking.

Hyatt is replacing that status benefit with a selectable Free Parking Award, first available at 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 Base Points. Each award will cover one qualifying stay of up to seven nights and can be gifted. The improvement is that the award will work on eligible paid stays too. The drawback is that members must select it instead of another reward.

“This decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit.”

After that, Globalist status alone will not provide free parking.

I appreciate the advance notice, but this is a devaluation for members who regularly drive to Hyatt properties and redeem points, a benefit I used regularly when I was still Globalist and still use on Guest of Honor awards today.

The ability to stack eligible awards is the most appealing part of this announcement and is a very positive change. Starting in 2027, members can combine a Suite Upgrade Award with a free night certificate, including Category 1–4, Category 1–7, Ultimate Free Night, and other eligible promotional certificates.

That addresses a frustrating restriction and having both a free night and a suite upgrade in your account should make it easier to plan a special stay. Other eligible combinations will include Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards, and Free Parking Awards on the same reservation.

For someone without Globalist status, combining a confirmed suite with Guest of Honor benefits could make for a very nice stay. For a Globalist, being able to confirm a suite while using a free night certificate is also very useful.

There are still restrictions. For example, the new Thompson Hotels and Premium Suite credits cannot be combined with a Free Night Award (I address the new milestone awards below). Hyatt has published the details on its 2027 updates page.

Awards issued beginning January 1, 2027, will expire 365 days after issuance.

That makes the rules easier to remember, but whether it helps depends on the award.

Some milestone free night certificates currently expire after 180 days. Doubling that window is welcome…six months can pass very quickly when you are trying to find the right opportunity to use a certificate.

But Suite Upgrade Awards, Club Access Awards, and Guest of Honor Awards currently can remain valid considerably longer, through the end of February of the second calendar year after they are earned. Reducing those to one year is a loss. Even today as I look to book stays in January and February of next year, I’ll be using those “older” Guest of Honor Awards.

That said, I would not call this change unreasonable and for most people it will be a net positive.

Milestone Rewards will begin at 10 qualifying nights or 20,000 Base Points, with additional milestones every 10 nights through 150.

Here are some notable new choices (which are in addition to the existing choices):

The $500 Premium Suite Credit awarded at 100 nights requires an eligible paid stay of at least two nights. I would evaluate that against what I would otherwise spend…a discount on an expensive suite is only useful if you would not otherwise get the upgrade anyway as a Globalist.

At 50 nights, the suite upgrade choice drops from two awards to one.

At 60 nights, My Hyatt Concierge becomes a selection rather than an automatic benefit (a worthless benefit, in my opinion). Members will choose two rewards from a menu that also includes suite upgrades, parking, points, and a skimpy Delta eCertificate.

If you value your concierge and want to retain the suite upgrades, that leaves no selection for parking…

The new Delta partnership adds eCertificates at milestones from 20–60 nights, two single-visit Sky Club passes at 70, 80, and 90 nights, and Medallion status options at higher thresholds. Of course the Delta Air Lines awards replace the American Airlines awards.

Members will need to link their Hyatt and Delta accounts. Hyatt is also enhancing “Pay My Way” so members can choose awards, points, cash, or Points + Cash for individual nights within a stay.

Hyatt’s technology has long lagged, but this is a nice new update.

The ability to combine free night certificates with suite upgrades is an excellent change. Earlier milestones and additional reward choices should also give members more opportunities to find something useful.

But the parking change is a loss for Globalists who regularly use that benefit. Shorter validity for some awards, fewer suite upgrades at 50 nights, and making concierge access a choice deserve attention too, as much I always loathed my own concierge agents.

I appreciate that Hyatt is providing notice and protecting existing parking benefits during the transition. All in all, I’d say these changes are positive, but will hurt some travelers a lot more than others.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Going to respectfully disagree here on the parking. And no, I am not some defensive fan boy.

As a many year Lifetime Globalist I have taken advantage of the free parking perhaps twice total on redemptions. I would say most are like me and that Hyatt is correct on those numbers they cited. The reality is that aspirational properties, the ones a Globalist would likely be wanting to use points at (I hope!) are rarely going to result in the need for parking. Maldives, Paris, London, New York, Milan, Tokyo, Any SE Asia property are all examples of Park Hyatts (which comprise the most percentage of aspirational hotels) and for which I imagine Hyatt’s number is conservative – betting parking comprises less than 5% of total check-ins on points. In fact, the only Park Hyatt I have ever redeemed points and used parking was in Sydney. And I have stayed at most all of them across the world. Properties like in Chicago are usually priced such as to not justify using points anyway.

I am actually much happier with the 7 day free parking milestone which I can use somewhere like in Chicago where I never redeem points.

Hyatt’s concierge service for globalists is generally useless.

So while having to choose concierge service over other benefits is a devaluation of globalist, it’s, practically speaking, not a huge loss for most members.

The loss of free parking on award-redemption stays is somewhat similar. On paper, it’s a significant devaluation. However, how many guests actually use it? If I’m going to a resort, I’m not arriving with a car. Same for if I’m redeeming points to stay at the Park Hyatt in Paris or wherever. So, practically speaking, it may not be a huge loss for many elites.

What I don’t understand is why wouldn’t you come up with better offerings for globalists who do 100, 120 or 150+ nights?

I wish they would have created a benefit to compensate for the growing number of Hyatt Regency and Grand Hyatt properties WITHOUT an open or operational club lounge.

I personally wish they’d get rid of the club passes since it seems that most properties I’ve been to sinve covid have closed them. I’d prefer free breakfast vouchers for the years I come up short of globalist.
