#6156. The Best Places to Go in Africa in 2027

While editing this year’s list, one thing quickly became very clear: 2027 is poised to be a banner one for cultural experiences across Africa. While chatting with our writers, I kept finding compelling reasons to go back to my favorite corners—the Kigali Triennale’s return to Rwanda in September, Jazzablanca’s 20th anniversary in Casablanca, and an even more vibrant creative landscape in Tunis than the one I reported on six years ago. But now I’m adding Benin to my list, thanks to four—yes, four—eagerly anticipated new museums debuting in the year ahead that will showcase everything from modern art to critical artifacts recently repatriated from Europe. Elsewhere on the continent there are fresh ways to experience some of its familiar pleasures, owing to a high-end resort boom on the beaches of Zanzibar, a host of safari lodge openings in Zambia, eight new marine reserves in São Tomé and Principe, and a groundbreaking five-country trans-frontier conservation area. Be sure to make some time for rarer incentives to travel too, like a once-in-a-generation “superbloom” in South Africa and the “eclipse of the century” over Luxor, Egypt (it also helps that there are some swish new places to stay at these places).But one of the most endearing stories of an African destination of the past year may be Cape Verde: Is the “World Cup effect” going to bring a wave of curious travelers to the archipelago? Read on to decide for yourself. —Sarah Khan

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: a museum boom and a vibrant cultural milieu

Home to ancient Kingdom of Dahomey, Benin has transformed into a destination for heritage tourism.

Benin is a place where history runs deep: It’s home to the ancient Kingdom of Dahomey, the spiritual traditions of Vodun, and Ouidah—one of West Africa’s significant ports in the transatlantic slave trade. Now the country is turning that history into a new era of cultural tourism, while creating ways for travelers, particularly people of African descent, to reconnect with their heritage.

Ouidah, an especially important destination for those tracing their ancestry, is central to that effort. In 2025 the government announced plans to invest $1.4 billion in tourism and cultural development, including for infrastructure, heritage restitution, and indigenous traditions. In 2027 that transformation is expected to become more visible with a host of new museum openings, like the Museum of Modern Art in Cotonou; the International Museum of Memory and Slavery in Ouidah; and the Museum of the Epic of the Amazons and Kings of Dahomey in Abomey. The latter of which is expected to house 26 royal artifacts repatriated by France in 2021.

Vodun Days, an eight-day celebration of Benin’s indigenous spiritual traditions taking place January 2–9, 2027, will showcase ceremonies, music, and dance. Meanwhile, Villa Karo in Grand-Popo—a bridge between artists and researchers from Finland, Sweden, and West Africa—will continue its residency program, which brings artists to its seaside research center to connect with the local community through workshops, concerts, and exhibitions. The famous stilt village of Ganvié, meanwhile, remains open to visitors as its Reinventing the Lakeside City of Ganvié project upgrades tourism infrastructure. Benin is also beginning to make appearances on cruise itineraries. Two new Swan Hellenic sailings in 2027 sailings feature the country, including an April voyage from Luanda to Accra and an October sailing from Ghana to Angola. —Harriet Akinyi

Go for: beaches, festivals, and new-found buzz

New Cabo Verde Airlines flight routes launched in May 2026, and coupled with the “World Cup effect,” will make travel to Cape Verde more appealing than ever.

During FIFA World Cup 2026, one of the most impressive performances came from Cape Verde, an archipelago of 10 islands off Africa’s Atlantic Ocean coast. Now the “World Cup effect” has gotten travelers curious about what the destination has to offer. It helps that getting there is easier than ever, thanks to new direct flights launched in May 2026 from Rhode Island’s T.F. Green International Airport on Cabo Verde Airlines. On the island of Sal, which boasts white-sand beaches and over 350 days of sunshine a year, adrenaline-driving activities range from swimming with lemon sharks to kite- and windsurfing, while those seeking a more relaxed experience can float in the saline pools of Pedra de Lume. The island’s luxury accommodation options are also getting an upgrade with Hyatt Regency Cape Verde Sal as well as a family-friendly all-inclusive Bahia Principe set to open in 2027. In March the 322-room Robinson Boa Vista will welcome its first guests to the easternmost island of Boa Vista, known as the Sahara in the Atlantic due to its desert-like flat plains. São Vicente and Praia are the islands to hit for local music—the samba-inspired São Vicente Carnival features dance performances, fireworks, and floats, while Praia hosts the annual Kriol Jazz Festival and the Atlantic Music Expo. Africa’s first Four Points by Sheraton resort opened in the port city of São Vicente last March, with 105 rooms and 22 suites overlooking either Laginha Beach, known for its turquoise waters, or the Monte Verde mountains. —Mazuba Kapambwe

Go for: a vibrant cultural and design scene

Casablanca's 2027 roster of cultural events include the 20th anniversary of Jazzablanca in July and the newly launched Morocco Design fair.

Casablanca stealthily enters 2027 as Africa’s most creative urban reinvention. It’s an apt year to visit, given the pioneering Royal Air Maroc flights, launched in June 2026, linking Casablanca with Los Angeles—the first African connection to America's Pacific Coast. It is a poetic bridge, connecting the dream factory that conjured Casablanca’s mythic character with the modern metropolis redefining itself as a vanguard of contemporary Maghrebi culture. A cornerstone of this cultural renaissance is the 20th anniversary of Jazzablanca in July: Once an intimate gathering, it has evolved into North Africa's best boutique music festival, hosting emerging Afrobeat, jazz, and urban artists beneath the modernist skyscrapers in Anfa Park and on stages in the palm-lined Arab League Park beside the Nevada skate park. Design lovers, meanwhile, can admire the Museum of Photography and Visual Arts, which was inaugurated in June in the medina and is Tadao Ando’s sole architectural project on the continent. The museum and the recently launched annual Morocco Design fair, which spotlights high-end design studios, establish Casablanca as an emerging destination for cutting-edge design, music, and art. The city's heritage sites are getting a revamp too. The iconic 1916 Neo-Moorish Lincoln Hotel by Radisson Collection is being masterfully revived by French Moroccan architects OUALALOU + CHOI, who are pairing its historic façade with an über-minimalist interior. From the hotel’s doorstep, a new tramline whisks you to the Casablanca Finance City (CFC), a glittering new commercial district composed of futuristic, climate-resilient buildings that pay homage to Casablanca’s legacy of concrete experimentation. Nearby, bougie restaurants like Le 7ème Ciel draw crowds and a new Radisson Red will open in 2027 to join an existing Radisson Blu. CFC is built on the old Anfa Airport, from which The Little Prince author and architecture school dropout Antoine de Saint-Exupéry flew a perilous mail route to Dakar in an open-cockpit Bréguet 14 biplane, returned for drinks at Le Petit Poucet, and lived with his fiery Salvadorean muse, Consuelo Suncín. Then, as now, the city was a nexus connecting continents and a frontier to the future. —Paula Hardy

Go for: a ground-breaking cross-border safari project and birding adventure

The Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area, or KAZA TFCA, is the world's largest terrestrial transboundary conservation area.

Zambia, which has forgone visa requirements of 53 countries and has increased international flights, will be the center of attention.

In a world where ecological degradation and global discord are reasons to despair, Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area, or KAZA TFCA, is more rising sun than ray of hope. Supported by five countries—Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, the world’s largest terrestrial transboundary conservation area encompasses a region roughly the size of France and is watered by the Kavango, Zambezi, Chobe, Kwando, and Kafue river systems. Officially launched in 2012, it languished as a plan on paper for years, but recent initiatives have seen it shake off bureaucratic paralysis: Green Growth for KAZA, the umbrella initiative, directly links community benefits to conservation. Several depleted parks have been rewilded; Africa’s first cross-border avitourism project, the Great Kavango Zambezi Birding Route, was recently launched; and connectivity improved—Shearzone Safari launched a charter service in Zambia in early 2026. Notably, Angola has entered the guided-safari arena with Luiana Plains Expedition Camp, the first to open in the 10.3-million-acre Luengue-Luiana National Park in July 2026. It will soon be followed by Natural Selection, which is developing a new 500,000-acre game reserve around Angola’s existing Cuatir Reserve. In Namibia’s unsung Zambezi Region, Thitake River Lodge opens on the banks of the Kwando in Bwabwara National Park late in 2026, while Nkasa Linyanti is the fabulous new linchpin in Nkasa Rupara National Park. But the KAZA TFCA region that’s experiencing the biggest proliferation is Zambia, buoyed by the scrapping of visa requirements of 53 countries and increased international flights. Ker & Downey launched its Zambia division with King Lewanika Lodge in remote Liuwa Plains National Park, the first luxury base from which to witness Africa’s second-largest wildebeest migration; its second location, Musesenji River Camp, opens in April 2027. And luring the well-heeled to 5.5-million-acre Kafue National Park are Anantara with Tented Camp Kafue River, and Classic Zambia with new Lwenge River Camp; both opened this summer. —Pippa de Bruyn

Go for: a wave of gallery and festival openings turning a gorilla trek stopover into an art capital

Kigali's art scene is ramping up as institutions like Kigali Triennial and Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art platform Rwandan and East African artists.

New Kigali properties are showcases for art, such as the nine-room Pinnacle hotel and members' club.

For years Kigali has been seen as little more than a pit stop before going gorilla trekking. Now the city is making a compelling case for staying awhile. The city’s vibrant food and fashion have already been putting it on the map, and now the art scene is getting noticed as several institutions build platforms for championing Rwandan and East African artists. September 2027 marks the second edition of the Kigali Triennial, which is primed to rival some of the continent’s more established art festivals, like ART X Lagos and Dak'Art Biennale. The Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art, which opened at the end of 2025, highlights artists from across Africa and its diasporas, with a focus on East Africa with two exhibitions: “Space Encounters,” exploring human connection and memory, which is currently on through December 2026; and a collection of contemporary work by Sudanese artists opening in January 2027. This follows the debut of the Inyuguti Art Hub this year, which brought together 19 artists from across Africa and the UK, including Rwandan Elisa Niyogisubizo (also the gallery’s founder), Burundi-based Peter Kamale, and Nigerian Pascal Ejiofor. The lines between the art and hotel scenes are beginning to blur too, with a new generation of properties doubling as cultural showcases. Among them is the nine-room Pinnacle hotel and members club that opened in early 2026 as Rwanda’s first women-led ultraluxury boutique property, showcasing the owner’s private art collection. Creative events are rippling beyond the capital, as Rwandan artists Willy Karekezi and Cedric Mizero are each launching new spaces in Musanze, the gateway town for gorilla trekking, in 2027: Karekezi will open a residency alongside his Indiba Arts Space in Kigali, and Mizero will open Umugenzi, an addition to the multisite Ikinyugunyugu art residency. —Vivienne Dovi

Go for: the eclipse of the century and nostalgia-soaked Nile cruises

Astrotourism is coming for Luxor and the Nile on August 2, 2027, thanks to the six-minute “eclipse of the century" and a wave of new boats promising prime viewing spots along the ancient waterway.

Dubbed the eclipse of the century, 2027’s much-anticipated celestial event will reach its zenith in Luxor, Egypt, on August 2, when the moon will block out the sun for a record-breaking 6 minutes and 23 seconds. Fitting, perhaps, for a place where the mystical has always loomed large, the mountains hold secret treasures, the temples and tombs have been perfectly preserved roughly 3,000 years after they were built, and the Nile exudes a life force of its own. Travelers have come to this transcendent stretch of Upper Egypt, nearly 400 miles south of Cairo, for millennia. Luxor itself served as Egypt’s capital from 1570 BCE to 1069 BCE, but today is better known as the home of the Valley of the Kings, and the start or end point of nostalgia-infused Nile cruises to and from Aswan, a leisurely four- or five-day sail away. Both destinations are primed for a momentous 2027: In Luxor the much-loved Winter Palace—archaeologist Howard Carter’s base during his 1922 Tutankhamen tomb discovery—will reopen in July as a Mandarin Oriental after an extensive renovation exactly 120 years after its official inauguration. Aswan’s own grande dame, the Old Cataract, which famously inspired Agatha Christie’s best-selling novel Death on the Nile, has also been taken over by Mandarin Oriental and will reopen its Nile Wing in 2027 after a thorough upgrade. Mandarin Oriental will launch its first Nile cruise that connects the two, joining a flurry of other new boats taking to the ancient waterway. Among them Oberoi’s Melouk and Malekat dahabiyas, with only seven cabins apiece, and homegrown operator Kemetale’s second boat, Deshret, with its Nile-view sauna, plunge pool, and spa treatments. —Selina Denman

Go for: a rare ‘superbloom’ of endemic flora and world-class wines at Africa’s southern tip.

Cape Agulhas, Africa's southernmost tip, offers a new interpretation center focused on the history and geology of Agulhas, as well as a 177-year-old lighthouse.

Chef Michael Broughton, formerly of Terroir in Stellenbosch, now leads the kitchen at historic Fisherman’s Cottage, putting seafood centerstage.

Cape Town. Winelands. Then head off on safari. That’s the typical circuit for travelers jetting into South Africa. But in 2027 look beyond to the Overberg—“over mountain” in Afrikaans—region, where wildfires have triggered a floral extravaganza not seen in decades. Base yourself in Hermanus for memorable whale watching from the seven-and-a-half-mile Cliff Path. The Marine Hotel, a seafront landmark since 1902, has unveiled a fynbos-inspired revamp of its public spaces and seafood-driven Pavilion Restaurant. There’s a new culinary energy in town too: Chef Michael Broughton, previously at Terroir in Stellenbosch, has turned the historic Fisherman’s Cottage into a hotbed of polished Cape coastal cuisine (don’t miss the spaghetti aglio e olio with local rock lobster). Broughton’s wine list leans into estates from the nearby Hemel-en-Aarde (Heaven and Earth) valley, where cellars are known for exceptional Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Creation Wines offers a new sculpture-led vineyard walk, and opens a private tasting room in May 2027 aimed at wine lovers looking for a deep dive into the cool-climate terroir. Bouchard Finlayson, one of the oldest estates in the valley, reopens in late 2027 after an extensive renovation, with a new tasting space and art collection.

Set in the heart of the Cape Floristic Region, Grootbos Private Nature Reserve is a biodiversity hot spot. Wildfires that swept the area in 2025 sparked a superbloom of new growth, including dormant species that haven’t flowered in decades like wild orchids and the fire-dependent Gladiolus overbergensis. Guided botanical walks and drives get you in the thick of the fynbos, but a new equestrian center also makes this a great choice for horse-riding holidays. Long popular with families, Coot Club, on the nearby Klein River Lagoon, expands in 2027 with a pair of new two-bedroom boathouses and brings a new wellness focus with outdoor yoga sessions and in-room wellness treatments. Toast it all with a sundowner in the refreshed Flamingo Bar upstairs in the original homestead. An hour’s drive east, Cape Agulhas, the southernmost tip of Africa, is a fitting finale. A new interpretation center delves into the history and geology of Agulhas, after which you can climb the 177-year-old lighthouse and stand on the rocky shoreline where the Indian and Atlantic Oceans meet. —Richard Holmes

Go for: new marine reserves and World Heritage Sites

Often known as the African Galapagos for its high concentration of endemic species, the island nation of São Tomé and Principe is surrounded by clear waters full of manta rays, sharks, and migrating humpback whales.

On the islands of São Tomé and Príncipe, more than 155 miles off the coast of Gabon in the Gulf of Guinea, a thick rainforest punctuated by needle-like rock formations meets shores of white and volcanic black sand. One of the world’s least visited countries, and known as the African Galapagos for its high concentration of endemic species, this island nation is surrounded by clear turquoise waters brimming with manta rays and reef and nurse sharks. Humpback whales migrate through seasonally, and turtles begin to nest on the beaches in November before hatching between February and April. In 2025 the first two of eight new dedicated marine reserves, Santana and Ilhéu das Rolas, were approved; in 2026, six roças, or former Portuguese plantations, were designated UNESCO World Heritage Sites, recognized for their role in shaping the social, economic, and cultural history of the nation, which was once the world’s preeminent supplier of cacao. Two of these roças are a part of the Príncipe Collection—the hospitality arm of sustainable development group HBD Príncipe—meaning you can stay at these historically significant sites. One of the properties on offer is Hotel Belo Monte, which opened in June and sits high up on a hillside overlooking the rainforest and sea. A stay in this eco-hideaway, chicly styled with splashes of bold color, comes with cultural insight and an immersion into the wild surroundings. Another outpost, Sundy Praia, is set within what was once part of Príncipe’s second-largest cocoa plantation on the remote northwest tip and hosts guests in tented villas backing the golden shores on the remote northwest tip of the island. —Lauren Burris Hill

Go for: ancient treasures and contemporary culture by the sea

Villa Kahina, an intimate guesthouse that opened in September in Tunis.

In the blue and white village of Sidi Bou Saïd, the six-room Villa Kahina offers views of the Mediterranean.

Designated 2027’s Arab Capital of Tourism, this languid North African city now pulses with the energy of a new generation of Tunisian creatives and entrepreneurs. Events planned in the historic Medina range from TedX Pasha Street talks and musical retreats to artisanal workshops, many organized by the beloved Dar Ben Gacem boutique hotel and cultural hub, which will also host a rooftop event for August’s solar eclipse. Across the Medina, near the Great Mosque of Zitouna, Dar Ben Turkia's early 2026 opening expands the luxury-hotel options that preserve the area’s history. The elegant eight-suite hideaway has an in-house hammam and spa, so it doubles as a wellness retreat in the heart of the Medina. Beyond the medieval city’s labyrinths, the sun-kissed ruins of ancient Carthage spill toward the coast. Anchoring these archaeological riches is the Carthage National Museum, slated to reopen by year-end after an eight-year overhaul. For more contemporary treasures, head downhill to the city’s leading art gallery, Selma Feriani, which in 2027 will exhibit major Tunisian artists Mohamed Amine Hamouda and Rafik El Kamel.

Nearby, sleek seaside city La Marsa gives way to the historically working-class neighborhood of Bhar Lazreg, where artists and makers have been repurposing spaces. Anchors like the B7L9 Art Centre (built by and for the area’s community), and Phosphor Creative District—showcasing local talent who specialize in everything from fine art to design—are transforming the area into a meeting place for artists, demonstrating why the neighborhood has become known as one of Tunis’s coolest. Meanwhile, fashionable La Marsa remains a firm favorite with the stylish set, and mid-2026 restaurant openings like Oto, a Japanese izakaya, and Sujet, a hybrid café and design store, keep things fresh. When you’re ready for a break, make your way up the coast to Birdie at The Clubhouse in Gammarth, which opened in August 2026, or south to Villa Kahina, an intimate guesthouse that began welcoming guests in September. Perched on the forested edge of the iconic blue and white village of Sidi Bou Saïd, this whitewashed six-room sanctuary with sweeping Mediterranean views feels almost untouched by time. —Lee Middleton

Go for: a host of new hotels from which to experience some of Africa’s best beaches

Beyond its beaches, Zanzibar is set to welcome two new luxury properties: Anantara Zanzibar Resort and Residences in 2027, followed by Four Seasons Resort Zanzibar at Pongwe in 2028.

Most visitors arrive in Zanzibar with postcard perfection already in mind—turquoise shallows, swaying palms, and dhows tipping into the sunset—but the island’s enduring drawcard is still Stone Town: a UNESCO-listed tangle of coral-rag limestone alleys, carved Omani doors, and clove-scented air, where Africa, Arabia, and India have intersected for centuries. In 2027 Zanzibar gets its most serious branded hotel wave yet with the 181-key Anantara Zanzibar Resort & Residences on the north coast, and in 2028 it will welcome, the 60-villa Four Seasons Resort Zanzibar at Pongwe, widely regarded as the loveliest beach on the east coast. The latter is a short flight from the brand’s Serengeti lodge and has been built with a bush-and-beach pairing in mind. The freshest energy is homegrown, though, and it has moved away from the overdeveloped north. In Jambiani, on the sunrise-facing southeast coast, the seven-villa Ma’a Salama (“go in peace”) opened in mid-2026 as a nonprofit that doubles as a hospitality school, training island youth in exchange for a year’s free education. Ma’a Salama’s spacious villas are named for spices and are cooled by bioclimatic design rather than air-conditioning, and four are crowned with rooftop teahouses, designed in Stone Town’s famous Emerson’s teahouses. On the quiet southwest coast at Kizimkazi, Kizikula is the antithesis of a resort: no sign, no jetty, just a jungly pathway leading to what feels more like a private home or artist’s enclave than a hotel. At low tide, guests access the beach through a secret gap in the coral cliff. Designed by Mumbai’s Case Design, its coral-limestone rooms sit in wild permaculture gardens. In 2026 the resort added 19 rooms, and in December it will open a new rooftop sunset bar and a three-floor wellness center, where treatments incorporate ingredients like Zanzibari cinnamon, turmeric, and cardamom. As of October 2026 Airlink flies the first-ever nonstop route between Cape Town and Zanzibar, with low-cost FlySafair rumored to be expanding its regular Johannesburg service to include Cape Town too. The UK gets its own first direct link in November 2027, courtesy of TUI Airways’s Gatwick service, along with a direct London flight from Air Tanzania. —Jane Broughton

#6155. Review: Austrian Airlines A320 Economy Class

After a lovely stay in Vienna, we continued our journey to Zürich onboard an Austrian Airlines A320 in economy class.

We arrived at the airport around 9:30 am, figuring there would be no need to get there early to use a lounge when we had just enjoyed an excellent breakfast at the Park Hyatt Vienna.

The airport was busy but we used the Star Gold corridor to enjoy expedited security and were soon at the gate, ready to board our short flight to Switzerland.

Stepping onboard, we headed to the back to find our seats in row 22.

The Austrian A320 has 180 seats arranged in a 3-3 configuration (same in business class, though the middle seat is blocked).

The Recaro BL3520 “NEK” slimline seats are very uncomfortable with very little padding. These are familiar seats if you have flown within Europe on Lufthansa Group carriers, with a literature pocket and a folding tray table on the seatback ahead.

Legroom varies by aircraft and row. Austrian lists a minimum economy class seat pitch of just 28 inches across its A320 fleet, so do not expect much room to stretch out, though it felt like we had 29 inches.

There are no power ports or USB ports on this aircraft. Thankfully, however, there are individual air vents, unlike on the 777.

In economy class, passengers receive a free glass of water and Austrian chocolate.

For those peckish, buy-on-board is available. I pre-ordered a hot meal from the carrier’s Austrian Melangerie menu.

What else would I order on Austrian Airlines but Wiener Schnitzel? While a proper Wiener Schnitzel is made with veal, Austrian uses chicken onboard, describing the dish as:

Golden-brown chicken schnitzel with parsley potatoes

The price was €13.80, though I received a 10% discount for pre-ordering.

Presentation was very much like economy class: the schnitzel and potatoes were served together in a cardboard box, but sometimes you have to look beyond the presentation. The chicken was tender, the breading remained surprisingly crisp, and the parsley potatoes were a nice accompaniment…my son Augustine and I both enjoyed it.

I highlighted this meal in a recent Meal of the Week feature.

> Read More: Austrian Airlines’ €13.80 Wiener Schnitzel On An 80-Minute Flight

I had also hoped to try the Julius Meinl Wiener Melange, a €5.20 coffee served with milk foam in a proper ceramic cup on a silver tray. Alas, Austrian only offers the Melange on flights of at least 80 minutes and our Vienna to Zürich flight was apparently five minutes too short according to the flight attendant.

Before landing I used the lavatory in the rear of the aircraft and it was messy by that point, with paper towels overflowing from the waste receptacle.

While there is no seatback screens or streaming movies and TV shows, Wi-Fi was available for purchase onboard. A high speed pass (Viasat) was 6€ while messaging was free. I had trouble connecting, initially, but ultimately was able to pay the 6€ and connect.

This was a quick, boring flight with a delicious lunch onboard thanks to the buy-on-board menu. I’d never go out of my way to fly Austrian shorthaul in economy class, but if you are stuck behind the curtain, do take advantage of the pre-order menu to make the flight go by a bit faster.

My original review, covering an Austrian Airlines A320 journey from Vienna to Yerevan, Armenian (fun trip!) in 2019 is below.

What is Austrian Airlines like on a mid-haul flight in economy class?

My business partner, John, and I spent a weekend in Yerevan, Armenia last month. We were in Vienna earlier in the week, so the nonstop Austrian flight from VIE to EVN made the most sense. We booked for 15,000 United miles each in economy class.

Business class would have been an extra 10,000 miles, but I figured 1.) the seat is the same, 2.) I already had lounge access, and 3.) we would be eating dinner just before the flight. So the upgrade did not make sense.

Vienna International Airport is such an easy airport to navigate. Check-in (John had to check a bag), security, and passport control took only a few moments. I’ll review the Austrian lounge in a separate post.

Boarding commenced precisely on schedule with business class passenger and Star Alliance Gold members invited to board first.

I’ll start with the seats and the following warning: these slimline seats are very uncomfortable. By the time we reached Yerevan three hours later, I could not wait to get off. The seats do recline slightly, but the lack of padding makes for an uncomfortable flying experience on flights longer than 60-90 minutes. But that’s hardly a unique experience to Austrian. Seat pitch is 30 inches.

Notice that the only difference in business class hard product is that the middle seat is blocked:

A sticker on the aircraft fuselage indicated wi-fi internet would be available, but it did not function. There are no in-seat power ports.

First, I appreciated the pillows and blankets, both of which were better than many airlines offer in economy class. Heck, United does not even offer pillows in domestic first class except on premium transcontinental flight.

That said, it was roasting outside and the cabin was not overly cool…not exactly heavy blanket weather.

Second, I appreciated the meal, as small as it was. A vegetarian cheese pasta with cake and bread was served after takeoff. Talk about a load of carbs! Passengers were not offered a choice of meal.

Flight attendants came around before the meal and also about 90 minutes before landing with a beverage serevice.

Finally, the lavatory was very clean…these pictures are toward the end of the flight.

I appreciate that Austrian is full service in the sense that blankets, pillows, and meals are provided. But three hours really pushes the limit for this type of slimline seat. I’ll happily fly Austrian again, but ideally on a shorthaul route or on a widebody jet in business class…

> Review: Austrian Airlines 767 Business Class from Beijing to Vienna

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

I have never understood who pays for the business class when it is the same seat, and if you have status you can get within a few rows of the front of the plane in economy.

I also don’t understand why all EU countries fly planes with no real business/first on flights that are this long, (2-4 hours) and are very much international. Almost all US planes have domestic first, even if they are only going an hour or two. How did things evolve so differently in the EU??

Many executives in Europe have business class travel as a part of their contracts. Non-cash perks like company cars, per diems, and travel perks are (and have historically been) more common there because they’re not taxed the same way (if at all) as wage/salary income.

These flex systems, although offering an inferior hard product, allow European carriers to flex their cabins to accommodate far more business class fliers. I’ve seen as many as the first 12 rows flexed to biz!

@Lara S, mallthus is correct that the present business class model allows for flexibility depending upon loads. Aeroflot, Tarom, and Turkish have real business class seats.

Iberia has also started incorporating ‘real’ business class seats on short to mid-haul flights on its A319..I had it from MAD-FLR, but I think its more commonly used on routes to Tel Aviv, Moscow Etc.

Looks and reminds me a lot of DLs old J seat on their 767s..

One reason to use it is when connecting with a long haul flight. Suppose you buy a business class ticket from New York to Yerevan via Vienna. You’d get the real thing in the trans Atlantic section, then a blocked middle seat.

The seats are the same as LH. After two hours on one recently I had back pain and a numb a*se. Apparently they are now being replaced by ones that according to the LH CEO Spohr are ‘even more comfortable’. I wait in fear!

Austrian unlike the other LH group carriers also use these seats on their long haul aircraft in economy. You have been warned!

I think Europeans find US Domestic premium cabins and products as strange and confusing as we find their intro-European premium product.

In the US, we call it First Class (but it’s closer to Business Class). You get a big seat with more leg room. Generally the plane is WiFi equipped with either IFE or streaming entertainment at no charge. You only get a meal if it’s over a certain length (2-3 hours) and during meal times. You also do not get Lounge access (but lounge access is commonly available through a credit card or membership program).

In the EU, you get a coach seat with a blocked middle. The leg room is less than what is available in the US in the Economy Plus, Main Cabin Extra, etc. cabins. You get Lounge access and a meal that is generally better than what you would get on a US carrier for the same stage length. WiFi and IFE/streaming entertainment is not as common.

I absolutely prefer the US model but it is what I am used to. I get my Lounge access through my credit cards. I would prefer an MCE seat to Euro Business any day and I can book those seats at ticketing. But I’m guessing some Euro business man would find the lack of a meal and complimentary lounge access disappointing.

FOLKS, note this is a brand new review that I just stacked on top of my old one.

#6154. At the Races: Regional realignment

By Daniela Altimari, Mary Ellen McIntire and Niels Lesniewski

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, New England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.)

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison?  Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

How Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The New York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#6153. Southeast Asia’s Coolest New Hotels Are Eco-Conscious Tented Camps

There's something exhilarating about bedding down under canvas: the fresh breeze drifting in, the sounds of distant rumbles and nearby rustling, and an untouched landscape unfurling right at the foot of your bed. For decades those experiences have been synonymous with the classic safari lodges pitched up around East and Southern Africa, but a new generation of small-scale camps are giving the concept a Southeast Asian spin. These intimate and wonderfully wild retreats, including one in a remote corner of northwest Cambodia and another in the forest-cloaked mountains of central Vietnam, trade the region's usual resort formula for a lighter footprint and, with it, a much deeper connection to its jungle perch.

A boat excursion on an underground river inside Vietnam’s largest cave network

In the shade of the camel-hump limestone karst formations of central Vietnam's Phong Nha–Ké Bàng National Park, Auko Eco recently opened as a plush base to wind down between mud-splattered mountain hikes and scrambles within the world's largest cave system. The camp's 30 canvas suites, each with mod cons like air-conditioning and an open-air bathtub, are built from local bamboo and timber reclaimed from fishing boats, and they are clustered so that most of the plots' native plant cover remains intact. Riverside yoga classes, hydrotherapy, and sound-healing sessions in the on-site meditation cave soothe minds and muscles after a day in the wild.

One of the 15 safari-style tents at Siempang Forest Lodge

Inside one of the guest tents at Siempang Forest Lodge

The songs of Cambodia's most elusive bird species make up the soundtrack to a stay at Siempang Forest Lodge, a camp of 15 safari-style tents on stilted decks that opened last fall in the heart of a 330,577-acre wildlife sanctuary of the same name. While there's a pool, a simple spa, and a well-stocked bar for sundowners, the camp's conservation-minded backstory is the real draw. Guests can join local rangers on forest walks and birding excursions to spot critically endangered critters such as wild bantengs (a species of cattle), Siamese crocodiles, and giant ibis, and learn firsthand how tourism helps revive and safeguard one of the country's last great swaths of wilderness.

At the entrance to Vietnam’s Hang So’n Đoòng, one of the largest natural caves in the world

Over the last few years, Koh Phangan has been shedding its Full Moon Party reputation by swapping the usual days of debauchery for holidays with a more mindful tilt. When Kaia, draped over a palm-heavy peninsula on the island's quiet northeast, opens, it will embrace that go-slow shift with 35 tented suites furnished with floorboards from reclaimed teak and decor from upcycled materials. Communal meals that center on homegrown produce cooked over an open fire will be served at the beach club and the breezy restaurant up the hill, while a stable of activities like ceramic workshops, guided foraging trips, and breath work sessions will tap into the local creative community.

#6152. Finding Unexpected Joy In Music And Hospitality From Los Angeles To Malibu

One of the beautiful things about traveling around the world is the chance to experience hospitality in different ways in different countries. I’ll never forget the hospitality I experienced In Iran or in Ukraine, but sometimes we don’t have to travel far to experience it, as I recently found out in Los Angeles.

I listen to music during the day as I work on this blog and on my other work. Some people require absolute silence to work, but I like music, specially Christian hymns. I primarily use YouTube and of course the algorithm gets to know you. There’s no music I like more than a powerful organ playing a beloved hymn. Lately, the algorithm has been suggesting a very gifted organist named Lauma Akmene, a Latvian-born musician who is the organist, conductor, and music director at St. Peter’s Episcopal Church in Salisbury, Maryland.

As I listened to her music all morning, one of her YouTube shorts noted that she would be performing a classical concert in Los Angeles, which immediately piqued my interest.

I obtained a ticket and found the concert would be held at a place called Stan’s Musical Parlor, which was actually a beautiful 1926 home in LA’s posh Lafayette Square neighborhood. Not knowing quite what to expect, I showed up and was warmly greeted by Stanley Harris himself, who I came to find out has opened his house since 1986 to showcase musical talents. Dr. Harris is a retired psychiatrist and was a longtime clinician and faculty member at the University of Southern California.

Stan has a Johannus-BachMen-Hauptwerk organ (including Hauptwerk virtual pipe organs) in his living room. Essentially, this digital organ can be set to emulate sounds from many of famous pipe organs around the world.

The concert began at 8:00 pm and was simply fabulous, with Lauma playing several classic and neo-classic works.

One of the guests mentioned that he was hosting Lauma the following evening at his home in Malibu, and invited me to attend. I had to be in Palm Springs for work that day, but I drove from Palms Springs all the way to Malibu via Pacific Coast Highway (took about three hours!) and made it just in time for the concert, another fabulous evening of food, fellowship, and great music.

Already, I’ve made friends through these two events, who I am staying in touch with, and will go to more of these concerts. Community is beautiful thing, as is hospitality, and all in my backyard, one of the many reasons I love Los Angeles and Southern California so much.

Truth be told, I almost did not go to either event. I was tired and probably could have used a couple extra hours of sleep. But I’m so glad I did go and I’m thankful to YouTube for suggesting Lauma and making these two possible in the first place.

Lauma is such a gifted organist. If you like classical music and especially sacred music, you can enjoy her work here.

American citizens do not need a visa to visit Tunisia for stays of 90 days or less, just a valid passport with at least six months’ validity and one blank page.

Tipping is appreciated but not expected, unlike in many neighboring countries such as Egypt. I generally added 10% to restaurant bills and rounded up taxi fares. For my tours, I tipped between 20 and 50 dinars, depending on the length and whether there was a separate driver.

Tunisia is essentially bilingual, with most people speaking Arabic and French fluently. In most tourist destinations and hotels, people spoke English, but the French I remembered from high school did help me in a few situations.

Ride-hailing apps like Uber are not available in Tunisia. Taxis are available, but ask for the fare upfront or confirm the meter is turned on before getting in. I pre-booked airport transfers through my hotels to avoid negotiating prices on the spot.

For my road trip, I found it easy to rent and drive a car throughout Tunisia. There is a major highway with toll booths running north to south through the country. In more rural parts of the south, roads are still well maintained — just watch out for sneaky speed bumps. All my hotels featured easy parking, but keep in mind that hotels inside medinas may not be accessible by car or might require navigating very narrow streets. Driving behavior is more erratic in Tunis, but generally, I found the rest of the country easy to drive in.

To visit mosques, you’ll need to cover your knees and shoulders — as well as hair if you’re a woman — but coverings are provided free of charge at most. To adapt to the heat and sun, wear loose layers of light-colored linen and be sure to bring a hat.

The U.S. Department of State lists Tunisia as a Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution, which contains areas with a higher security risk, the same as Turkey and Egypt. Save for a few curious stares from men and one overzealous self-appointed medina guide who demanded a tip, I felt perfectly safe as a solo female traveler. It is best to avoid wandering around medinas after dark since most shops and restaurants are closed anyway. I felt most comfortable with pre-arranged guides, but more because they knew exactly where to go, and I didn’t have to navigate things solo.

For the most comfortable weather with a low chance of rain, visit Tunisia between March and May or between October and November. If you do decide to visit for the Aug. 2, 2027 solar eclipse, keep in mind it can get up to 120 degrees Fahrenheit in the middle of the day out in the desert. During my visit in August, I also experienced rolling blackouts and bottled water shortages.

Tunisia is about to have a big year. On the morning of Aug. 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse will cut a path across the central part of the North African nation, bringing several minutes of darkness to sites like the ancient Roman amphitheater in El Jem, the Great Mosque of Kairouan and the dramatic Sahara Desert dunes and canyons surrounding Tozeur.

The latter will also draw “Star Wars” fans to many of the Tatooine filming locations to mark the franchise’s 50th anniversary of the movie’s release in 2027. The capital of Tunis isn’t in the path of totality, but any trip in 2027 should also include a stop in the picturesque cliffside village of Sidi Bou Said, which UNESCO recently added to its World Heritage list, joining other culturally significant sites like the Medina of Tunis and the Archaeological Site of Carthage.

This 7-day itinerary covers a tour of Tunisia’s most important cultural and historic landmarks in a road trip from Tunis to Tozeur and back, plus tips for where to be during the 2027 eclipse and how to maximize the perks and benefits of the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) along the way.

Currently, there are no nonstop flights between the United States and Tunisia, so you’ll need to plan for at least one layover before connecting to Tunis-Carthage International Airport (TUN), the country’s largest airport.

I flew to TUN on Air France via Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), since I’m loyal to the SkyTeam alliance and it offered the most frequent connections. However, if you’re loyal to another airline alliance, you can also find connections to TUN on Lufthansa via Frankfurt, ITA via Rome, Royal Air Maroc via Casablanca and Turkish Airlines via Istanbul.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: When booking flights, check the Chase Travel℠ portal to see what routes and airlines are available to book using the Points Boost feature. I found several business-class fares offering the maximum Points Boost value of 2 cents per point. I ultimately transferred 142,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue after finding an amazing round-trip business-class fare directly on the Air France website, yielding a value of 5.83 cents per mile.

I landed in Tunis around 5 p.m. after a red-eye flight from New York and a relaxed connection in Paris.

A pre-arranged car transfer whisked me to the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis, a luxury beachfront resort in the suburb of Gammarth, about 30 minutes from the airport. Upon arrival, staff greeted me warmly and took me directly to my upgraded Deluxe Sea-View Room for an in-room check-in. The spacious room had a balcony overlooking the Mediterranean, a walk-in closet and a marble bathroom with a separate tub and a shower.

After a quick rinse, I wandered down to Blu, the hotel’s alfresco poolside restaurant, where I enjoyed a refreshing salad of a soft local cheese, tomatoes, onions and peppers served with a glass of Tunisian rosé. Since it was my first day in the country, the friendly staff made sure I tried some spicy Tunisian harissa, a smoky chili paste drizzled in olive oil that I sopped up with fluffy squares of focaccia.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Book the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis through The Edit to use one of the twice-annual, up-to-$250 credits toward prepaid hotel stays of two or more nights reserved through Chase Travel. By booking through The Edit, I also received other perks like complimentary hotel breakfast for two and up to $100 property credit, which I used for meals but could have used toward spa treatments like the ceremonial hammam experience, which comes out to approximately $100.

Since I only had one full day in Tunis, I headed out bright and early for a private tour of the capital’s major sites, booked through Chase Travel with Didon Tours. My guide, Baligh, and a private driver picked me up for a full 8-hour day that included lunch and fascinating storytelling about the city’s ancient and modern history and politics.

To beat the cruise groups and midday heat, we visited the ancient ruins of Carthage first, taking in the views from Byrsa Hill before heading down to the circular Punic port and the massive seaside complex of the Baths of Antoninus.

From there, we drove to the charming blue-and-white village of Sidi Bou Said, Tunisia’s newest UNESCO World Heritage site, for fresh juice and almond cakes at Cafe des Delices and iconic views of the beach below. While we didn’t have much time to browse the cliffside town’s shops, I did pick up some handmade souvenirs at the ceramic store at 16 Rue Habib Thameur.

For lunch, we stopped in the coastal suburb of Le Goulette at Restaurant La Victoire for a traditional Tunisian meal of brick à l’oeuf, a deep-fried pastry stuffed with egg, tuna and onion and a freshly grilled dorade fish served with rice and carrots.

Next, we turned inland toward the western side of the city to visit the Bardo Museum, set in a former palace and home to the world’s largest collection of Roman mosaics. (Don’t miss the mosaic of the Roman poet Virgil, flanked by the muses of history and tragedy, as it’s considered to be the Mona Lisa of Tunisia.)

Finally, we hit the medina of Tunis, where we visited the courtyard of the Zitouna Mosque and made a quick pass through the souk's meandering lanes before returning to the hotel for a much-deserved swim in the indoor pool and a nap before a quiet room-service dinner.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Earn 8 points per dollar spent on Chase Travel purchases, including activities and tours like the one I booked. Those with more time can add another day in Tunis and split this itinerary into two for a more relaxed pace in each location.

Around midday, I returned to the airport to pick up a rental car from Avis and set the GPS to drive two hours south to Kairouan, a UNESCO-recognized city famous for its picturesque medina and Great Mosque, which dates to the 9th century AD. While Kairouan is considered one of the holy cities of Islam, film buffs may recognize it from “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” where it stood in for 1930s Cairo. It lies along the northern boundary of the 2027 solar eclipse’s path of totality.

La Kasbah Hotel, booked via Chase Travel, provided a soft landing with its private parking lot, pool and strong air conditioning. The shops and sites in the medina tend to close in the late afternoon, so if you arrive after then, plan on a quiet night in the hotel, cooling off in the pool or lounging on woven rugs in its vintage café, drinking mint tea.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Pay for car rentals with Chase Sapphire Reserve to receive primary auto rental coverage (just be sure to decline the agency's collision insurance). Though I didn’t end up needing it, I had peace of mind knowing I was covered for up to $75,000 of theft or collision damage to the rental car.

Having arrived the previous afternoon after the mosque closed, I went first thing the next morning to admire the column-lined courtyard and three-tiered minaret before the tour groups arrived. The ticket to the mosque also included admission to the nearby Sidi Abid el Ghariani Mausoleum, built in the Moorish style with black and white marble arches. A few doors down, I stopped by the former home of the governor of Kairouan, an ornately decorated mansion that now serves as a rug shop. While I wasn’t in the market for a carpet, I enjoyed the architecture and left with a handwoven scarf for 40 dinars ($14).

After checking out, I hit the road again for the 4.5-hour drive south to Tozeur, a city in the heart of the Sahara Desert. Though I drove straight through, making brief stops at gas stations along the way, it’s also possible to break up the drive with stops at either the well-preserved archaeological site of Sbeitla or the Roman baths of Gafsa.

Just be mindful of timing: I wouldn’t recommend driving at night. Though the roads are well-maintained, speed bumps are common and harder to spot after dark.

Once in Tozeur, I checked into Dar Saida Beya, a traditional Tunisian guesthouse, booked through Chase Travel. After a long drive, I had a quiet evening to walk around and explore the nearby old town center.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Though the upscale Mora Sahara Tozeur resort west of town isn’t bookable via Chase Travel currently, it’s still possible to earn 4 points per dollar spent on direct hotel bookings made with the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The Atlas Mountains meet the salt flats and sands of the Sahara Desert in Tozeur, creating an otherworldly landscape that inspired many film directors. Most notably, the canyons and dunes around Tozeur served as the filming location for the desert planet of Tatooine in the “Star Wars” movies. The epic sci-fi series is celebrating the 50th anniversary of its release in 2027, and fans can experience the eclipse from here, since Tozeur falls along the southern boundary of the path of totality.

I booked a 7-hour tour with Attractive Discoveries via Chase Travel to see everything the area had to offer. Before diving into the area’s cinematic legacy, my driver and guide, Firas, began the day at Chebika Oasis, where a 45-minute hike wound through the ruins of a former Berber village and down to the oasis and its waterfall.

Our next stop was the Grand Canyon of Tunisia, Mides Canyon, roughly a mile from the Algerian border and featured in films like “The English Patient.” During the 30-minute hike along the dry riverbed, I spotted no fewer than six falcons diving in and out of the cliff face while hunting.

To avoid the worst heat of the day, the tour included a break from 1 to 5 p.m., during which we stopped to pick some dates from my guide’s family’s oasis of palm trees. I also tried a makloub sandwich filled with chicken, cheese and harissa and took a short nap.

At 5 p.m. on the dot, Firas picked me up again in his 4x4 to head out into the desert to watch the sunset over the dunes. Along our drive, we spotted a herd of camels, stopped to climb the Ong Jmal or “Camel’s Neck” rock formation and did some adrenaline-inducing 4x4 driving. We arrived at the remaining film sets that served as the desert trading post of Mos Espa in “The Phantom Menace” just before sunset.

To cap off the day, we drank fresh mint tea with almonds — a local treat — and watched the sun set behind the dunes before heading back into town.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Put the card's up to $300 annual credit to work on travel purchases like the tour I booked. The credit is applied automatically to eligible purchases each account anniversary year.

The biggest Star Wars fans may want to stay another day to visit other nearby filming locations, such as Sidi Bouhlel Canyon and the Lars family homestead exterior near the town of Nefta.

Since I had another 4.5-hour drive ahead of me that day, I left around 11 a.m. to drive back north to the city of El Jem via Chott el Djerid. Before heading off across the massive salt lake, I filled up my gas tank and packed snacks for the long drive since there aren’t many places to stop in the first couple of hours.

Built about 1,800 years ago, the Roman amphitheater of El Jem is roughly 70% the size of Rome’s amphitheater but has significantly fewer crowds and offers wide-open access to each level — even the underground level where animals were kept before they fought gladiators.

After checking into Hotel Julius, booked through Chase Travel, I dropped my bags and took the five-minute walk to the amphitheater before it closed. The 20 dinar ($7) ticket includes entrance to both the amphitheater and the nearby El Jem Archaeological Museum on the same day. Since I arrived a little later in the afternoon, I went to the museum first thing the next morning and justified the extra $7 by spending a leisurely morning taking in the incredibly detailed mosaics without being rushed.

El Jem falls within the path of totality for the 2027 solar eclipse, so history buffs may want to make this city their home base for the celestial event.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Tunisia is still a predominantly cash-based society, so it may be hard to find restaurants that accept cards. I couldn’t earn 3 points per dollar spent on dining worldwide with my Chase Sapphire Reserve in El Jem, but the two fricassee (fried dough buns stuffed with egg, tuna, potato and harissa) I ordered at a street food stall on the way back from the amphitheater only cost 7 cents total (yes, really), so I wasn’t worried about missing out on too many points.

After checking out the museum, I loaded up my rental car one last time for the two-hour drive back to Tunis. Those with more time and desire to sit on the beach than I did could easily add a day or two in the coastal town of Hammamet, which sits about two-thirds of the way back to Tunis from El Jem.

Once I handed off my rental car keys at the airport, I met the taxi driver I had prearranged with my final hotel, Dar Ben Gacem, a traditional guesthouse in the Tunis medina. Since my tour of Tunis at the beginning of the trip only included a brief visit to the medina, I was glad to have the rest of the afternoon and evening to poke around the shops and alleys of the historic city center and do some final souvenir shopping before flying home the next day.

Keep in mind that most stalls in the medina are open from around 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with more closed on Fridays and Sundays, so plan your visit accordingly. (Plus, many restaurants are closed for dinner on Sunday nights as well.)

Though some flights depart in the evening, I opted to take a connecting flight back to Paris in the morning and stay an extra night to avoid a rushed final day.

During my week-long road trip, I explored Tunisia’s ancient ruins, UNESCO-recognized Islamic architecture and otherworldly desert landscapes, many of which lie in the path of totality of the 2027 solar eclipse. Booking through Chase Travel maximized my Ultimate Rewards earnings, while the card benefits helped offset travel expenses along the way, like the $300 annual travel credit on tours, The Edit perks and $250 statement credit at the Four Seasons and primary rental car coverage through Avis. When I returned to New York, I was glad I had enrolled in Global Entry before my trip. The Sapphire Reserve's $120 Global Entry application fee statement credit helped offset the cost, and the program made reentering the U.S. much easier.

#6150. Starlux Adds First Route to Australia, New Zealand

Taiwanese carrier Starlux is branching out to Australia and New Zealand with a new, one-stop connection.

Starting March 23, 2027, the airline will fly from Taipei to Sydney to Auckland. Flights will initially operate four times weekly, then switch to daily on May 1. Starlux will operate the route using Airbus A330-900 aircraft.

Taipei-Sydney-Auckland will be the airline’s first one-stop or through route; all other flights are nonstop from Taiwan. Officials said the one-stop approach will give travelers access to “two incredible destinations in one journey.”

Starlux said it is working with Qantas to arrange connecting flights to other destinations in Australia, New Zealand, and Fiji.

Starlux is headquartered in Taipei and mainly flies within East and Southeast Asia, though it also offers service to North America and Europe. In the U.S., it serves Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix, and Ontario, California.
